# What is Backpack? 🤔

Backpack is an initiative to make developing serverless apps on AWS easier and more enjoyable. Its goal is to deliver a
smooth, consistent, modern development experience.

## When to use?

Backpack is currently intended for serverless projects at NS that are:

* using AWS as cloud platform;
* using [AWS CDK][aws-cdk] for infrastructure-as-code;
* running on AWS Lambda functions with Node.js as runtime.

## What Backpack offers:

* A [CLI] for bootstrapping new projects;
* [How-to guides] explaining how to use Backpack for building apps;
* A collection of [Typescript libraries] to support common use cases;
* [Demo projects] featuring practical examples;
* [In-depth guides] on our common practices to expand our collective knowledge base.

[Typescript libraries]: ../packages/index.md

[How-to guides]: ../how-tos/lambda.md

[CLI]: ../packages/@backpack/cli/index.md

[Demo projects]: ./demo-projects.md

[In-depth guides]: ../guides/index.md

## Community-driven

Backpack is a community-driven initiative. Instead of a single team dictating how you should build your app, we
encourage collaboration and shared approaches. "Best practices" should be shaped by consensus.

Missing something? Feel free to discuss it in [our Slack channel][slack] or contribute by opening\
[a pull request][contributing].

[aws-cdk]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/work-with-cdk-typescript.html

[slack]: https://ns-topaas.slack.com/archives/C097QFAUBUP

[contributing]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/CONTRIBUTING.md&_a=preview

# Backpack requirements 📋

Before you start using Backpack, make sure your environment and project setup meet the following prerequisites.

## System prerequisites

These system-level requirements and the tools and you need installed:

* You have installed [Node.js 24] or higher;
* You have configured [access to Nexus];
* You have set up [AWS CLI with SSO].

[Node.js 24]: https://nodejs.org/en/download

[access to Nexus]: ../guides/tooling/using-nexus.md

[AWS CLI with SSO]: ../guides/tooling/aws-cli-sso.md

## Project requirements

If you want to use Backpack in your existing project, these are the requirements:

* You are using [AWS CDK v2] to create your cloud infrastructure;
* Your project uses [ECMAScript modules (ESM)][ESM] as module system;
* You are using AWS Lambda with Node.js v24 or higher as runtime
* You are using [TypeScript 6.0](https://www.typescriptlang.org/) or higher;
* You are using [Vitest 4](https://vitest.dev/) as test framework.

Please refer to our [migration guide](../guides/migrating/existing-project-to-backpack.md) for more information.

[AWS CDK v2]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/work-with-cdk-typescript.html

[ESM]: ../guides/tooling/ecmascript-modules.md

[//]: # "peer-deps: update the versions on this page when we create a new release train"

# Demo projects 📁

Demo projects are fully functioning, end-to-end examples that can serve as inspiration for your work.

You can find them in the [Backpack repository](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/apps) under
[`/apps`](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/apps).

## `@backpack/bookstore-rest-api`

The [Bookstore REST API] demonstrates Backpack best practices for building a REST API.

[Bookstore REST API]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/apps/bookstore-rest-api

It includes the following:

* AWS Lambdas with API Gateway
* Endpoint handlers implemented using [`@backpack/aws-lambda`](../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md)
* Environment-specific app configs
* Error handling with [`@backpack/error-handling`](../packages/@backpack/error-handling/index.md)
* Dependency injection with Needle DI
* Local development using [`@backpack/hono`](../packages/@backpack/hono/index.md)
* OpenAPI specs with generated Zod schemas
* Unit tests and coverage with Vitest
* Acceptance tests with fixtures and test builders
* CI/CD: Azure DevOps pipeline with API Management
* Logging, metrics, and a dashboard with Datadog

### Infrastructure architecture

The infrastructure of the API is specified as Infrastructure as Code (IaC) using CDK. It uses Lambda functions, a
DynamoDB table, and an AWS API Gateway.

An overview of how all the AWS infrastructure components work together in the Bookstore Demo API can be found in the
following figure:
![Bookstore Demo REST API infrastructure architecture](/diagrams/architecture-bookstore-demo.drawio.png)

### Not in scope (yet)

The following features are not (yet) part of the Bookstore Demo API:

* Caching
* Authentication & Authorization
* Resiliency patterns

# Getting started 🚀

## Creating a new Backpack project

To use Backpack, make sure to [use Nexus](../guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) as npm registry.
Additionally, ensure that Node.js 24 is installed on your system. For more details, check out our
[requirements page](./requirements.md).

Once your environment is ready, you can generate a new project skeleton using
the [Backpack CLI](./../packages/@backpack/cli/index.md) with the following command:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli generate-project my-project
```

Replace "my-project" with the name of your project.

## Migrating an existing project to Backpack

For existing projects, we recommend to adopt Backpack gradually, in a step-by-step manner.

Please check out our dedicated [migration guide] to learn how you can do this.

[migration guide]: ../guides/migrating/existing-project-to-backpack.md

::: tip Using `@ns/common-serverless-library`?
We adopted most utilities of this existing library, and provide them in Backpack as well. Please look
at [this migration guide](../guides/migrating/common-serverless-library.md) to learn
more.
:::

## Demo projects

For inspiration, take a look at our [demo projects](./demo-projects.md) and explore the examples.

## How-to guides

To build your own serverless app with Backpack we offer some how-to guides. To get started, have a look
at [setting up a Lambda function](../how-tos/lambda.md).

# Upgrade guides

This section helps you upgrade an existing Backpack project to a newer version.

## When do I need an upgrade guide?

You should check the upgrade guides if:

* you are already using Backpack
* you want to upgrade to a newer minor or major version
* a release mentions **breaking changes** or **required actions**

If you are **new to Backpack**, or migrating from other libraries, see the [Migration guides](../migrating/index.md)
instead.

## How upgrade guides work

Each upgrade guide covers **one version step**.

For example:

* **v0.9 → v0.10** assumes your project is currently on **v0.9**
* **v0.8 → v0.9** assumes your project is currently on **v0.8**

If you are multiple versions behind, apply the guides **step by step**, in order.

## What you will find in an upgrade guide

Each guide typically contains:

* **Required actions**\
  Changes you must apply for your project to keep working.

* **Optional actions**\
  Improvements or new features you may want to adopt.

* **Links to detailed guides**\
  For example, registry migrations or tooling changes.

* **Context and rationale**\
  Why the change was introduced.

---

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/upgrading/v0.13.md'
---
# Upgrade guide: `0.12.x` to `0.13.x`

If you are upgrading from `0.12.x` to `0.13.x`, you will need to make the following changes.

## Required actions

### Upgrade your Backpack packages

Update all `@backpack/*` dependencies to `~0.13.0`.

For example, using `npm-check-updates`:

```bash
npx npm-check-updates '@backpack/*' -u
npm update
```

### Upgrade Vite-based tooling

Backpack `0.13.x` uses Vite 8.

If your project declares a direct `vite` dependency, update it to `^8.0.0`:

```bash
npm install -D vite@^8.0.0
```

### Add the Backpack Vite plugin if you use decorators

If your project uses ECMAScript decorators in code processed by Vite or Vitest, add `@backpack/vite` and configure
`backpackVitePlugin()`.

```bash
npm install -D @backpack/vite
```

::: code-group

```ts [vitest.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";
import { backpackVitePlugin } from "@backpack/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [backpackVitePlugin()],
  test: {
    // project-specific Vitest options
  },
});
```

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import { backpackVitePlugin } from "@backpack/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [backpackVitePlugin()],
});
```

:::

If your `vitest.config.ts` already imports and merges your `vite.config.ts`, adding the plugin to `vite.config.ts` is
enough.

This compatibility layer is needed because Vite 8 uses Rolldown/Oxc, and Oxc [does not yet support][issue] stage 3
decorators directly. The plugin is provided by [`@backpack/vite`](../../packages/@backpack/vite/index.md).

[issue]: https://github.com/vitejs/vite/discussions/21891

### Migrate deprecated local development setup when needed

`@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda` is **deprecated** in Backpack `0.13.x`.

Existing Lambda handlers can stay as they are. However, if your project still uses the old Express-based local
development setup, migrate that local setup to Hono when upgrading your local development tooling.

Use the [Hono migration guide](../migrating/hono.md) for the required steps.

## No required application changes

The following Backpack 0.13 changes do not require application code changes in a standard project:

* automatic Datadog instrumentation support for AWS SDK clients in `LambdaFunction`;
* `LambdaFunction` now defaults to the `ARM_64` Lambda architecture for lower runtime costs, which can be overridden in
  the construct when a project needs a different architecture;
* the new REST client OAuth bearer token middleware;
* generated example project snapshots;
* interface mocking support in `createMockedObject()`;
* SNS batch publishing utilities;
* DynamoDB projected reads and transactional writes;
* prettier Backpack config validation errors;
* Datadog Lambda/Fargate layer and agent updates.

---

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/upgrading/v0.12.md'
---
# Upgrade guide: `0.11.x` to `0.12.x`

If you are upgrading from `0.11.x` to `0.12.x`, you will need to make the following changes.

## Required actions

### Upgrade your Backpack packages

Update all `@backpack/*` dependencies to `~0.12.0`.

For example, using `npm-check-updates`:

```bash
npx npm-check-updates '@backpack/*' -u
npm update
```

### Updated peer dependencies

Backpack `0.12.x` now requires `aws-cdk-lib@2.253.0` or higher and `datadog-cdk-constructs-v2@4.0.0` or higher.

This update fixes an incompatibility between `aws-cdk-lib@2.253.0` and older versions of `datadog-cdk-constructs-v2`,
which could cause `cdk synth` or `cdk deploy` to fail when Datadog source code integration is enabled.

If your project uses AWS CDK, update `aws-cdk-lib` together with your Backpack packages:

```bash
npm install aws-cdk-lib@^2.253.0
```

If your project uses Datadog CDK constructs directly, also update `datadog-cdk-constructs-v2`:

```bash
npm install datadog-cdk-constructs-v2@^4.0.0
```

### Check your ESLint configuration

The `recommended` ESLint preset now includes type-aware rules from `typescript-eslint`.

For most projects, no configuration changes are required if you already use the default Backpack ESLint setup:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";
import backpack from "@backpack/eslint-config";

export default defineConfig(...backpack.configs.recommended);
```

However, type-aware linting may surface new issues that were not detected before. We recommend fixing these issues where
possible, as they usually point to unsafe values, floating promises, or incorrect type-driven usage patterns.

If your project is not ready for type-aware linting yet, you can temporarily switch to the `legacy` preset:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";
import backpack from "@backpack/eslint-config";

export default defineConfig(...backpack.configs.legacy);
```

The `legacy` preset keeps the previous non-type-aware behavior available while allowing the `recommended` preset to move
forward with stronger defaults.

## Optional actions

The following steps are optional but recommended if they apply to your project.

### Adopt the new test builder utility

If your project creates a lot of nested test data, consider using the new test builder utility from `@backpack/testing`.

Check out the [`@backpack/testing` API reference](../../packages/@backpack/testing/index.md) to learn more.

### Adopt the new HTTP caching utilities

If your project returns HTTP responses from `@backpack/aws-lambda`, you can now use the new caching options on
`jsonResult()` and `jsonOk()`.

Check out the [dedicated caching guide](../../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md#http-caching) for more details.

### Update APIM deploy brick usage

As of `v8.15.0` of the CI/CD pipeline templates, the APIM deploy brick supports multiple products through the new
`productIds` parameter.

If your pipeline uses API Management, migrate to `productIds`:

```diff
- productId: "backpack-public"
+ productIds:
+   - "backpack-public"
```

The existing `productId` parameter has been deprecated.

# Upgrade guide: `0.10.x` to `0.11.x`

If you are upgrading from `0.10.x` to `0.11.x`, you will need to make the following changes.

## Required actions

### Upgrade your Backpack packages

Update all `@backpack/*` dependencies to `~0.11.0`.

For example, using `npm-check-updates`:

```bash
npx npm-check-updates '@backpack/*' -u
npm update
```

### Upgrade to TypeScript 6

* Update `typescript` to `~6.0.0`

If you are using `@backpack/typescript-config`, no additional changes are required.

### Upgrade to ESLint 10

* Update `eslint` to `^10.0.0`
* Update `typescript-eslint` to `^8.58.0`

We migrated from `eslint-plugin-import` to `eslint-plugin-import-x`.

In most cases, you only need to replace rule names:

```diff
- import/no-extraneous-dependencies
+ import-x/no-extraneous-dependencies
```

Make sure to update any custom ESLint rules or overrides accordingly.

## Optional actions

### Remove Gitleaks CI/CD brick from your pipeline

The Gitleaks CI/CD brick [has been deprecated][deprecation] in favor of SonarQube.

If you are using the standard Backpack pipeline, you can remove it from:

```
.azure-devops/pipelines/ci/build.yml
```

[deprecation]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/TECHWIKI/pages/2088239148/Secret+Detection+in+SonarQube

### Mockserver changes

To stabilize the Backpack mockserver, we made some changes that may require you to adjust a few things.

* Replace all `mockserver.mock...()` calls with their `mockserver.when...()` counterparts.
* Make sure to import any Vitest-related utilities from `@backpack/mockserver-client/vitest`.

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/upgrading/v0.10.md'

# Upgrade guide: `0.9.x` to `0.10.x`

If you are upgrading from `0.9.x` to `0.10.x`, you will need to make the following changes.

## Required actions

### Migrate to our new Nexus registry ⚠️

Before you can upgrade, you need to migrate to our new Nexus registry.

* Change your `.npmrc` file;
* Adjust your service connections in Azure DevOps accordingly;
* Adjust your `npm audit` scripts.

Check out our dedicated migration guide for [migrating to the new Nexus registry](../migrating/nexus-registry.md).

### Upgrade to Node.js 24

Backpack `0.10.x` requires Node.js 24 to align with the latest AWS Lambda runtime and modern ECMAScript features.

* Install [Node.js 24] or use [nvm] to switch to v24.
* Upgrade your `aws-cdk-lib` to `v2.224.0` or higher.
* Upgrade your `datadog-cdk-constructs-v2` to `v3.7.0` or higher.
* If you are not using `@backpack/cdk-constructs`, change the runtime of your Lambda functions to `nodejs24.x`.
* If you are not using `@backpack/typescript-config`, make the following changes to your `tsconfig.json`:
  * Change `target` to `es2024`
  * Change `lib` to `es2024`
  * Optionally add the following libs: `ESNext.Array`, `ESNext.Collection`, `ESNext.Error`, `ESNext.Iterator`,
    `ESNext.Promise`
* In your CI/CD pipelines, change `NODE_VERSION` to a Node.js 24 version (for example `24.13.0`).

[Node.js 24]: https://nodejs.org/en/download

[nvm]: https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm

### Upgrade your Backpack packages

Update all `@backpack/*` dependencies to `~0.10.0`.

For example, using `npm-check-updates`:

```bash
npx npm-check-updates '@backpack/*' -u
npm install
```

## Optional actions

The following steps are optional but recommended if they apply to your project.

### Adopt `@backpack/i18n`

If your project is doing something with translations, you can use our
new [@backpack/i18n](../../packages/@backpack/i18n/index.md) package.

### Adopt `@backpack/mockserver-client`

If your project is doing something with HTTP mocking, check out the
new [@backpack/mockserver-client](../../packages/@backpack/mockserver-client/index.md) package.

---

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/upgrading/v0.9.md'

# Upgrade guide: `0.8.x` to `0.9.x`

If you are upgrading from `0.8.x` to `0.9.x`, you will need to make the following changes.

## Required actions

### Upgrade your Backpack packages

Update all `@backpack/*` dependencies to `~0.9.0`.

For example, using `npm-check-updates`:

```bash
npx npm-check-updates '@backpack/*' -u
npm install
```

## Optional actions

The following steps are optional but recommended if they apply to your project.

### Update your linting & formatting workflow

We published a dedicated guide on [linting/formatting]. To get the best experience:

* Make sure your IDE automatically applies lint fixes and formatting on save.
* Consider adopting `husky` and `lint-staged` to run linting and formatting as a pre-commit hook.
* Align your npm scripts with the [latest naming conventions], and apply them consistently in CI/CD pipelines.

[linting/formatting]: ../../guides/tooling/linting-and-formatting.md

[latest naming conventions]: ../../guides/tooling/linting-and-formatting.md#using-npm-scripts

### Use `FileApiDefinition` from `@backpack/cdk-constructs`

For API Gateway, you can now import your OpenAPI file directly:

```ts
import { FileApiDefinition } from "@backpack/cdk-constructs";

new ApiGateway(this, "BookstoreApiGateway", {
  restApiName: "Bookstore API",
  // ...
  apiDefinition: new FileApiDefinition("./path/to/openapi.yaml"), // (or JSON)
});
```

### Align your `renovate.json`

We tweaked our default `renovate.json` a bit. Check out the [latest version](../cicd/renovate.md) to see what changed.

# Upgrade guide: `0.7.x` to `0.8.x`

If you are upgrading from `0.7.x` to `0.8.x`, you will need to make the following changes.

## Required actions

### Upgrade your Backpack packages

Update all `@backpack/*` dependencies to `~0.8.0`.

In addition, upgrade to `vitest@^4.0.0` (required peer dependency).

For example:

```bash
npx npm-check-updates '@backpack/*' -u
npm install vitest@^4
npm install
```

Make sure to double-check additional Vitest-related dependencies (such as reporters or plugins).

For more information, see [Vitest v4](https://vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4).

## Optional actions

### Use the APIM CI/CD brick

If applicable, consider using the new CI/CD brick for API Management! Check how to use API Management in
Backpack [here](../../how-tos/rest-apis/api-management.md#cicd-integration).

# Upgrade guide: `0.6.x` to `0.7.x`

If you are upgrading from `0.6.x` to `0.7.x`, you will need to make the following changes.

## Required actions

### Upgrade your Backpack packages

Update all `@backpack/*` dependencies to `~0.7.0`.

In addition, upgrade to `zod@^4.0.0` (required peer dependency).

For example:

```bash
npx npm-check-updates '@backpack/*' -u

npm install
```

For more information, see [Zod v4](https://zod.dev/v4).

If you rely on `@backpack/rest-client` and you use additional middleware or custom error handlers, this upgrade may
require changes.

See the [Wretch 3 migration guide](https://github.com/elbywan/wretch/blob/master/MIGRATION_V2_V3.md).

# Compatibility matrix

This page describes which versions of Node.js, infrastructure tooling, and developer tooling are officially supported by
Backpack.

## How to read this matrix

* **Required** versions must be used to run Backpack-supported projects
* **Supported** versions are tested and expected to work
* Versions outside this matrix may work but are not guaranteed

Backpack supports **only the latest Backpack version**, but this matrix is useful when upgrading existing projects.

## Platform compatibility

This table shows the required platform-level dependencies per Backpack version range.

| Backpack version | Node.js | AWS Lambda runtime | aws-cdk-lib | datadog-cdk-constructs-v2 |
|------------------|---------|--------------------|-------------|---------------------------|
| 0.13.x, 0.12.x   | 24      | nodejs24.x         | >= 2.253.0  | >= 4.0.0                  |
| 0.11.x, 0.10.x   | 24      | nodejs24.x         | >= 2.224.0  | >= 3.4.0                  |
| 0.3–0.9.x        | 22      | nodejs22.x         | >= 2.168.0  | >= 1.121.0                |

### Notes

* Node.js major upgrades are the primary driver for Backpack major releases
* Dropping support for a Node.js or CDK major version is always considered a breaking change
* AWS Lambda runtime versions follow AWS availability and may lag Node.js releases

## Tooling compatibility

This table shows the recommended and supported tooling versions for Backpack projects.

| Backpack versions    | TypeScript | ESLint | Vitest | Vite |
|----------------------|------------|--------|--------|------|
| 0.13.x               | 6.0.x      | 10.x   | 4.x    | 8.x  |
| 0.12.x, 0.11.x       | 6.0.x      | 10.x   | 4.x    | 7.x  |
| 0.10.x, 0.9.x, 0.8.x | 5.9.x      | 9.x    | 4.x    | 7.x  |
| 0.7.x                | 5.9.x      | 9.x    | 3.x    | 7.x  |
| 0.6.x                | 5.9.x      | 9.x    | 3.x    | 7.x  |
| 0.5.x, 0.4.x         | 5.8.x      | 9.x    | 3.x    | 6.x  |
| 0.3.x                | 5.7.x      | 9.x    | 2.x    | 6.x  |

### Notes

* These versions are tested and used in Backpack templates and examples
* Minor or patch upgrades within these ranges are typically safe
* Major upgrades may require changes and are reflected in Backpack minor or major releases

# Migration guides

This section helps you migrate an existing project or setup to Backpack.

## When do I need a migration guide?

You should check the migration guides if:

* you are not using Backpack yet
* you are migrating from legacy or alternative libraries
* you need to change a core part of your project setup

If you are already using Backpack and only want to move between versions,
see the [Upgrade guides](../upgrading/index.md) instead.

## How migration guides work

Migration guides are **context-specific**, not version-specific. Unlike upgrade guides, migration guides usually **do
not need to be followed in sequence**.

## Overview

* New to Backpack?\
  Start with [Existing project to Backpack](./existing-project-to-backpack.md).

* Still using the old Nexus registry?\
  Migrate to our new registry using [the Nexus migration guide](./nexus-registry.md).

* Using `@ns/cdk-helper`?\
  Check out [Migrating from @ns/cdk-helper](./cdk-helper.md).

* Using `@ns/common-serverless-library`?\
  Check out [Migrating from @ns/common-serverless-library](./common-serverless-library.md).

---

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/migrating/existing-project-to-backpack.md'
---

# Migrating an existing project to Backpack

This migration guide explains how to migrate your existing project to Backpack.

## Basics

Let's begin with some basics that require minimal changes to your code.

### Upgrade to Node.js v24

Backpack expects Node.js v24 for both local development and your Lambda runtime.

* Install Node.js v24 on your machine (using [Homebrew], [n], or [nvm]).
* In your project, ensure `aws-cdk-lib` is upgraded to `v2.224.0` or higher.
* Update the `runtime` of your Lambda CDK construct to `NODEJS_24_X`.
* Use `"es2024"` for the `lib` option in your `tsconfig.json`.

[Homebrew]: https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/node

[n]: https://github.com/tj/n

[nvm]: https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm

### Start using ES modules

It is recommended to switch to ECMAScript modules (ESM).

* Add `"type": "module"` to your `package.json`.
* Configure your Lambda bundling options to output ES modules with `format: OutputFormat.ESM`.
* Update your code to be ESM-compliant (e.g. instead of use Node.js global `__dir`, use `import.meta.dirname`)

For more details, see our [guide on ES modules](../tooling/ecmascript-modules.md).

### Migrate to Vitest

If you are still using [Jest] for testing, you may run into some issues with ES modules. This is because its support
for ECMAScript modules is still [experimental] and requires a specific setup.

We recommend replacing Jest with [Vitest], a modern testing tool with built-in support for TypeScript and ESM. It
requires minimal configuration, has fewer dependencies, and runs faster.

Migrating from Jest to Vitest is simple, as Vitest closely resembles Jest’s API.

[Jest]: https://jestjs.io/

[experimental]: https://jestjs.io/docs/ecmascript-modules

[Vitest]: https://vitest.dev/

### Adopt TypeScript practices

You can simplify your `tsconfig.json` setup by using one of the presets provided by [`@backpack/typescript-config`].

```jsonc
{
  "extends": "@backpack/typescript-config/bundler",
  "include": ["**/*.ts"],
  "compilerOptions": {
    // Overrides if needed
  }
}
```

This approach ensures reasonable defaults, while still allowing you to override settings as necessary.

[`@backpack/typescript-config`]: ../../packages/@backpack/typescript-config/index.md

### Use ESLint with Prettier

This step is optional, especially if you're satisfied with your current ESLint setup. However, if you already use many
of the "recommended" presets and aim to reduce dependency clutter, consider adopting [`@backpack/eslint-config`]:

```javascript
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";
import backpack from "@backpack/eslint-config";

export default defineConfig(
  ...backpack.configs.recommended,
  {
    rules: {
      // Additional rule overrides here...
    },
  }
);
```

This config includes reasonable [default presets][`@backpack/eslint-config`], but you can still customise or extend it.

Additionally, we recommend [Prettier] for consistent code formatting. You might also consider adding a pre-commit hook
to enforce this.

[`@backpack/eslint-config`]: ../../packages/@backpack/eslint-config/index.md

[Prettier]: https://prettier.io/

::: tip\
**Looking for examples?**\
Here are some pull requests showcasing the migration process:

* [PR 327010 - Adopting
  `@backpack/typescript-config`](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/NSAPP/_git/ns-push-api-v2/pullrequest/327010)
* [PR 327112 - Adopting
  `@backpack/eslint-config`](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/NSAPP/_git/ns-push-api-v2/pullrequest/327112)\
  :::

### Adopting the CI/CD pipeline (optional)

Backpack provides a default CI/CD pipeline for Azure DevOps, which you can easily adopt if you want to. If you are
unsure about switching, keep in mind that you can run it in parallel to your existing pipeline to try it out without
any disruption.

Use the [`generate-pipeline`][generate-pipeline] command of the Backpack CLI to generate the brick-based CI/CD pipeline.

[generate-pipeline]: ../../packages/@backpack/cli/index.md#generating-a-ci-cd-pipeline

## Migrate your code

Once the basics are in place, you can begin adopting Backpack libraries and best practices.

### Improve your app configuration

If you are relying on global environment variables, consider reorganising your app to use a single (externalised) source
for configuration. This approach streamlines environment management, makes setting up integration tests easier, and
simplifies local development.

Check out [`@backpack/config`](../../packages/@backpack/config/index.md) to learn more!

### Use dependency injection

Improving your codebase by applying inversion of control patterns or using a dependency injection library is another
step to consider. Although not mandatory, these practices improve maintainability and reduce boilerplate code.

For more information, see our guide on [dependency injection].

[dependency injection]: ../development/dependency-injection.md

### AWS Lambda utilities

Backpack offers the `@backpack/aws-lambda` library, which contains utilities to enhance your Lambda functions,
especially for REST APIs.

Refer to the API documentation of [`@backpack/aws-lambda`].

[`@backpack/aws-lambda`]: ../../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md

### Other AWS utilities

Backpack also provides libraries for working with AWS services like Secrets Manager, DynamoDB, and S3. You can explore
all our [AWS packages].

If you are currently using utilities from `@ns/common-serverless-library`, consider migrating to their Backpack
counterparts.

Refer to the dedicated [migration guide] for details.

[AWS packages]: ../../packages/index.md

[migration guide]: ./common-serverless-library.md

# Nexus registry migration guide

This document explains the migration of Backpack to the new Nexus npm group, why this change was made,
and what developers need to update.

## Summary

Starting from v0.10.0, Backpack has migrated from its original NSAPP-specific Nexus registry to
a dedicated registry location for Backpack. All our packages are now available using the following group:

`https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup`

* All previous Backpack versions remain available via this group;
* **Newer versions (≥ v0.10.0) are published exclusively via this group**;
* Migration is therefore **required** to keep receiving updates.

## What changed and why

### Background

Backpack originally emerged within the **NSAPP community**. Because of that, packages were published to a Nexus registry
closely tied to the NSAPP environment.

This setup worked well initially, but over time Backpack grew beyond that original scope:

* more teams started using it
* use cases expanded beyond NSAPP
* visibility and accessibility became more important

### What changed

* Backpack packages are now published to a **dedicated Nexus npm group**
* This group acts as a **single, generic npm entry point**
* Every TOPAAS user has default read access to this group

### Why a Nexus group

Using a Nexus group gives us much more flexibility:

* It can serve:
  * public packages (via npmjs.org proxy)
  * private NS-specific packages (including Backpack)
* We can **add or change underlying registries** without requiring users to:
  * reconfigure npm scopes
  * update local `.npmrc` files
  * create additional CI/CD service connections in Azure DevOps

In short: fewer moving parts for users, more freedom for maintainers.

## How to use the new registry

The new Nexus group can be used in **two ways**. We recommend the first option, but both are fully supported.

### Option 1: use as primary npm registry (recommended)

Configure the Backpack Nexus group as your **primary npm registry**.

This is the recommended approach because:

* there is a single registry for **all** dependencies
* both public and private packages are resolved consistently
* CI/CD pipelines are simpler and more predictable
* tools like `npx` and `postinstall` scripts work without additional configuration

### Option 2: use only for Backpack packages

If you prefer, you can scope the registry to Backpack packages only. This allows you to keep another registry
(for example npmjs.org) as your primary registry.

Both approaches are supported; the primary-registry approach is recommended to minimize configuration and edge cases.

## What developers need to update

### 1. Local npm configuration

Your personal npm configuration must be updated to point to the new Nexus group.

#### `~/.npmrc` (primary registry, recommended)

```text
registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
//nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/:_auth=YOUR_TOKEN_HERE
```

Make sure to remove the old registry:

```text
@backpack:registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_NSAPP_NPM/
```

Your token is the base64 representation of `username:password`, available from your Nexus profile.

#### `~/.npmrc` (scoped registry)

If you prefer the scoped approach, you only need to update the scoped registry entry:

```text
@backpack:registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
//nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/:_auth=YOUR_TOKEN_HERE
```

### 2. Project configuration

Projects should define the registry in a repository-level `.npmrc`:

```text
registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
```

This ensures consistent dependency resolution for both Backpack and transitive dependencies.

Make sure to also delete your `package-lock.json` file, since it may contain outdated references to the old registry.
Then, run `npm install` to generate a new lock file.

If you have a `renovate.json` file, also update your "npmrc" entry:

```json5
{
  // ...
  "npmrc": "https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/:_auth={{ secrets.NEXUS_TOKEN }}",
  "npmrcMerge": true,
  // ...
}
```

### 3. CI/CD (Azure DevOps)

Pipelines should both authenticate against Nexus **and** pass the service connection to the `npm ci` step.

This ensures authentication is applied consistently for:

* `npm ci`
* `npx` calls
* nested npm calls, such as `postinstall` scripts

```yaml
- task: npmAuthenticate@0
  displayName: "Nexus authentication"
  inputs:
    workingFile: ".npmrc"
    customEndpoint: "your-backpack-nexus-service-connection"

- task: Npm@1
  displayName: "npm ci"
  inputs:
    command: ci
    customEndpoint: "your-backpack-nexus-service-connection"
```

***

If you are also doing an `npm audit` in your pipeline, you will need to make a small adjustment and add
`--registry=https://registry.npmjs.org`. For example:

```yaml
- task: Npm@1
  displayName: "npm audit"
  inputs:
    command: custom
    customCommand: "audit --omit=dev --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org"
```

This is because Nexus requires Sonatype Repository Firewall, a paid product that NS currently has no license for.

***

Happy hacking! 🚀

---

# Migrating from `@ns/cdk-helper`

If you are using `@ns/cdk-helper`, you may want to migrate your project to use `@backpack/config` instead.
If you are also using the `DatadogEcsMonitoring` construct from `@ns/cdk-helper`, see the dedicated [DatadogFargate migration guide](/guides/migrating/datadog-fargate) for how to migrate to the new `DatadogFargate` construct.

## Do I need to migrate?

Not necessarily — `@ns/cdk-helper` and Backpack can be used side by side. However, we've decided to adopt
most of its functionality to ensure compatibility and to stay aligned with current best practices.

`@backpack/config` brings more type-safety to your CDK config, especially when you are using additional properties. It
also provides improved runtime safety using schema validation, making sure you have the right values in your YAML files.

For more information on `@backpack/config`, check out its [API reference](../../packages/@backpack/config/index.md).

## How to migrate

### 1. Create a Zod schema

Add a [Zod] schema representing your current configuration model:

::: code-group

```ts [cdk/config/BuildConfig.ts]
import { z } from "zod";

export type BuildConfig = z.infer<typeof BuildConfig>;
export const BuildConfig = z.object({
  App: z.string(),
  AwsAccount: z.string(),
  AwsRegion: z.string(),
  Environment: z.enum(["dev", "stg", "prd"]),
  Tags: z.record(z.string(), z.string()),
});
```

:::

::: tip
This example uses the same naming convention as `@ns/cdk-helper`. Feel free to use a different naming convention
(e.g. "camelCase" over "PascalCase") for your property keys.

The `@backpack/config` library provides lenient matching, accepting different casing in your config files.
If you do so, remember to update all references in your code.
:::

### 2. Replace config loading

Change your existing code:

::: code-group

```ts [bin/cdk.ts]
import { App } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { Config } from "@ns/cdk-helper";

const cdk = new App();

const buildConfig = Config(cdk);

// ...
```

:::

Replace this with the `loadConfig()` function from `@backpack/config`. You can use the `cdkLoader()` to load
both YAML files and [CDK context] variables.

::: code-group

```ts [bin/cdk.ts]
import { App } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { loadConfig, cdkLoader } from "@backpack/config";

import { BuildConfig } from "../config";

const cdk = new App();

const buildConfig = await loadConfig({
  schema: BuildConfig,
  loaders: [
    cdkLoader(cdk, { configDirectory: "./cdk/config" }),
  ]
});

// ...
```

:::

### 3. Apply `envSuffix` (optional)

If you are using the `envSuffix` from `@ns/cdk-helper` somewhere in your project, make sure to explicitly apply it
where you need it.

First, add it to your config schema. This will automatically pick up `-c envSuffix=foo` as CDK command-line argument.

You can use Zod transforms to make sure it converts to a certain case, such as kebab-case:

::: code-group

```ts [cdk/config/BuildConfig.ts]
import { z } from "zod";

export type BuildConfig = z.infer<typeof BuildConfig>;
export const BuildConfig = z.object({
  // ...
  envSuffix: z.string().slugify().optional(),
});
```

:::

Everywhere you are relying on the `App` property, and you want to apply the suffix, make sure to do so explicitly.

For example:

```ts
// add the suffix if needed:
const stackPrefix = buildConfig.envSuffix
  ? `${buildConfig.App}-${buildConfig.envSuffix}`
  : `${buildConfig.App}`;

// apply it:
const appStack = new AppStack(cdk, `${stackPrefix}-app-stack`, {
  env: {
    region: buildConfig.AWSRegion,
    account: buildConfig.AWSAccount,
  },
  buildConfig: buildConfig,
  tags: buildConfig.Tags,
  // ...
});
```

### 4: Double-check tags

In contrast to `@ns/cdk-helper`, the `@backpack/config` library contains no CDK-specific logic such as validating
[CDK tags]. If you still want to validate your tags, you can leverage Zod validation for this, by adjusting your schema:

```ts
export const BuildConfig = z.object({
  // ...
  Tags: z.object({
    App: z.string(),
    Team: z.string(),
    // ...
  })
});
```

More information on resource tagging can be found in
our [Tagging guide](../../guides/infrastructure/resource-tagging.md).

[Zod]: https://zod.dev/

[CDK context]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/context.html

[CDK tags]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/tagging.html

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/migrating/common-serverless-library.md'

# Migrating from `common-serverless-library`

If you are currently using `@ns/common-serverless-library`, you may want to migrate your code to use Backpack instead.

#### Table of contents

\[\[toc]]

## Do I need to migrate?

Not necessarily — `@ns/common-serverless-library` and Backpack can be used side by side. However, we've decided to adopt
most of its utilities to ensure compatibility and to stay aligned with current best practices.

Here are some key differences in our approach:

* Utilities are now published in separate packages, allowing for more granular dependency management.
* Most utility classes support constructor injection, facilitating inversion of control and seamless integration with
  dependency injection (DI) frameworks.
* For decorators, we prefer [Stage 3 ECMAScript decorators][decorator comparison] over legacy TypeScript decorators.

[decorator comparison]: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-5-0-beta/#differences-with-experimental-legacy-decorators

## AWS Secrets Manager

### Updating imports

Utilities for AWS Secrets Manager have been moved to [
`@backpack/aws-secrets-manager`](../../packages/@backpack/aws-secrets-manager/index.md), so make sure
to install the package and update your imports.

```ts
import {
  SecretsManagerService,
  CachedSecretsManagerService
} from '@backpack/aws-secrets-manager';
```

### Changes to `SecretsManagerService`

* added constructor injection, make sure to provide a `SecretsManagerClient`;
* `getSecretValue()` is deprecated in favour of `getJsonSecret(secretId, { required: false })` (will be removed in a
  future version)
* `getRequiredSecretValue()` is deprecated in favour of `getJsonSecret()` (will be removed in a future version)
* `batchGetSecretValue()` has been removed (barely used in existing projects).

### Changes to `CachedSecretManagerService`

* renamed from `CachedSecretManagerService` to `CachedSecretsManagerService`
* added constructor injection, make sure to provide a `SecretsManagerClient`;
* `cacheExpirySeconds` moved to options object as `cacheExpiryDurationSeconds`
* it now extends `SecretsManagerService`, make sure to check those changes as well.

## Amazon DynamoDB

### Updating imports

Utilities for DynamoDB have been moved to [`@backpack/amazon-dynamodb`][backpack-amazon-dynamodb], so make sure to
install the package and update your imports.

[backpack-amazon-dynamodb]: ../../packages/@backpack/amazon-dynamodb/index.md

```ts
import { DynamoDbRepository } from '@backpack/amazon-dynamodb';
```

### Changes to `DynamoRepository`

* has been renamed to `DynamoDbRepository`;
* constructor injection was added, make sure to provide your own `DynamoDBDocumentClient`;
* the `tableName` method parameter has moved to an options object which can be passed in the constructor;
* two generic types `TItem` and `TKey` were added, reflecting the types of the item and its (composite) key;
* logging has been made optional, to enable it you only need to pass your logger instance to the constructor options;
* `error` logging has changed to `debug` level, since errors are still propagated;
* since `tableName` was moved to the constructor, the existing methods have been deprecated, allowing us to improve
  naming a bit:
  * `putItem(key, tableName)` was deprecated in favour of `putItem(key, options)`
  * `getItem(key, tableName)` was deprecated in favour of `findItemById(key)`
  * `removeItem(key, tableName)` was deprecated in favour of `deleteItemById(key)`
  * `itemExists(key, tableName)` was deprecated in favour of `itemExistsById(key)`
  * `getAllItems(tableName)` was deprecated in favour of `scanAllItems(options)`
* it is now possible to add your mapping functions `writeItem()` and `readItem()`, allowing mapping and/or validation
  with Zod.
* `saveItem(options)` was added to perform a `Save` command.

### Changes to `DynamoQueryRepository`

* this class has merged with `DynamoDbRepository`, please review those changes;
* the existing mapping function has been moved to the option `itemMapper.readItem()` and is a bit stricter, now
  accepting
  a `Record<string, unknown>` instead of `Record<string, any>`;
* `queryTable()` was deprecated in favour of `queryItems(options)`, which now has an options object accepting all
  `QueryCommandInput` parameters.

## Amazon SNS

### Updating imports

Utilities for SNS have been moved to [`@backpack/amazon-sns`](../../packages/@backpack/amazon-sns/index.md), so make
sure to install the package and update your imports.

```ts
import { SnsPublisher } from '@backpack/amazon-sns';
```

### Changes to `SnsPublisher`

* constructor injection was added, make sure to pass your own `SNSClient`;
* the `topicArn` method parameter has been deprecated and moved to the constructor;
* logging has been made optional, to enable it you only need to pass your logger instance to the constructor;
* `info` and `error` logging has been changed to `debug` level;
* any errors are now propagated, make sure to catch your errors properly if you need to retain resilience.
* since `topicArn` has moved to the constructor, `publish(message, topicArn)` is now deprecated in favour of
  `publishRaw(message)` and `publishJson(message)`

## Amazon SQS

### Updating imports

Utilities for SQS have been moved to [`@backpack/amazon-sqs`](../../packages/@backpack/amazon-sqs/index.md), so make
sure to install the package and update your imports.

```ts
import { SqsPublisher } from '@backpack/amazon-sqs';
```

### Changes to `SqsPublisher`

* constructor injection was added, make sure to pass your own `SQSClient`;
* the `queueUrl` method parameter has been deprecated and moved to the constructor;
* logging has been made optional, to enable it you only need to pass your logger instance to the constructor;
* `info` and `error` logging has been changed to `debug` level;
* any errors are now propagated, make sure to catch your errors properly if you need to retain resilience.
* since `queueUrl` has moved to the constructor, `publish(message, queueUrl)` is now deprecated in favour of
  `sendRaw(message)` and `sendJson(message)`

## Amazon S3

### Updating imports

Utilities for S3 have been moved to [`@backpack/amazon-s3`](../../packages/@backpack/amazon-s3/index.md), so make sure
to install the package and update your imports.

```ts
import { S3Service } from '@backpack/amazon-s3';
```

### Changes to `S3Service`

* constructor injection was added, make sure to pass your own `S3Client`;
* the `bucketName` method parameter has been deprecated and moved to the constructor;
  * NOTE: for `putObject()`, instead of deprecating, we removed the old method signature entirely;
* logging has been made optional, to enable it you only need to pass your logger instance to the constructor;
* `info` and `error` logging has been changed to `debug` level;
* `deleteVersionedObject()` has not been migrated (yet) due to unclear use case;
* `getObject()` now accepts a `type` option to convert the stream to a `buffer`, `text`, `arrayBuffer`, `blob` or
  `json`;
* `getObjectStream()` has been deprecated in favour of `getObject(key, { type: "stream" )`
* The `NoSuchKey` error is still caught for `deleteObject()`, however, this error is not translated to the custom
  `NotFoundException` anymore.

## `Exception` classes and error handling

For error handling, `@ns/common-serverless-library` provides an `Exception` class (including some subclasses) that
represent HTTP errors.

Since Backpack advocates the [RFC 9457 Problem Detail] web standard, it provides the `ProblemError` class instead. You
can use generic subclasses like `NotFoundProblem` to throw a similar generic error, representing a HTTP 404:

```ts
import { NotFoundProblem } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

if (myBook === undefined) {
  throw new NotFoundProblem("Could not find book 123")
}
```

Alternatively, you can define your own error classes by extending `ProblemError`:

```ts
import { ProblemError, HttpStatus } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

class BookNotFoundProblem extends ProblemError {
  constructor(bookId: string) {
    super({
      title: "Book not found",
      detail: `Could not find book ${bookId}`,
      type: "/problems/book-not-found",
      status: HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND,
    });
  }
}

// ...

if (myBook === undefined) {
  throw new BookNotFoundProblem("123")
}
```

To handle these errors properly, you can use the default `defaultErrorHandler` from `@backpack/aws-lambda`, in
combination with the utilities from `@backpack/error-handling`:

```ts
import { defaultErrorHandler } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import { catchErrors } from "@backpack/error-handling/promises";

class MyLambda {
  @catchErrors(defaultErrorHandler())
  public async handle(): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult> {
    // ...
  }
}
```

Note that if you need to retain the original response body structure, you can still do so by implementing a
[custom error converter].

[RFC 9457 Problem Detail]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html

[custom error converter]: ../../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md#error-handling

---

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/migrating/datadog-fargate.md'
---

# Migrating from the CDK helper `DatadogEcsMonitoring` construct

If you are currently using the `DatadogEcsMonitoring` construct from `@ns/cdk-helper`, this guide helps you migrate to the new `DatadogFargate` construct from `@backpack/cdk-constructs`.

For more information on the new construct, check out the [API reference](../../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/classes/DatadogFargate.md).

## Do I need to migrate?

Not necessarily — the CDK helper and Backpack can be used side by side.
However, the CDK helper is not actively maintained and does not include some of the latest best practices for ECS monitoring.
If you want to benefit from ongoing improvements and a more streamlined integration, we recommend migrating to `DatadogFargate`.

Here are some key differences in approach:

* Backpack will own the versions of the Datadog agent and Fluent Bit images, ensuring you get the latest features and security updates when upgrading the construct.
* The new construct is no longer tied to `buildConfig`, giving you more flexibility in how you define service identity and tags.
* The new construct uses the official `DatadogECSFargate` construct underwater instead of manually configuring the agent and log router.
* The new construct no longer logs application logs to CloudWatch by default, but you can enable this by passing along a `cloudwatchLogGroup` if desired.

## Side by side comparison

### Before

```ts
import { DatadogEcsMonitoring } from "../constructs/datadog-ecs-monitoring";

const taskDefinition = new FargateTaskDefinition(this, "TaskDef", {
  cpu: 512,
  memoryLimitMiB: 1024,
});

taskDefinition.addContainer("app", {
  image: ecs.ContainerImage.fromRegistry("my-app:latest"),
  logging: new ecs.FireLensLogDriver({ /* manual config */ }),
});

new DatadogEcsMonitoring(this, "Datadog", {
  buildConfig: buildConfig,
  ecsTaskDefinition: taskDefinition,
  ecsClusterArn: cluster.clusterArn,
  version: "1.0.0",
  isJsonLogs: true,
});

const service = new FargateService(this, "Service", {
  taskDefinition: taskDefinition,
});
```

### After

```ts
import { DatadogFargate } from "@backpack/cdk-constructs";

// first, define the Datadog construct:
const monitoring = new DatadogFargate(this, "DatadogFargate", {
  service: "bookstore-api",
  env: "development",
  version: "1.0.0",
  source: "java",
  tags: {
    team: "team_fundamentals",
    application: "NS App Core",
    applicationserviceid: "ASID0007799",
    department: "RG2",
    owner: "my.po@ns.nl",
    ...
  },
  taskDefinitionProps: { cpu: 512, memoryLimitMiB: 1024 },
});

// Then, add your application container to the instrumented task definition.
// The log driver is configured automatically.
const appContainer = monitoring.taskDefinition.addContainer("app", {
  image: ecs.ContainerImage.fromRegistry("my-app:latest"),
});

// Explicitly set the default container for ALB target-group registration
monitoring.taskDefinition.defaultContainer = appContainer;

// Finally, define your Fargate service using the instrumented task definition
const service = new FargateService(this, "Service", {
  taskDefinition: monitoring.taskDefinition,
});
```

## Updating imports

`DatadogEcsMonitoring` and its helpers have been replaced by `DatadogFargate`, so make sure to install the package and
update your imports.

```ts
import { DatadogFargate } from "@backpack/cdk-constructs";
```

You can remove any imports of `@ns/cdk-helper`, such as:

* `DatadogEcsMonitoring`
* `datadog-helper.ts` functions (`datadogTags`, `datadogECSAgentTags`, `defineDatadogServiceTag`)

If your project had its own copies of the Fluent Bit config files (`extra.conf`, `longTextLogs.conf`), they can be
removed.

## Task definition

The old construct expected you to create a `FargateTaskDefinition` and pass it in. The new construct creates the task
definition for you. Pass task-level settings (CPU, memory, IAM roles) via `taskDefinitionProps` instead, and use
`monitoring.taskDefinition` wherever you previously referenced your own task definition (e.g. when creating a Fargate
service).

After adding your application container, you must explicitly set it as the default container on the task definition.
This ensures ALB target-group registration works correctly.

```ts
const appContainer = monitoring.taskDefinition.addContainer("app", {
  image: ecs.ContainerImage.fromRegistry("my-app:latest"),
  portMappings: [{ containerPort: 8080 }],
});

monitoring.taskDefinition.defaultContainer = appContainer;
```

> \[!WARNING]
> Make sure to set the default container to the application container. Without it, CDK picks the Datadog agent as the default.

## Tags and `buildConfig`

The old construct pulled tags from `buildConfig`. The new construct uses explicit props:

* `buildConfig.Environment` is now `env`
* `buildConfig.Tags.Service` or `buildConfig.Tags.Application` (service tag) is now `service`
* `buildConfig.AdditionalDatadogTags` is no longer needed, you can pass along your own `tags` (a plain `Record<string, string>`)
* `buildConfig.AdditionalDatadogTags.source` is now a dedicated `source` prop, which falls back to `tags.source`, then
  `service`

## Changes to optional props

* `ecsClusterArn` has been removed and is no longer needed.
* `isJsonLogs` has been removed; JSON log parsing is always enabled.
* `disableLongTextLogs` has been removed; multiline reassembly is always enabled.
* `specificEnvVars` has been renamed to `agentEnvVars`.
* `fireLensLogGroup` and `dataDogAgentLogGroup` have been removed; these log groups are no longer created by the construct.
* `firelensImageVersion` and `datadogImageVersion` have been removed and are now managed by the construct.
* `datadogSecretName` has been removed; the API key is always read from the Landing Zone secret.
* `source` was added to set the Datadog log source (`ddsource`) for integration pipeline matching (e.g. `"nodejs"`,
  `"java"`). Falls back to `tags.source`, then `service`.
* `tracing` was added to configure APM tracing. Tracing is enabled by default; set `tracing: { enabled: false }` to
  disable. Use `tracing: { ignoreTraceResources: ["GET /actuator/health"] }` to exclude noisy endpoints from trace
  collection.
* `cloudwatchLogGroup` was added to optionally send logs to CloudWatch as a secondary output alongside Datadog.

## Log driver configuration

The old construct required you to set up `FireLensLogDriver` on your application containers manually. The new construct
does this automatically — just call `monitoring.taskDefinition.addContainer(...)` without a `logging` property.

## Behavioural changes

* **API key source**: the API key is always retrieved from the Landing Zone (`LandingZone.datadogApiKeySecret`).
  Per-service secret names derived from `buildConfig` are no longer supported.
* **Multiline reassembly**: always enabled. The old `disableLongTextLogs` toggle has been removed.
* **Log parsing**: JSON log parsing is always enabled.
* **APM tracing**: enabled by default. Set `tracing: { enabled: false }` to disable if needed. When enabled, you must
  also instrument your application with a Datadog tracing library (e.g. the [Java tracer](https://docs.datadoghq.com/tracing/trace_collection/dd_libraries/java/?tab=wget#add-the-java-tracer-to-the-jvm)).
  No extra environment variables need to be set on the application container — the construct configures the agent to
  receive traces automatically.
* **CloudWatch logging**: CloudWatch logging for the app container is disabled by default. Pass `cloudwatchLogGroup` to enable it as a secondary output alongside Datadog.
* **Tag normalization**: tag keys and values are automatically normalized to comply with Datadog's tag format (lowercased, disallowed characters replaced with underscores, truncated to 200 characters). For example, `"NS App Core"` becomes `"ns_app_core"`.

## Verification after deployment

After deploying, confirm:

* Tags are correct for logs and traces in Datadog.
* APM traces appear (if tracing is enabled) and are connected to logs and metrics.
* CloudWatch logs appear in the specified log group (if `cloudwatchLogGroup` was provided).

---

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/migrating/hono.md'
---
# Migrating to Hono

This guide explains how to migrate your Backpack project to a [Hono]-based setup.

## When to use this guide

Use this guide if your project:

* has a local development setup based on [@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda] with Express.

## Local development

The `@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda` package has been **deprecated**. For local development, use Hono together
with [@backpack/hono] instead.

### Before

The old setup uses `@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda`, Express and `lambdaHandlers()`.

::: code-group

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import { VitePluginLambda } from "@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    VitePluginLambda({
      appPath: "./server.ts",
    }),
  ],
});
```

```ts [server.ts]
import express from "express";
import { lambdaHandlers } from "@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda";

export const app = express();

app.use(
  lambdaHandlers({
    handlers: {
      "/api/v1/persons": {
        get: {
          handler: () =>
            import("./app/lambdas/get-persons.handler").then((it) => it.handler),
        },
        post: {
          handler: () =>
            import("./app/lambdas/add-person.lambda").then((it) => it.handler),
        },
      },
    },
  }),
);

export default app;
```

:::

### After

The new setup uses Hono, `@backpack/hono` and `@hono/vite-dev-server`.

::: code-group

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import devServer from "@hono/vite-dev-server";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    devServer({
      entry: "./server.ts",
    }),
  ],
});
```

```ts [server.ts]
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { fromAwsLambdaHandler } from "@backpack/hono";

import { handler as getPersons } from "./app/lambdas/get-persons.handler";
import { handler as addPerson } from "./app/lambdas/add-person.lambda";

const app = new Hono();

app.get("/api/v1/persons", fromAwsLambdaHandler(getPersons));
app.post("/api/v1/persons", fromAwsLambdaHandler(addPerson));

export default app;
```

:::

### Steps

Install the new dependencies:

```bash
npm install -D hono @backpack/hono vite @hono/vite-dev-server
```

Remove Express, along with the deprecated package:

```bash
npm uninstall express @types/express @backpack/vite-plugin-lambda
```

Then:

1. Replace `VitePluginLambda()` with `devServer()` from `@hono/vite-dev-server`.
2. Replace the Express app with a Hono app.
3. Replace `lambdaHandlers()` entries with Hono routes using `fromAwsLambdaHandler()`.
4. Keep your existing Lambda handlers unchanged.

### Swagger UI and OpenAPI

If your old Express server contained local-only routes, such as Swagger UI or an OpenAPI endpoint, move those routes to
Hono as well.

For example:

```ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

import { swaggerUI } from "@hono/swagger-ui";
import { parse } from "yaml";

app.get("/", (c) => c.redirect("/swagger-ui"));
app.get("/swagger-ui", swaggerUI({ url: "/openapi" }));
app.get("/openapi", (c) =>
  c.json(parse(readFileSync("./openapi.yaml", "utf-8"))),
);
```

### Testing

Hono apps can be tested directly with `app.request()`.

```ts
const response = await app.request("/api/v1/persons");

expect(response.status).toBe(200);
```

You can also use `createTestRestClient()` from `@backpack/hono` to test through the familiar `@backpack/rest-client`
API.

```ts
import { createTestRestClient } from "@backpack/hono";

const restClient = createTestRestClient(app);

const person = await restClient
  .url("/api/v1/persons")
  .post({ name: "Vera" })
  .json();
```

[Hono]: https://hono.dev/

[@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda]: ../../packages/@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda/index.md

[@backpack/hono]: ../../packages/@backpack/hono/index.md

---

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/how-tos/lambda.md'
---
# Setting up an AWS Lambda function

## Defining the handler

Every AWS Lambda function that uses Node.js as runtime can essentially be written as a regular JavaScript function.

Make sure it is exported properly. For example, consider a `hello-world.handler.ts`:

```ts
export const handler = async function() {
  // ...
};
```

Depending on the Lambda integration you choose, this function will accept an event argument and will need to
return a specific value.

## Choosing a Lambda integration

In most cases, you will need to decide on a specific Lambda integration. Examples include scheduled events, REST APIs,
or handling SQS events.

Depending on the integration you choose, the handler function will accept an additional event parameter and
will need to return a specific result. To ensure the parameters and return values are correctly typed, you
can use the utilities provided by [`@backpack/aws-lambda`].

For example, for [REST integration] it takes an `APIGatewayProxyEvent`:

![REST integration](/diagrams/lambda-integrations-api-gateway.drawio.png)

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda } from "@backpack/aws-lambda";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  //                                           ^?
  return { statusCode: 200, body: "Hello world!" };
});
```

Or, with [SQS integration] it takes an `SQSEvent`:

![SQS integration](/diagrams/lambda-integrations-sqs.drawio.png)

```ts twoslash
import { defineSqsLambda } from "@backpack/aws-lambda";

export const handler = defineSqsLambda(async (event) => {
  //                                          ^?
  // ...
});
```

Check out [`@backpack/aws-lambda`] to learn more.

## Object-oriented approach

When your serverless app grows larger, it might be useful to adopt an object-oriented approach.

This enables you to leverage inversion of control with constructor injection, making it suitable for dependency
injection frameworks.

::: code-group

```ts [hello-world.handler.ts]
// on cold start, bootstrap a new instance (e.g. with a DI framework)
const helloWorldLambda = new HelloWorldLambda(/* ... */);

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  // delegate the event to your class instance
  return helloWorldLambda.handle(event);
});
```

```ts [hello-world.lambda.ts]
export class HelloWorldLambda {
  constructor(private readonly helloService: HelloService) {
  }

  public async handle(event: APIGatewayProxyEvent): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult> {
    // ...

    return { statusCode: 200, body: "Hello world!" };
  }
}
```

:::

Read more about [dependency injection].

[dependency injection]: ../guides/development/dependency-injection.md

[REST integration]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/set-up-lambda-integrations.html

[SQS integration]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html

[`@backpack/aws-lambda`]: ../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md

## Adding a CDK construct

To deploy your code to AWS Lambda, you will need to define a CDK construct for it.

Our recommendation is to use the `LambdaFunction` construct from [`@backpack/cdk-constructs`][cdk-constructs],
which leverages [esbuild] to bundle the code of your Lambda.

Ensure the `entryPath` option points to the file where your handler function is exported:

```ts twoslash
import { Stack, StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { Construct } from "constructs";
import { LambdaFunction } from "@backpack/cdk-constructs";

export class AppStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    new LambdaFunction(this, "MyLambda", {
      // 👇 your lambda entry point
      entryPath: "./app/lambdas/hello.handler.ts",
      handler: "handler",
      environment: {
        APP_PROFILE: `AWS_DEV`
      }
    });
  }
}
```

[cdk-constructs]: ../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/index.md

[esbuild]: https://esbuild.github.io/

## Deploying with CDK

Now use the [CDK CLI] to deploy your Lambda to your preferred environment:

```bash
npx cdk deploy -c config=dev
```

After a successful deployment, you can trigger your Lambda from the [AWS console].

[CDK CLI]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/cli.html

[AWS console]: https://eu-west-1.console.aws.amazon.com/lambda/home?region=eu-west-1#/functions

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/how-tos/rest-api.md'
---
# Building a REST API

## Choosing an architecture

When building a serverless REST API, there are several [architectural patterns](./rest-apis/architecture.md) you can
apply. For most cases we recommend using an [API Gateway] with individual Lambda functions for each endpoint.

[API Gateway]: https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/

## Adding API Gateway to CDK

To set up an API Gateway in your infrastructure code, we recommend using the `ApiGateway` construct from [`@backpack/cdk-constructs`][cdk-constructs].

This construct enables you to define your API mapping using OpenAPI specs and provides
a smooth integration for custom domains.

```ts twoslash
import { Stack, StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { Construct } from "constructs";
import { ApiGateway, AccountDomainName, FileApiDefinition } from "@backpack/cdk-constructs";

export class AppStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    new ApiGateway(this, "MyRestApi", {
      restApiName: "My REST API",

      // optionally, provide an OpenAPI spec file used for routing,
      // with optionally, serving a Swagger UI in its gateway
      apiDefinition: new FileApiDefinition("./path/to/openapi.yaml"), // (or JSON)
      swaggerUI: true,
      
      // optionally, pass your Lambda functions to arrange invocation permissions.
      lambdaFunctions: [ /* lambda functions here  */ ],
      
      // enable API Management ACL
      enableApiManagementAcl: true,
      
      // optionally, enable a custom domain
      customDomain: {
        // automatically creates api.my-service.<aws-account-name>.cla.ns.nl:
        accountDomainName: new AccountDomainName(this, "AccountDomainName", {
          subDomain: "api.my-service"
        })
      }
    });
  }
}
```

[cdk-constructs]: ../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/index.md

[aws-apigateway]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/docs/aws-cdk-lib.aws_apigateway-readme.html

## Writing OpenAPI specs

You can use the [OpenAPI extensions for API Gateway] to add additional API Gateway metadata to your OpenAPI definitions.

A simple OpenAPI document with a single endpoint might look like this:

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.1
info:
  title: Sample API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /hello:
    get:
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A greeting
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  message:
                    type: string
      # OpenAPI extension for API Gateway integration
      x-amazon-apigateway-integration:
        httpMethod: POST # AWS integration method - must be POST regardless of endpoint method
        passthroughBehavior: "when_no_match"
        type: aws_proxy
        uri:
          Fn::Sub: "arn:aws:apigateway:${AWS::Region}:lambda:path/2015-03-31/functions/${HelloWorld.Arn}/invocations"
```

In this case, the `${HelloWorld.Arn}` refers to a Lambda function called "HelloWorld" that exists in the same CDK stack.

[OpenAPI extensions for API Gateway]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-swagger-extensions.html

::: tip
If you are writing your OpenAPI specifications manually, you can use [Swagger Editor](https://editor.swagger.io/) for
validation and previewing.

Alternatively, you can generate your OpenAPI specifications using a code-first approach with libraries such
as [asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi](https://github.com/asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi).
:::

[asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi]: https://github.com/asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi

## Implementing a REST endpoint

To implement a REST endpoint, just add a Lambda function with [REST integration].

When dealing with REST Lambdas, you will likely run into common problems that often require repetitive
boilerplate code, such as normalising request headers, parsing and validating request parameters or handling errors.

Most of these challenges can be addressed with utilities from [`@backpack/aws-lambda`]:

```ts
import { defineRestLambda } from "@backpack/aws-lambda";
import { parseRequest, jsonOk, defaultErrorHandler } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import { AsyncResult } from "@backpack/error-handling/async-result";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  return AsyncResult
    // using `AsyncResult` from `@backpack/error-handling` to handle (async) errors
    .try(() => {
      const request = parseRequest(event);

      // parse a required header
      const callerId = request.getHeader("X-Caller-Id", { required: true });
      
      // parse a JSON body and validate it against a Zod schema 
      const book = request.getBody().json({ validated: BookSchema });

      // return a HTTP 200 result
      return jsonOk({ message: "Hello world" });
    })
    // apply the default error handler from `@backpack/aws-lambda/rest`
    .recover(defaultErrorHandler());
});
```

Check out the API reference of [`@backpack/aws-lambda`] to learn more.  Or have a look at the [Bookstore REST API] demo.

[REST integration]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/set-up-lambda-integrations.html

[`@backpack/aws-lambda`]: ../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md

[Bookstore REST API]: ../introduction/demo-projects.md#backpackbookstore-rest-api

## Deploying with CDK

Now use the [CDK CLI] to deploy your API Gateway to your preferred environment:

```bash
npx cdk deploy -c config=dev
```

After a successful deployment, you can trigger your endpoint from the [AWS console].

[CDK CLI]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/cli.html

[AWS console]: https://eu-west-1.console.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/main/apis?region=eu-west-1

## Security and API Management

By default, your REST endpoints are publicly accessible. If you want to restrict access, you can integrate
it with the [API Management portal](./rest-apis/api-management.md).

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/how-tos/rest-apis/architecture.md'
---
# Choosing a REST architecture

When building a serverless REST API, there are several architectural patterns you can apply:

\[\[toc]]

## API Gateway with Single-purpose Lambdas (recommended)

![API Gateway with Single-purpose Lambda](/diagrams/single-purpose-lambdas.drawio.png)

Each Lambda function handles exactly one endpoint. The API Gateway routes each endpoint to its dedicated Lambda.

Pros:

* Clean separation of concerns – each function is small, focused, and easier to test.
* Easier to scale, deploy, and debug individual endpoints.

Cons:

* More functions to manage – might feel cluttered.
* Slightly more complex deployment setup (e.g., lots of handlers and infrastructure code).

## API Gateway with Multi-purpose Lambdas

![API Gateway with Multi-purpose Lambda](/diagrams/multi-purpose-lambdas-api-gateway.drawio.png)

One single Lambda handles multiple endpoints or routes (also called *lambdalith* or *monolambda*). It uses internal
routing (e.g. via a framework like [Hono]) to delegate logic based on the incoming request.

Pros:

* Fewer functions to manage.
* Easier to get started with if you're used to monolithic backends or express-style routing.

Cons:

* Harder to test, scale, and deploy granularly.
* Only one URL per Lambda, so routing logic must be handled manually inside the function.
* All logic is bundled together – one failing route can affect others.
* Cold starts might take longer due to larger bundle sizes.

[Hono]: https://hono.dev/

## Multi-purpose Lambdas with Lambda Function URL

![API Gateway with Multi-purpose Lambda and function url](/diagrams/multi-purpose-lambdas-function-url.drawio.png)

Skip API Gateway entirely. A single Lambda handles all routing and is invoked directly via a Lambda Function URL.

Pros:

* Simpler and cheaper – no API Gateway in between.
* Great for simple or internal apps with minimal complexity.

Cons:

* No advanced API features like rate limiting, custom auth, throttling, etc. (you’d have to implement them yourself).
* Only one URL per Lambda, so routing logic must be handled manually inside the function.
* There is currently no option to use a custom domain name, unless you route your traffic through CloudFront.

---

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/how-tos/rest-apis/api-management.md'
---
# Integrating with API Management

To expose your REST API to other services or to the outside world, you can integrate your REST API with
the [Azure API Management] portal. This solution will manage the authentication and authorization of your
REST API.

[Azure API Management]: https://apiportal.ns.nl/

## Getting started

To onboard your project, you can find more information in [the APIM cookbook][cookbook].

[cookbook]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/APIM/pages/149422169/Azure+API+Management+Cookbook

## CI/CD integration

To integrate API Management with your CI/CD pipeline, you can use [this CI/CD brick][brick].

* If you generated your Backpack project with `@backpack/cli` v0.8 or higher, it is already included in your project.
* To add it to your existing project:
  * generate [a new CI/CD pipeline] with the Backpack CLI;
  * or integrate it manually, by looking at the CI/CD pipeline of the [Bookstore demo project].

[a new CI/CD pipeline]: ../../packages/@backpack/cli/index.md#generating-a-ci-cd-pipeline

[Bookstore demo project]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/apps/bookstore-rest-api/.azure-devops/pipelines/ci.yaml

> \[!IMPORTANT]
> The CI/CD brick requires you to have an existing API Management product to deploy to.

[brick]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/CICD/_git/pipeline-templates?path=/jobs/deploy/api-management/apim-deploy.md

## Prevent access using an ACL

By adding the `FMIncludeAPIMgtWebACL` tag to your API Gateway or CloudFront distribution construct, you can restrict
access to it and only allow the Azure API Management Portal access to it:

```ts
Tags.of(apiGateway).add("FMIncludeAPIMgtWebACL", "true");
Tags.of(cloudFrontDistribution).add("FMIncludeAPIMgtWebACL", "true");
```

If you are using the [ApiGateway construct] from `@backpack/cdk-constructs`, you can enable this ACL using the
`enableApiManagementAcl` option.

[ApiGateway construct]: ../../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/classes/ApiGateway.md

# Using DynamoDB

DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database service offered by AWS. It's designed for
high-performance, low-latency applications that need to scale seamlessly.

## Adding your DynamoDB table to CDK

To create your DynamoDB table, you need to define a CDK construct for it.

Our recommendation is to use the `Table` construct from `aws-cdk-lib/aws-dynamodb`.

```ts twoslash
import { Stack, StackProps } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { Construct } from 'constructs';
import { NodejsFunction, OutputFormat } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs';
import { AttributeType, BillingMode, Table } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-dynamodb";

export class AppStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    // const myLambdaFunction = ...

    const myTable = new Table(this, id, {
      partitionKey: { name: "id", type: AttributeType.STRING },
      billingMode: BillingMode.PAY_PER_REQUEST
    });

    // since the table name is created dynamically, 
    // you may want to pass it to your lambda as environment variable:
    // myLambdaFunction.addEnvironment("MY_TABLE_NAME", myTable.tableName);
  }
}
```

A more detailed example of this construct can be found on our [CDK snippet page].

[CDK snippet page]: ../guides/infrastructure/cdk-snippets.md#amazon-dynamodb

## Writing a repository

To interact with DynamoDB, we recommend using [`@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb`]. This library simplifies the process by
removing the need to manually marshal and unmarshal DynamoDB attribute values.

If you prefer, you can even use the default repository implementation from [`@backpack/amazon-dynamodb`], which
streamlines common DynamoDB operations:

```ts
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb";
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb";
import { DynamoDbRepository } from "@backpack/amazon-dynamodb";

// Create a client
const client = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient());

// Define a repository
const booksRepository = new DynamoDbRepository<Book>(
  client,
  { tableName: 'Books' }
);

// Retrieve an item by ID
const book = await booksRepository.getItemById({ isbn: "9789027439642" });
```

Check out [`@backpack/amazon-dynamodb`] to learn more. Or have a look at the [Bookstore REST API] demo.

[`@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb`]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSJavaScriptSDK/v3/latest/Package/-aws-sdk-lib-dynamodb/

[`@backpack/amazon-dynamodb`]: ../packages/@backpack/amazon-dynamodb/index.md

[Bookstore REST API]: ../introduction/demo-projects.md#backpackbookstore-rest-api
