# Building a REST client

When consuming REST APIs you can use the built-in [Fetch API] or opt for a third-party library.

## Recommended library: Wretch

An implementation based on the Fetch API is preferred, due its lightweight nature and lack of external dependencies,
making it ideal for minimal and maintainable applications. However, using the Fetch API alone, without any library, has
its limitations. It easily leads to verbose syntax, awkward error handling and there is no built-in support for
middleware.

[Wretch] addresses these issues by providing a more expressive API, enabling fluent method chaining, automatic response
parsing, and cleaner error handling, reducing boilerplate:

```ts
import wretch from "wretch";

const bookStoreClient = wretch()
  .url("https://my-book-store.com")
  .headers({ "X-Some-Api-Key": "..." });

const books = await bookStoreClient
  .get("/api/v1/books")
  .json();

await bookStoreClient
  .body({ isbn: "1234", title: "My book" })
  .put("/api/v1/books");
```

::: info What about Axios?
In the past, Axios was the go-to solution for making HTTP requests in JavaScript and TypeScript. However, its
implementation is based on `XMLHttpRequest`, requiring more code and increasing your bundle size. It also has no
automatic JSON handling, and requires more boilerplate code. Therefore, we recommend a more modern library instead.
:::

## Pre-configured REST client from Backpack

You can use the pre-configured REST client from `@backpack/rest-client`, which is based on Wretch and ships with a few
add-ons and middlewares enabled by default:

```ts
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";

const bookStoreClient = createRestClient({
  baseUrl: "https://my-book-store.com",
  apiManagementApiKey: '...',
  timeout: 5_000,
  // ...
});

const books = await bookStoreClient
  .get("/api/v1/books")
  .json();
```

Check out the [API reference][backpack/rest-client] of `@backpack/rest-client` to learn more.

## OAuth bearer tokens

Use the `bearerToken()` middleware when a downstream API expects an `Authorization: Bearer` header.

For Azure Entra ID client credentials, use `azureClientCredentials()`. This provider uses the v2 token endpoint with
`scope`; it does not support legacy `resource` based token requests. Tokens are cached until shortly before expiry.

```ts
import { SecretsManagerClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-secrets-manager";
import { CachedSecretsManagerService } from "@backpack/aws-secrets-manager";
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";
import {
  azureClientCredentials,
  bearerToken,
  fromAwsSecretsManager,
} from "@backpack/rest-client/middleware";

const secretsManager = new CachedSecretsManagerService(
  new SecretsManagerClient(),
);

const bookStoreClient = createRestClient({
  baseUrl: "https://my-book-store.com",
  middlewares: [
    bearerToken(
      azureClientCredentials({
        tenantId: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000",
        clientId: "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
        clientSecret: fromAwsSecretsManager<{ clientSecret: string }>({
          secretsManager,
          secretId: "/bookstore/oauth/client-credentials",
          select: (secret) => secret.clientSecret,
        }),
        scope: "api://bookstore/.default",
      }),
    ),
  ],
});
```

For local development, use required environment variables instead of AWS Secrets Manager:

```ts
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";
import {
  azureClientCredentials,
  bearerToken,
  fromEnv,
} from "@backpack/rest-client/middleware";

const bookStoreClient = createRestClient({
  baseUrl: "https://my-book-store.com",
  middlewares: [
    bearerToken(
      azureClientCredentials({
        tenantId: fromEnv("AZURE_TENANT_ID"),
        clientId: fromEnv("AZURE_CLIENT_ID"),
        clientSecret: fromEnv("AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET"),
        scope: fromEnv("AZURE_SCOPE"),
      }),
    ),
  ],
});
```

## Response validation

One way to make your response data type-safe, is by passing a generic type to the `json()` method:

```ts
import { createRestClient } from '@backpack/rest-client';

const books = await createRestClient()
  .get("/api/v1/books")
  .json<BooksResponse>();

books
// ^ inferred as `BooksResponse`, but unsafe! ⚠️
```

However, since you are now basically type-casting your JSON result, it might be better to perform actual runtime
validation to the response instead.

To achieve this, we recommend you to parse the result against a schema, using [Zod]:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { createRestClient } from '@backpack/rest-client';

// define a Zod schema for your response
const BooksResponse = z.object({
  isbn: z.string()
  // ...
});

const books = await createRestClient()
  .get("/api/v1/books")
  .json()
  .then(json => BooksResponse.parse(json));
//      ^ `json` is `unknown` but can be parsed by Zod

books;
// ^ still inferred as `BooksResponse`, but now it's safe! 🚀
```

With the pre-configured REST client from Backpack, you can even use the shorthand `.validatedJson()` instead:

```ts
const books = await createRestClient()
  .get("/api/v1/books")
  .validatedJson(BooksResponse);
```

For more information on Zod and validation, see [Schema validation](../guides/development/zod-validation.md).

## Configuring a timeout

To prevent hanging requests and handle failures gracefully, it is important to configure a timeout for your REST client.

With Wretch, you can achieve this by using the [AbortAddon]:

```ts
import wretch from 'wretch';
import AbortAddon from 'wretch/addons/abort';

const restClient = await wretch()
  .addon(AbortAddon())
  .setTimeout(3_000) // 3 seconds

const books = await restClient
  .get("/api/v1/books")
  // additional helper method to recover from an aborted request:
  .onAbort(() => console.log("Aborted!"))
```

If you use the pre-configured REST client from [`@backpack/rest-client`][backpack/rest-client], you don't have to worry
about this:

```ts
import { createRestClient } from '@backpack/rest-client';

const restClient = createRestClient({
  timeout: 3_000
});

const books = await restClient.get("/api/v1/books")
```

## Error handling

How errors should be handled in your REST client, depends on the type of error and your use case.

To handle expected errors such as HTTP 404 responses gracefully, you can use the [built-in helper methods] of Wretch:

[built-in helper methods]: https://github.com/elbywan/wretch#catchers-

```ts
import { createRestClient } from '@backpack/rest-client';

const result = await createRestClient()
  .get("/api/v1/books")
  .notFound(() => {
    // recover from a HTTP 404
    return "some fallback";
  })
  .json()
```

Another way to handle errors is to propagate them through a chain of Promises:

```typescript [using Promise]
const result = createRestClient()
  .get("/api/v1/books")
  .json()
  .then(json => BooksResponse.parse(json))
  .then(data => /* do other stuff */)
  .catch(error => {
    logger.warn('Got unexpected error', error);
    return "some fallback";
  })
```

With the `AsyncResult` utility from `@backpack/error-handling` you can even handle every kind of error differently:

```typescript
import { createRestClient } from '@backpack/rest-client';
import { AsyncResult } from "@backpack/error-handling/async-result";

const result = await AsyncResult
  .try(() =>
    createRestClient()
      .get("/api/books")
      .json()
  )
  .map((json) => BooksResponse.parse(json))
  .map(data => /* do other stuff */)
  .onFailureIfInstanceOf(ZodError, (error) => /* ... */)
  .onFailureIfInstanceOf(WretchError, (error) => /* ... */)
  .recover(() => "some fallback");
```

## Logging

Given how easily logging becomes opinionated, the default REST client in Backpack avoids it entirely.

However, if you do want to add some logging, you can easily do so using a middleware function. If you are using
the [Powertools Logger], you can use the existing logging middleware from Backpack:

```ts
import {
  createRestClient,
  powertoolsLoggingMiddleware
} from "@backpack/rest-client";

const myRestClient = createRestClient()
  .middlewares([
    powertoolsLoggingMiddleware({
      logger: myLogger, // pass your logger instance to the middleware
      logRequests: true,
      // to see all options, check the API reference
    })
  ]);

const result = myRestClient
  .get("/api/books")
  .json()
```

Check out our in-depth guide [Logging & metrics](./../guides/observability/logging-and-metrics.md) to learn more.

## Adding custom middleware

You can also add your own middleware:

```ts
import type { Middleware } from "@backpack/rest-client";

// Add custom options to this factory when needed.
export const myMiddleware = (): Middleware => {
  return (next) => async (url, options) => {
    // do something with the request...

    const response = await next(url, options);

    // do something with the response...

    return response;
  };
};
```

[Fetch API]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch

[Wretch]: https://github.com/elbywan/wretch

[Zod]: https://zod.dev/

[AbortAddon]: https://github.com/elbywan/wretch#abort-

[Powertools Logger]: https://docs.powertools.aws.dev/lambda/typescript/latest/core/logger/

[backpack/rest-client]: ../packages/@backpack/rest-client/index.md

# Messaging & event-driven architectures

Messaging is a key part of building scalable and decoupled systems in AWS, and allows you to create
an event-driven architecture.

## Choosing your architecture

### SQS-only

![SQS only](/diagrams/messaging-sqs.drawio.png)

You can publish a message directly to an [SQS queue][SQS]. This is useful for point-to-point communication.

* Decouples producers and consumers
* Supports dead-letter queues, retries, delay queues

### SNS with optionally SQS

![SNS](/diagrams/messaging-sns.drawio.png)

Alternatively, you can publish a message to an [SNS topic][SNS] instead. This is useful for a pub/sub model,
e.g. when different systems will need to subscribe to a topic independently. Every subscriber can have its
own [SQS queue][SQS].

* Pushes messages to multiple subscribers (email, HTTP, Lambda, SQS, etc.)
* Good for broadcasting events to multiple systems

### EventBridge

![EventBridge](/diagrams/messaging-event-bridge.drawio.png)

[EventBridge] is an event bus for event-driven architectures, and can be used in combination with SQS queues.

* Schema registry, event routing with rules
* Ideal for loosely coupled microservices

[SQS]: https://aws.amazon.com/sqs/

[SNS]: https://aws.amazon.com/sns/

[EventBridge]: https://aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/

## Adding CDK constructs

To add your SQS queue, you can use the constructs from `aws-cdk-lib/aws-sqs`:

```ts
import { Stack, StackProps, Duration } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { Construct } from "constructs";
import { Queue } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-sqs";
import { SqsEventSource } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-event-sources";

export class AppStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    // const myLambdaFunction = ...

    const myQueue = new Queue(this, "MyQueue", {
      queueName: "my-queue"
    });

    // Add the SQS queue as event source for your Lambda
    myLambdaFunction.addEventSource(new SqsEventSource(myQueue));
  }
}
```

To add an SNS topic to your infrastructure code, you can use the CDK constructs from `aws-cdk-lib/aws-sns`.

You can either create your own topic, or import an existing one with `Topic.fromTopicArn`:

```ts
import { Stack, StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { Construct } from "constructs";
import { Topic } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-sns";
import { SqsSubscription } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-sns-subscriptions";

export class AppStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    // create your own SNS topic:
    const myTopic = new Topic(this, "MyTopic", {
      displayName: "my-topic",
      topicName: "my-topic"
    });

    // make sure to arrange additional permissions to publish to your topic 

    // ...or import an existing one, e.g. from another project:
    // const myTopic = Topic.fromTopicArn(...)

    // add a subscription to your queue:
    // const myQueue = ...  (see previous example)
    myQueue.addSubscription(new SqsSubscription(queue));
  }
}
```

More examples of these constructs can be found on our [CDK snippet page].

[CDK snippet page]: ../guides/infrastructure/cdk-snippets.md

## Publishing messages

Publishing messages to [SQS] or [SNS] can be done with the corresponding AWS SDK clients.

You can additionally use utilities from [`@backpack/amazon-sqs`] and [`@backpack/amazon-sqs`] to make it even
simpler:

```ts
import { SNSClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-sns";
import { SnsPublisher } from "@backpack/amazon-sns";

const client = new SNSClient();
const publisher = new SnsPublisher(client, "my-topic-arn");

// publishes the message as JSON payload
await publisher.publishJson({ foo: "Foo" });
```

Check out the [API reference] section to learn more.

[`@backpack/amazon-sqs`]: ../packages/@backpack/amazon-sqs/index.md

[`@backpack/amazon-sns`]: ../packages/@backpack/amazon-sns/index.md

[API reference]: ../packages/index.md

## Handling messages

To handle SNS or SQS messages, you will need to create an AWS Lambda with the correct integration.

With the utilities from [`@backpack/aws-lambda`] you can do this easily:

```ts twoslash
import { defineSqsLambda } from "@backpack/aws-lambda";

export const handler = defineSqsLambda(async function(event) {
  //                                                   ^?
  // ...
});
```

Check out [`@backpack/aws-lambda`] to learn more.

[`@backpack/aws-lambda`]: ../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md

# Recommended tools

To offer a consistent developer experience, we recommend the following tools.

## Package manager: npm

We recommend using [npm](https://docs.npmjs.com/downloading-and-installing-node-js-and-npm), the default package
manager of Node.js. Other package managers (like [Yarn] or [PNPM]) usually work fine, but are not recommended to
maintain consistency between projects.

## Code formatting: Prettier

[Prettier](https://prettier.io/) is an opinionated code formatter that is widely adopted in the industry and
integrated into most IDEs. Maintaining a consistent code style across all Backpack-powered projects eliminates
discussions about code style during code reviews.

Although Prettier is [configurable](https://prettier.io/docs/en/options), Backpack does not currently provide a specific
preset. We recommend sticking to the default settings, but feel free to tweak it to your likings.

> \[!TIP]
> For more tips on how to use Prettier effectively, check out our [Linting & formatting] guide.

## Code linting: ESLint

[ESLint](https://eslint.org/) is the recommended linting tool. It checks your code for common mistakes and
bad practices, making your code safer and improving consistency.

Backpack provides [a preset](../../packages/@backpack/eslint-config/index.md) for your ESLint config that includes most recommended
rules and saves you some dependency management.

> \[!TIP]
> For more tips on how to use ESLint effectively, check out our [Linting & formatting] guide.

## Testing: Vitest

[Vitest](https://vitest.dev/) is a modern testing framework that supports TypeScript out-of-the-box and makes testing
easier, demanding little to no configuration and requiring only a single dependency.

> \[!TIP]
> For more tips on how to use Vitest effectively, check out our [Vitest guide].

## Local development: Vite

[Vite](https://vite.dev/) is a build tool that speeds up local development. It is mostly adopted by frontend
projects, but with [`@backpack/hono`](../../packages/@backpack/hono/index.md) you can also
use it to run your AWS Lambda functions locally.

> \[!TIP]
> For more tips on local development, check out our [local development guide].

[Yarn]: https://yarnpkg.com/

[PNPM]: https://pnpm.io/

[Linting & formatting]: ./linting-and-formatting.md

[Vitest guide]: ../testing/using-vitest.md

[local development guide]: ./local-development.md

# Using AI in Backpack projects

This guide explains how to use AI coding assistants and agents effectively in Backpack projects.

Backpack provides AI-readable documentation and project-level agent instructions so AI tools can use current Backpack
guidance instead of relying on outdated assumptions.

## What Backpack provides

Backpack exposes AI-ready documentation through:

* [`llms.txt`](/llms.txt)
* [`llms-full.txt`](/llms-full.txt)
* [AI agent instructions](/ai/agents.html)

These files help AI tools find current Backpack documentation, package APIs, upgrade guides, migration guides, and
examples.

## Add agent instructions to your project

To make your project easier for AI coding agents to understand, add an `AGENTS.md` file to the project root.

The recommended way is to use the Backpack CLI:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli agents init
```

This creates an `AGENTS.md` file with Backpack-specific instructions for AI coding agents.

The file points agents to the current Backpack documentation and tells them to verify package APIs, imports, migrations,
and examples before changing code.

## Existing AGENTS.md files

If your project already has an `AGENTS.md` file, the command will not overwrite it.

To add a Backpack section to the existing file, run:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli agents init --merge
```

Existing local instructions are preserved.

## Check whether your project is ready

To check whether your project already contains Backpack agent guidance, run:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli agents init --check
```

This checks whether `AGENTS.md` is present and contains Backpack-specific guidance.

## When to use this

Use this setup when:

* working with AI coding agents in a Backpack project
* asking an agent to perform migrations
* upgrading Backpack packages
* changing REST API, Lambda, CDK, or testing code
* asking questions about Backpack APIs or examples

## Recommended workflow

1. Install Backpack agent instructions:

   ```shell
   npx @backpack/cli agents init
   ```

2. Ask your AI tool to read the local `AGENTS.md`.

3. Ask it to verify Backpack-specific answers against the Backpack docs.

4. Review generated changes like any other code change.

AI tools can help with implementation, migration, and documentation work, but generated changes should still be reviewed
by a developer.

## Example prompt

```text
Hey, check AGENTS.md and investigate if this project needs
important Backpack migrations.

Check the Backpack docs, and give me a short migration plan
before changing anything.
```

Or, more specific:

```text
Hi, do you know which packages are included in Backpack?

What is the latest Backpack version right now?

Which Node.js version should I use for this Backpack project?
```

# Setting up AWS CLI with SSO

## Instructions

1. Install the [AWS CLI].

2. Run `aws configure sso`.

3. Enter the following SSO settings:
   * **SSO session name**: choose a suitable name, e.g., `NS`.
   * **SSO start URL**: `https://ns-sso.awsapps.com/start`.
   * **SSO region**: `eu-west-1`.
   * **SSO registration scopes**: press "Enter" to accept the defaults.

4. Log in using your credentials and approve any prompts.

5. Complete the wizard:
   * **CLI default client Region**: press "Enter" to accept the defaults.
   * **CLI default output format**: press "Enter" to accept the defaults.
   * **CLI profile name**: use `default` if this is your first time setting up SSO.

[AWS CLI]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html

# Linting & formatting

Linting and formatting keep a codebase consistent, readable, and easier to change safely. They reduce noise in reviews,
catch common bugs early.

## Using ESLint with Prettier

* **[ESLint]** is our recommended tool for code-quality rules (possible bugs, unsafe patterns, unused vars, bad imports,
  etc.).
* **[Prettier]** is our recommended tool for code style (indentation, line wrapping, quotes, etc.).

The recommended setup is: **let Prettier handle all styling**, and configure ESLint so it **doesn’t fight** Prettier and
only reports actual code issues.

> \[!NOTE] Why "ESLint for linting, Prettier for formatting"?
> If ESLint is also enforcing style rules, you’ll get lots of lint errors just because someone’s line-wrapping differs.
> That creates noisy PRs and encourages people to ignore ESLint output ("it’s yelling again").
> With Prettier doing style, formatting becomes a non-event: it either matches or it gets auto-fixed.

## Customization

For ESLint, we provide [a preset](../../packages/@backpack/eslint-config/index.md) that includes most
[recommended rules][eslint-recommended] and saves you some dependency management.

You can still override or add additional rules in your `eslint.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";
import backpack from "@backpack/eslint-config";

export default defineConfig(...backpack.configs.recommended, {
  rules: {
    // your overrides/tweaks here, e.g.:
    "import/order": "off"
  }
});
```

For Prettier, you can add a `.prettierrc` to override the [default settings][default prettier]:

```json
{
  "printWidth": 120
}
```

[default prettier]: https://prettier.io/docs/options

[eslint-recommended]: https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/

## Recommended workflow

There are multiple ways to apply linting and formatting. Ideally you combine them:

* **Running npm scripts** (so you can run all checks locally)
* **Auto-format on save** (so styling stays invisible and effortless)
* **Auto-fix lint on save** (so trivial issues get fixed immediately)
* **Optionally: add pre-commit hooks** (so you don’t run full checks manually)
* **Optionally: enforce everything in CI** (so nothing sneaks in)

### Using npm scripts

Example npm scripts for your `package.json`:

```jsonc
{
  "scripts": {
    "check": "npm-run-all --continue-on-error check:types check:lint check:format",
    "check:types": "tsc",
    "check:types:watch": "tsc -w",
    "check:lint": "eslint",
    "check:format": "prettier . --ignore-unknown --check",
    "format": "prettier . --ignore-unknown --write",
    "lint": "eslint",
    "lint:fix": "eslint --fix",
  },
}
```

### Using IDE (run on save)

We recommend enabling format on save (Prettier) and auto-fix lint on save (ESLint).

#### IntelliJ IDEA (and other JetBrains IDEs)

* Prettier
  * Enable the Prettier plugin.
  * Configure: *Languages & Frameworks* → *JavaScript* → *Prettier*
  * Turn on **Run on save**.
* ESLint
  * Configure: *Languages & Frameworks* → *JavaScript* → *Code Quality Tools* → *ESLint*
  * Enable *Automatic ESLint configuration*.
  * Enable **Run eslint --fix on save**.

#### VS Code

Install extensions:

* ESLint (by Microsoft)
* Prettier - Code formatter (by Prettier)

Recommended `.vscode/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode",
  "eslint.useFlatConfig": true,
  "editor.codeActionsOnSave": {
    "source.fixAll.eslint": "explicit"
  }
}
```

### Using pre-commit hooks

Pre-commit hooks help you avoid running full `npm run check` all the time by only processing staged files.

Here follows a simple setup using [Husky] (to manage Git hooks) with [lint-staged] (to run commands only on staged
files).

Install dependencies:

```bash
npm i -D husky lint-staged
```

Enable husky:

```bash
npx husky init
```

Configure lint-staged (example in `package.json`):

```json
{
  "lint-staged": {
    "*": [
      "eslint --fix",
      "prettier --ignore-unknown --write"
    ]
  }
}
```

Update the pre-commit hook (`.husky/pre-commit`) to run lint-staged:

```bash
npx lint-staged
```

How it behaves:

* On `git commit`, only staged files are formatted and lint-fixed.
* If anything can’t be auto-fixed, the commit is blocked and you’ll see the errors.
* This keeps the feedback loop tight and prevents the classic "CI failed because someone committed a file with 3 spaces
  instead of 2" scenario.

[ESLint]: https://eslint.org/

[Prettier]: https://prettier.io/

[Husky]: https://typicode.github.io/husky/

[lint-staged]: https://github.com/lint-staged/lint-staged

---

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/tooling/typescript.md'
---
# Configuring TypeScript

Backpack does not force you to use TypeScript, but we recommend doing so to maximize the type-safety of your code.

However, configuring your `tsconfig.json` properly can be challenging. On this page, you find some tips and tricks.

## Using a preset (recommended)

The easiest way to configure TypeScript for your project is to use [
`@backpack/typescript-config`](../../packages/@backpack/typescript-config/index.md) which offers a preset for your
`tsconfig.json`.

## Important compiler settings

If you rather like to use your own `tsconfig.json`, or if you want to understand why we recommend certain compiler
settings, you can find the most important settings below.

### `strict`

To maximize type-safety, make sure to set this option to `true` so
that [most recommended](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#strict) strict settings are enabled.

### `module`

For Node.js it is recommended to use `NodeNext` if TypeScript is used as transpiler, but since we use CDK / esbuild,
the best option here is `preserve`. This makes `tsc` less strict in its module resolution, e.g. allowing you to omit
file extensions in imports.

### `noEmit`

Since we use `tsc` only as type-checker (CDK / esbuild is used for transpiling), it's important to set this option
to `true`. This makes sure that `tsc` won't emit any JavaScript files, causing all kinds of issues (for example, when no
`outDir` is set,
the `.js` files taking presedence over `.ts` files).

### `lib`

Specifies which standard libraries are available in your runtime. In the preset, this is configured to `es2024`,
assuming a runtime with Node.js v24. If you are using a different version of Node.js, you may want to override
this option.

[//]: # "peer-deps: update the paragraph above when we change to a newer version of Node.js, and upgrade the `lib` option accordingly."

It's recommended to NOT include `DOM` as library, since we're not running in a browser. Please install
`@types/node` instead (aligning the version with your Node.js runtime) to use type definitions for Node.js APIs.

---

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md'
---
# Using Nexus as npm registry 🛠

To use Backpack, you need to configure [Sonatype Nexus] as npm registry.

> \[!WARNING]
> We recently migrated the location of our npm registry.
> Please check out [this migration guide](../migrating/nexus-registry.md) for more information.

## What is Nexus?

Nexus is a repository manager that stores and serves packages. In our case, Nexus acts as an npm registry with a proxy
between your project and external package sources (such as npmjs.org). It ensures packages are resolved through an
NS-managed registry, where access, caching, and security policies can be enforced.

### What are Nexus groups?

Using a Nexus group gives us more flexibility:

* It can serve:
  * public packages (via npmjs.org proxy)
  * private NS-specific packages (including Backpack)
* We can **add or change underlying registries** without requiring users to:
  * reconfigure npm scopes
  * update local `.npmrc` files
  * create additional CI/CD service connections in Azure DevOps

In short: fewer moving parts for users, more freedom for maintainers.

## Current registry location

Backpack packages are available via the following Nexus group:

`https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup`

All TOPAAS users can access this group.

## How to use this registry

This Nexus group can be used in **two ways**. We strongly recommend the first option, but both are fully supported.

### Available options

When you run `npm install`, npm downloads packages from a registry.

There is always a primary registry, but you can configure npm to use a different registry for specific package scopes
via your `.npmrc` file.

We recommend configuring **the Backpack Nexus group as your primary npm registry**, meaning all packages are resolved
through it.

Alternatively, you can configure it only for the `@backpack` scope. An npm scope is a namespace (e.g.
`@backpack/package-name`) that allows specific packages to be resolved from a different registry.

### Option 1: use as primary npm registry (recommended)

Configure the Backpack Nexus group as your **primary npm registry** (in your personal `~/.npmrc` and project-level
`.npmrc` file):

::: code-group

```text [personal ~/.npmrc]
registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
//nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/:_auth=YOUR_PERSONAL_TOKEN_HERE
```

```text [project-level .npmrc]
registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
```

:::

**Why this is recommended:**

* One single registry for **all** dependencies:
  * public packages (via npmjs.org proxy)
  * private NS-specific packages (such as Backpack)
* We can **add or change underlying registries** without requiring users to:
  * reconfigure npm scopes
  * update local `.npmrc` files
  * create additional CI/CD service connections in Azure DevOps

In short: fewer moving parts for users, more freedom for maintainers.

> \[!NOTE]
> If you are using a private package that is not accessible through this group yet, let us know and we will make it
> available. Alternatively, you can use `@some-scope:registry=` to override the registry for a specific scope.

### Option 2: use only for Backpack packages

If you prefer, you can configure the Backpack Nexus group only for the `@backpack` scope in both your personal
`~/.npmrc` and your project-level `.npmrc` file:

::: code-group

```text [personal ~/.npmrc]
@backpack:registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
//nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/:_auth=YOUR_PERSONAL_TOKEN_HERE
```

```text [project-level .npmrc]
@backpack:registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
```

:::

This allows you to keep another registry (for example npmjs.org) as your primary registry.

## Local environment

### 1. Retrieve your personal access token from Nexus

Log in to [Sonatype Nexus] and copy your access token from your profile.

Make sure to use the base64 representation of `username:password`, as shown on the screenshot below:

![nexus-token.png](/screenshots/nexus-token.png)

### 2. Update your personal `~/.npmrc` file

#### Using `npm config` commands (recommended)

The easiest way to update your npm settings is by running the following commands:

```bash
npm config set registry https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
npm config set //nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/:_auth=$ACCESS_TOKEN
```

Replace `$ACCESS_TOKEN` with your personal token retrieved from Nexus.

These commands will update your personal `~/.npmrc` file.

#### Manually

Optionally, you can update your `~/.npmrc` manually. Make sure it looks like this:

```text
registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
//nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/:_auth=YOUR_PERSONAL_TOKEN_HERE
```

> \[!IMPORTANT]
> For security reasons, do not put your personal access token in your project’s `.npmrc`. Otherwise, you risk leaking it
> in version control.

## npm audits

When using Nexus as the primary npm registry, `npm audit` may not work as expected. You may see an error like:

```
Nexus Lifecycle or Nexus Firewall must be configured. Please contact your NXRM administrator.
```

This happens because Nexus requires **Sonatype Repository Firewall** to support `npm audit`. Repository Firewall is a
paid add-on, and NS currently does not have a license for it. We are investigating the possibility of acquiring one.

### Workaround

As a workaround, you can run `npm audit` directly against the public npm registry:

```bash
npm audit --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org
```

⚠️ Do **not** run `npm audit fix --registry=...`.

Using `--registry` with `npm audit fix` may update your `package-lock.json` with incorrect registry URLs, which can lead
to inconsistent or broken installs.

For Backpack projects, prefer `npm update` over `npm audit fix --registry=...`. See
also [Using npm in Backpack projects](./working-with-npm.md) for more guidance on resolving audit findings.

## CI/CD environment

To use Nexus in your CI/CD pipeline, follow these steps.

### 1. Functional account and permissions

First, arrange a functional account: an account that can be used for CI/CD purposes. More information can be found
[here][WPOL accounts].

### 2. Set up a service connection in Azure DevOps

Create a service connection in Azure DevOps that points to the Nexus group:

`https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup`

Remember the name of this service connection.

### 3. Configure your CI/CD pipeline

Make sure your project has an `.npmrc` file in the root of its repository with:

```text
registry=https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/repository/NS_BACKPACK_NPMGroup/
```

In your YAML pipeline, always authenticate **and** pass the service connection to the `npm ci` step.

This ensures:

* `npm ci` is authenticated
* any `npx` calls are authenticated
* `postinstall` scripts work reliably
* all dependency resolution goes through the expected registry
*

```yaml
- task: npmAuthenticate@0
  displayName: "Nexus authentication"
  inputs:
    workingFile: ".npmrc"
    # any additional connections should be comma-separated
    customEndpoint: "name-of-your-service-connection, other-service-connection"

- task: Npm@1
  displayName: "npm ci"
  inputs:
    command: ci
    # any additional connections should be comma-separated
    customEndpoint: "name-of-your-service-connection, other-service-connection"
```

[Sonatype Nexus]: https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/

[mutate membership]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/49/create/225

[WPOL accounts]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/TECHWIKI/pages/155097024

# Using npm in Backpack projects

This guide explains the npm concepts and commands that matter most in day-to-day Backpack development.

## package.json vs package-lock.json

`package.json` describes your **intent**. It lists which packages your project depends on and which version ranges are
acceptable.

Example:

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "zod": "^4.1.0"
  }
}
```

This does **not** pin one exact install result forever. It says: this project is compatible with Zod `4.x`, starting
from `4.1.0`.

`package-lock.json` describes the **exact resolved dependency tree** that was installed at a given moment, including
transitive dependencies.

That means:

* `package.json` = what we want
* `package-lock.json` = what we actually installed

## Why commit package-lock.json?

You should commit `package-lock.json` to version control because it makes installs reproducible.

Without a lockfile, two developers or a CI pipeline may install slightly different dependency trees on different days,
even when `package.json` did not change. That can lead to "works on my machine" issues, unexpected build failures, or
subtle behavior changes caused by transitive dependency updates.

Committing the lockfile gives the team:

* deterministic installs
* fewer surprises in CI
* easier debugging when dependency updates cause problems
* explicit reviewable diffs when dependencies change

## Version constraints

npm uses semantic versioning ranges in `package.json`.

Common examples:

* `1.2.3` → exactly this version
* `^1.2.3` → allow updates that stay within major version `1`
* `~1.2.3` → allow updates that stay within minor version `1.2`

In practice:

* `^1.2.3` can become `1.9.0`, but not `2.0.0`
* `~1.2.3` can become `1.2.9`, but not `1.3.0`

As a rule of thumb:

* use `^` when compatible minor and patch updates are acceptable
* use `~` when you want to be more conservative
* use an exact version only when you have a specific reason to pin it

## dependencies vs devDependencies

`dependencies` are packages required at runtime.

Typical examples:

* application libraries
* HTTP frameworks
* validation libraries
* SDKs used by production code

`devDependencies` are packages only needed to develop, test, build, lint, or synthesize the project.

Typical examples:

* TypeScript
* Vitest
* ESLint
* Prettier
* build tooling

This is partly **context dependent**. In Backpack, we often treat CDK constructs as `devDependencies`, because one
package commonly contains both the application code and the infrastructure code. In that setup, CDK is needed for
development, synthesis, and deployment, but not as a runtime dependency of the deployed app itself.

So the real question is not "what kind of package is this in general?", but rather: **does the deployed runtime need
it?**

## Core npm commands

### npm install

`npm install` installs dependencies using the current lockfile where possible, and updates the lockfile when dependency
changes require it.

Use it when:

* you added or removed a dependency
* you changed version constraints in `package.json`
* you want npm to resolve and write a new lockfile state

In short: `npm install` is the normal command for day-to-day dependency changes.

### npm ci

`npm ci` installs strictly from the current `package-lock.json`. It does not modify the lockfile and fails if
`package.json` and `package-lock.json` are out of sync.

Use it when:

* you want a clean reproducible install
* you are running in CI
* you want to verify the project exactly as locked

In short: `npm ci` = install according to the current lockfile.

### npm update

`npm update` updates installed packages to newer versions that still match the current version constraints in
`package.json`.

It does **not** mean "upgrade everything to the latest major". It stays within the intent already declared.

Use it when:

* you want fresher dependency versions without broad manual changes
* you want to pick up compatible fixes
* you want to address many audit findings in a controlled way

In many Backpack projects, `npm update` is often the most sensible first step when resolving vulnerable or outdated
dependencies.

## Extraneous dependencies

Extraneous dependencies are packages that are present in `node_modules` but not declared in your own `package.json`.

A common cause is importing a package directly in your code even though it only exists as a transitive dependency of
another package. If your code imports a package, you should declare it explicitly in your own `dependencies` or
`devDependencies`, even if it “happens to work” because another package pulled it in.

Relying on transitive dependencies is fragile:

* they can disappear after an update
* they make your dependency graph unclear
* they can break builds in CI or other environments

To enforce this, we use an ESLint rule that warns when you import packages that are not declared in your `package.json`.

## What is a peer dependency error?

A peer dependency error means one package expects your project to provide a compatible version of another package, but
npm cannot satisfy that expectation.

Common example:

* package A says it works with `typescript@^5`
* your project installs `typescript@6`
* npm reports a peer dependency conflict

This usually happens with plugins, adapters, and ecosystem tooling such as ESLint, TypeScript, or Vite
integrations.

In practice, a peer dependency error means:

* the package author has declared compatibility expectations
* your dependency tree currently violates them
* npm is warning that the combination may not work correctly

The right fix is usually to align versions or upgrade the packages involved, not to blindly suppress the error.

## npm scripts

npm scripts are commands defined in `package.json` under the `scripts` field.

Example:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "check": "run-p check:types check:lint check:format",
    "check:format": "prettier . --ignore-unknown --check",
    "check:lint": "eslint",
    "check:types": "tsc",
    "format": "prettier . --ignore-unknown --write",
    "lint": "eslint",
    "lint:fix": "eslint --fix",
    "test": "vitest run",
    "test:coverage": "vitest run --coverage",
    "test:watch": "vitest"
  }
}
```

Run them with:

```bash
npm run check
npm run check:lint
npm run test
```

### Passing flags to npm scripts

Use `--` to pass flags through to the underlying command.

Example:

```bash
npm run test -- --watch
npm run lint -- --fix
```

Everything after `--` is forwarded to the actual script command.

## npx

`npx` runs a package executable without requiring a global install.

Examples:

```bash
npx vitest
npx tsc --version
npx npm-check-updates
```

This is useful for one-off commands and local tooling. It helps avoid global version drift and ensures you run the tool
version appropriate for the project.

## npm audit

`npm audit` checks installed dependencies for known security vulnerabilities.

In our environment, this typically needs npmjs.org as an explicit registry:

```bash
npm audit --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org
```

This happens because Nexus requires **Sonatype Repository Firewall** to support `npm audit`, for which NS currently has
no license yet.

There is also:

```bash
npm audit fix --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org
```

However, that is often **not** what we want in Backpack projects as it is not compatible with our Nexus setup.

In practice, the better first step usually is:

```bash
npm update
```

Why?

* it updates packages within the currently declared version constraints
* it is often enough to resolve a large part of audit findings
* it keeps changes more aligned with the project's declared intent

So for Backpack, a common pattern is:

1. run `npm audit --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org`
2. inspect the findings
3. run `npm update`
4. re-run the audit
5. only make more targeted changes if needed

## npm ls

`npm ls` shows the installed dependency tree and is very useful for debugging.

Examples:

```bash
npm ls
npm ls typescript
npm ls eslint
```

This helps answer questions like:

* which version is actually installed?
* why is this package present?
* which package pulled in this transitive dependency?
* do I have duplicate versions in the tree?

When dependency behavior is confusing, `npm ls` is often one of the fastest ways to understand what npm actually
resolved.

## npm registries

We are using [Sonatype Nexus] as npm registry. This allows us to use private packages and to use custom npm mirrors.

Read more about Nexus in our dedicated [Nexus guide](./using-nexus.md).

[Sonatype Nexus]: https://nexus.topaas.ns.nl/

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/tooling/local-development.md'
---
# Local development

This how-to guide explains how to run and test Backpack serverless projects locally.

For REST APIs, the recommended approach is to use [Hono] together with `@backpack/hono`. This lets you mount existing
API Gateway Lambda handlers in a local Hono application, run them through [Vite], and test them without deploying to
AWS.

> \[!NOTE]
> This guide focuses on local development for REST APIs. Other Lambda event sources, such as SQS, EventBridge or
> DynamoDB streams, usually require a different local testing strategy.

## REST APIs

Backpack REST APIs often use AWS Lambda handlers behind API Gateway. In production, API Gateway receives the HTTP
request and invokes your Lambda handler with an API Gateway event.

For local development, you can use Hono as the local HTTP layer:

```txt
HTTP request
  -> Hono route
  -> fromAwsLambdaHandler()
  -> existing AWS Lambda handler
  -> HTTP response
```

This keeps your production handler unchanged, while giving you a fast local development server.

### Install Hono and `@backpack/hono`

First, install Hono and `@backpack/hono`:

```bash
npm install -D hono @backpack/hono
```

### Create a local Hono app

Create a `server.ts` file in the root of your project:

```ts
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { fromAwsLambdaHandler } from "@backpack/hono";

import { handler as helloWorld } from "./app/hello-world.lambda";
import { handler as updateBook } from "./app/update-book.lambda";

const app = new Hono();

app.get("/api/v1/hello", fromAwsLambdaHandler(helloWorld));
app.put("/api/v1/books/:isbn", fromAwsLambdaHandler(updateBook));

export default app;
```

The `fromAwsLambdaHandler()` adapter converts requests handled by Hono to API Gateway-style events and invokes your
existing Lambda handler.

> \[!WARNING]
> The local Hono app is intended for local development and tests. It does not fully emulate API Gateway.

### Add Vite

Install `vite` and `@hono/vite-dev-server`:

```bash
npm install -D vite @hono/vite-dev-server
```

Then add a `vite.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import devServer from "@hono/vite-dev-server";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    devServer({
      entry: "./server.ts",
    }),
  ],
});
```

You can also configure the Vite server, for example to use a fixed port:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import devServer from "@hono/vite-dev-server";

export default defineConfig({
  server: {
    port: 3000,
  },
  plugins: [
    devServer({
      entry: "./server.ts",
    }),
  ],
});
```

### Add an npm script

Add a `dev` script to your `package.json`:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite"
  }
}
```

Now start the local development server:

```bash
npm run dev
```

Your API is now available locally through the Hono dev server.

## Add local-only routes

Because your local server is a regular Hono app, you can add local-only routes next to your Lambda-backed routes. This
is useful for development helpers such as redirects, Swagger UI or serving an OpenAPI document.

For example:

```ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

import { Hono } from "hono";
import { swaggerUI } from "@hono/swagger-ui";
import { parse } from "yaml";

const app = new Hono();

// ...

app.get("/", (c) => c.redirect("/swagger-ui"));
app.get("/swagger-ui", swaggerUI({ url: "/openapi" }));
app.get("/openapi", (c) =>
  c.json(parse(readFileSync("./openapi.yaml", "utf-8"))),
);

export default app;
```

## Test your local Hono app

Hono apps can be tested directly through `app.request()`. This is useful when you want to test your local HTTP layer
without starting a real server.

```ts
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import app from "../server";

describe("server", () => {
  it("handles requests locally", async () => {
    const response = await app.request("/api/v1/hello");

    expect(response.status).toBe(200);
  });
});
```

If you prefer the familiar `@backpack/rest-client` API, use `createTestRestClient()` from `@backpack/hono`:

```ts
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import { createTestRestClient } from "@backpack/hono";

import app from "../server";

const restClient = createTestRestClient(app);

describe("server", () => {
  it("updates a book locally", async () => {
    const updatedBook = await restClient
      .url("/api/v1/books/978-6-2270-9353-7")
      .put({ title: "Man in the Mist" })
      .json();

    expect(updatedBook).toEqual({
      isbn: "978-6-2270-9353-7",
      title: "Man in the Mist",
    });
  });
});
```

## Mocking

Most serverless applications depend on cloud infrastructure and remote services. When running locally, you need to
decide which dependencies are real and which dependencies are mocked.

There is no single best option. A pragmatic local setup often combines a local HTTP server with either real cloud
infrastructure, local emulators or mocks.

## Cloud infrastructure

For cloud infrastructure such as DynamoDB tables, S3 buckets or SQS queues, there are two common approaches.

### Connect to a deployed AWS environment

You can run the API locally while connecting to real AWS resources in a development environment.

This is often the simplest option when:

* the infrastructure already exists;
* the data is safe to use from a local machine;
* personal AWS credentials are available;
* the risk of interfering with other developers is acceptable.

For example, your local config (`app-config.local-dev.ts`, `.env.local`) might point to a table in a development AWS
account:

```dotenv
BOOKS_TABLE_NAME=my-dev-stack-BooksTable123ABC
```

If multiple developers use the same AWS resources, make sure the application data is isolated. For example, use
developer-specific prefixes, test users or a separate stack.

### Run infrastructure locally

Alternatively, you can run local infrastructure using tools such as Docker Compose or service-specific emulators.

This is useful when:

* tests should not depend on a deployed AWS environment;
* developers need to work offline;
* the application needs isolated local state;
* using shared cloud resources would be risky or expensive.

For example, a project may run a local DynamoDB-compatible service and configure the AWS SDK client with a local
endpoint.

```dotenv
BOOKS_TABLE_NAME=books
DYNAMODB_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:8000
```

Keep in mind that local emulators may behave differently from real AWS services. Use them for fast feedback, but still
test important flows against real infrastructure.

## Remote services

For remote HTTP services, prefer mocking at the HTTP boundary.

Backpack provides `@backpack/mockserver-client` to configure and verify mock HTTP interactions in tests and local
development setups. This is useful when your API calls another service and you want deterministic local behavior.

A typical setup looks like this:

```txt
Local Hono API
  -> REST client
  -> Mock server
  -> configured mock response
```

For local development, you can run a mock server and point your service client to it through an environment variable:

```dotenv
REMOTE_SERVICE_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080
```

Then configure the responses needed for your scenario before calling your local API.

Use this approach when:

* the remote service is unavailable from your local machine;
* the remote service is slow or unstable;
* you need predictable responses for development or tests;
* you want to reproduce edge cases that are hard to trigger against the real service.

For more information, see the [
`@backpack/mockserver-client` API reference](/packages/@backpack/mockserver-client/index.md).

## Recommended local development setup

For most Backpack REST APIs, start with this setup:

1. Use Hono and `@backpack/hono` to run API Gateway Lambda handlers locally.
2. Use Vite and `@hono/vite-dev-server` for the local development server.
3. Setup a local configuration (e.g. `app-config.local-dev.ts` or `.env.local`).
4. Connect to real AWS development resources when that is safe and practical.
5. Mock remote HTTP services when deterministic behavior is more useful than calling the real service.
6. Add tests using either Hono's `app.request()` or `createTestRestClient()`.

This keeps local development close to the production Lambda handler model, while still giving you a fast feedback loop.

[Hono]: https://hono.dev/

[Vite]: https://vite.dev/

---

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/tooling/ecmascript-modules.md'
---
# Using ECMAScript modules (ESM)

Using native [ECMAScript modules] is the official way of developing JavaScript software today.
More and more projects and libraries are adopting this as industry standard.

Since support for [CommonJS] is declining, we recommend you
to move away from it.

## Migrating to ESM

The recommended way to use ESM in Node.js, is by adding `"type": "module"` to your `package.json`. This makes it the
default for your entire project:

```json
{
  "type": "module"
}
```

Make sure to also configure your Lambda Node.js CDK Construct accordingly:

```ts
new NodejsFunction(this, id, {
  bundling: {
    format: OutputFormat.ESM,
    // ...

    // enable if you find any issues with CommonJS modules that need "require()"
    //banner: "import { createRequire } from 'module';const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);",
  },
});
```

If you are using the `LambdaFunction` construct from `@backpack/cdk-constructs`, you don't have to do anything.

## TypeScript

In TypeScript, make sure to have `"module": "preserve"` in your `tsconfig.json`. This is because we're
transpiling with AWS CDK which uses [esbuild] under the hood.

> \[!TIP]
> You can also use [`@backpack/typescript-config`](../../packages/@backpack/typescript-config/index.md) which contains
> presets for your TSConfig.

Read more on [best practices for TypeScript](typescript.md).

## Switch from Jest to Vitest (recommended)

Jest has [experimental support for ESM][jest], which requires a lot of additional configuration. Therefore, we recommend
to use [Vitest] instead, which supports ESM out of the box.

Please read more about our [recommended tooling](./recommended-tools.md).

[ECMAScript modules]: https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html

[CommonJS]: https://blog.logrocket.com/commonjs-vs-es-modules-node-js/

[esbuild]: https://esbuild.github.io

[jest]: https://jestjs.io/docs/ecmascript-modules

[Vitest]: https://vitest.dev/

# Docker images

On this page, you can find some relevant Docker images. This might be useful for local development or
for integration testing.

## `amazon/dynamodb-local`

The [official Docker image][`amazon/dynamodb-local`] provided by Amazon to run DynamoDB locally.

Example of a `compose.yaml`, exposing it on port 4567 of your host:

```yaml
services:
  dynamodb:
    command: "-jar DynamoDBLocal.jar -sharedDb -inMemory"
    image: "amazon/dynamodb-local:latest"
    ports:
      - "4567:8000"
```

Note that this will not initialize any tables. To do so, you could set up another service that initializes your table
based on a JSON schema, using the AWS CLI. Example:

```yaml
services:
  dynamodb:
    command: "-jar DynamoDBLocal.jar -sharedDb -inMemory"
    image: "amazon/dynamodb-local:latest"
    ports:
      - "4567:8000"
    healthcheck:
      test:
        [
          "CMD-SHELL",
          '[ "$(curl -s -o /dev/null -I -w ''%{http_code}'' http://localhost:8000)" == "400" ]',
        ]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3

  dynamodb-setup:
    image: "amazon/aws-cli:latest"
    volumes:
      - "./app/resources/dynamodb-schemas:/tmp/dynamo"
    depends_on:
      dynamodb:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: "FAKEID"
      AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "FAKEKEY"
      AWS_REGION: "eu-west-1"
    entrypoint:
      - bash
    command: '-c "for f in /tmp/dynamo/*.schema.json; do aws dynamodb create-table --endpoint-url "http://dynamodb:8000" --cli-input-json file://"$${f#./}"; done"'
```

This will mount your local directory `app/resources/dynamodb-schemas` and search for `*.schema.json` files to create
tables.

For example, a `my-table.schema.json`:

```json
{
  "TableName": "MyTable",
  "AttributeDefinitions": [
    {
      "AttributeName": "foo",
      "AttributeType": "S"
    },
    {
      "AttributeName": "bar",
      "AttributeType": "S"
    }
  ],
  "KeySchema": [
    {
      "AttributeName": "foo",
      "KeyType": "HASH"
    },
    {
      "AttributeName": "bar",
      "KeyType": "RANGE"
    }
  ],
  "BillingMode": "PAY_PER_REQUEST"
}
```

[`amazon/dynamodb-local`]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DynamoDBLocal.UsageNotes.html

## `wiremock/wiremock`

A [Docker version][`wiremock/wiremock`] of [WireMock], useful to mock remote endpoints.

Example of a `compose.yaml`, exposing it on port 8081 of your host:

```yaml
services:
  wiremock:
    image: "wiremock/wiremock:latest"
    ports:
      - "8081:8080"
```

To interact with WireMock from a Vitest script, we
recommend [WireMock Captain](https://www.npmjs.com/package/wiremock-captain).

[`wiremock/wiremock`]: https://wiremock.org/docs/standalone/docker/

[WireMock]: https://wiremock.org/

## `localstack/localstack`

[LocalStack] is a fully functional local AWS cloud stack that allows you to develop and test cloud applications on your
local machine without actually using AWS services. It emulates a wide range of AWS services such as S3, Lambda,
DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, API Gateway, and many more.

Example of `compose.yaml` with LocalStack, mounting some DynamoDB schemas from `./app/resources/dynamodb-schemas` and
running `./init-aws-local.sh`. It has a custom health check added that waits for the init script to be completed.

```yaml
services:
  localstack:
    image: localstack/localstack:4.14.0
    volumes:
      - "./app/resources/dynamodb-schemas:/tmp/dynamo"
      - "./init-aws-local.sh:/etc/localstack/init/ready.d/init-aws.sh"
    environment:
      - DYNAMODB_IN_MEMORY=1
      - DYNAMODB_SHARE_DB=1
    ports:
      - '4566:4566'
      - '4510-4559:4510-4559'
    healthcheck:
      test: >
        curl -s http://localhost:4566/_localstack/init/ready | grep -q '"completed": true'
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 1m
      retries: 5
```

Example of `./init-aws-local.sh`, using [awslocal] from LocalStack.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
for f in /tmp/dynamo/*.schema.json; do
  awslocal dynamodb create-table --cli-input-json file://"${f#./}";
done
awslocal s3api create-bucket --bucket my-bucket
```

[LocalStack]: https://docs.localstack.cloud/

[awslocal]: https://github.com/localstack/awscli-local

# Standard CI/CD pipeline

Backpack provides a standard CI/CD pipeline for Azure DevOps.

> \[!NOTE]
> Platforms other than Azure DevOps are currently not supported.

## What's included?

* Quality checks (linting, formatting, testing)
* Security checks (npm audit)
* Static analysis (coverage reporting, SonarQube)
* Deployments (CDK deploy, Change API, API Management)
* Renovate for automatic dependency updates

## New projects

When generating a new Backpack project, a fully functional YAML pipeline is included automatically.

### Registering the pipeline

Make sure to register this YAML pipeline through the UI of Azure DevOps:

* Go to *Pipelines*, click *New pipeline*, select *Azure Repos Git* and choose your repository;
* Select *Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file*;
* Choose `.azure-devops/pipelines/ci.yml`;
* On the first run, you may need to authorize your service connections.

### Adding as Build Validation for Pull Requests

To make sure your pipeline runs as a validation step for your Pull Request:

* In Azure DevOps, go to *Settings* ⇒ *Repositories* and select your repository;
* Go to the *Policies* tab, scroll down and select your main branch;
* Add a **Build Validation** step and select your YAML pipeline.

## Existing projects

Use the `npx @backpack/cli generate-pipeline` Backpack CLI command to generate a fresh YAML pipeline
for your existing project. More information about this command can be found in the
[Backpack CLI documentation][generate-pipeline].

If you are unsure about switching, keep in mind that you can try it out in parallel to your existing pipeline without
any disruption.

[generate-pipeline]: ../../packages/@backpack/cli/index.md#generating-a-ci-cd-pipeline

## Service connections and variables

The standard pipeline depends on a number of **service connections** and **variables**
in Azure DevOps to work properly. Here is an overview.

Service connections:

* Nexus service connection — used to download npm packages from Nexus;
* AWS Service Connection — used to access your AWS account (provided by NS Cloud)
* Azure service connection — used for API Management deployments
* SonarQube service connection — to send code quality reports to SonarQube

Secrets:

* Azure DevOps PAT — to trigger API Management pipelines
* Change API credentials — to register changes in ServiceNow
* Nexus token — needed for Renovate to access Nexus
* GitHub PAT — for Renovate (optional)

Secrets should be stored in Variable Groups or in an Azure Key Vault.

## Example pipeline

You can check out our [Bookstore REST API] for an example of a CI/CD pipeline.

[Bookstore REST API]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/apps/bookstore-rest-api

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/cicd/renovate.md'
---
# Using Renovate

To keep your dependencies up to date, we recommend using [Renovate].

## How Backpack uses Renovate

The CI/CD team maintains a dedicated [Renovate guide on Confluence], which explains the standard setup and recommended
practices. Please refer to that guide for general background and usage details.

Backpack largely follows this approach, with one intentional deviation.

The Confluence guide promotes the use of centralized repositories:

* a `renovate-bot` repository for the Renovate pipeline, and
* a `renovate-config` repository for shared Renovate configuration.

Backpack, however, aims for fully self-contained repositories. For that reason, Renovate is configured to run from
within your project’s own repository and pipeline, rather than relying on centrally managed Renovate repositories.

However, this approach does not prevent you from using centralized repositories if you prefer.

## Setup a pipeline schedule

Ensure that Renovate runs daily. Note that most Renovate pre-defined schedules assume you are running before 4 AM (UTC
time by default).

Therefore, we recommend running it midnight.

```yaml
schedules:
  - cron: "0 0 * * *" # 12:00 AM UTC time
    displayName: Daily midnight schedule for Renovate
    always: true
    branches:
      include:
        - main
```

## Using the CI/CD brick

The following CI/CD brick can be used to run Renovate:

```yaml
- template: steps/maintain/renovate.yml@CICD
  parameters:
    # to only run Renovate for your own repository, make sure to include: 
    autodiscover: false
    repositories:
      - $(System.TeamProject)/$(Build.Repository.Name)
    # optional, but recommended (see CI/CD guide):
    githubToken: $(YOUR_GITHUB_TOKEN)
    # to pass a Nexus token to Renovate,
    # allowing it to update private packages such as Backpack:
    secrets:
      NEXUS_TOKEN: $(YOUR_NEXUS_TOKEN)
```

Check out its [documentation][Renovate CI/CD brick] for more details.

## Renovate config

You can use the following configuration as a starting point for your `renovate.json`:

```yaml
{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "extends": [ "config:recommended" ],
  "hostRules": [
    {
      "hostType": "npm",
      "matchHost": "nexus.topaas.ns.nl",
      "token": "{{ secrets.NEXUS_TOKEN }}",
      "authType": "Basic"
    }
  ],
  "addLabels": [ "renovate" ],
  "azure-pipelines": {
    "enabled": true
  },
  "packageRules": [
    {
      "matchPackagePatterns": [ "*" ],
      "matchManagers": [ "npm" ],
      "matchUpdateTypes": [ "patch", "minor" ],
      "groupName": "all minor and patch dependencies",
      "groupSlug": "all-minor-patch",
      "automerge": true,
      "autoApprove": true
    },
    {
      "extends": [ "schedule:weekly" ],
      "matchManagers": [ "azure-pipelines" ],
      "matchDepNames": [ "CICD/pipeline-templates" ],
      "versioning": "semver",
      "automerge": true,
      "autoApprove": true
    },
    {
      "matchDatasources": [ "azure-pipelines-tasks" ],
      "extractVersion": "^(?<version>\\d+)"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Renovate workflow

You can use the `automerge` and `autoApprove` options to automatically merge pull requests created by Renovate. However,
you should still regularly check for open Renovate PRs with failing jobs.

Also, make sure to deploy your project to production regularly to ensure that all dependencies are up to date.

[Renovate]: https://docs.renovatebot.com/

[Renovate guide on Confluence]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/TECHWIKI/pages/1253573344/CI+CD+-+Renovate+Tutorial

[Renovate CI/CD brick]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/CICD/_git/pipeline-templates?path=/steps/maintain/renovate.md&_a=preview

# Publishing documentation to Confluence

Want to get your documentation published to Confluence quickly and smoothly? Follow these steps!

## Step 1: Add the documentation template 📖

Start by creating a `docs` folder in your repo. Inside this folder, [copy these files](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/apps/docs/how-tos/docs-to-confluence/docs):

* `nsdocs.yml` — configures where in Confluence your docs will be published
* `_attributes.adoc` — for setting key attributes which are used in the template
* `apihomepage.adoc` — your API content

Make sure to replace all the `TODO` comments in these files with your API specific information.

::: code-group

```yml
# pick the page ID of the parent page you want to publish *under* from the page URL. This page will not be modified.
# Find it in Confluence by navigating to the page and looking at the URL in your browser.
default-parent-id: 153026795 # The default parent ID under which we document NSAPP apis

# your own space (e.g. ~john.doe), or a team space (e.g. MLAB)
space: MLAB

# pick any string that makes your project unique; e.g. a git URL
tenant: #TODO: add unique string
```

```adoc
:SONARQUBE_ID: //TODO: Add SonarQube ID, for example NSAPP_bookstore-demo-api
:SONARQUBE_TOKEN: ${SONARQUBE_TOKEN} # Injected by the build pipeline
:SONARQUBE_URL: https://sonarqube.topaas.ns.nl
:API_NAME: //TODO: Add API name in Azure API Management, for example bookstore-demo-api
:API_FRIENDLY_NAME: //TODO: Add human readable API name, for example Bookstore Demo API
:SLACK_CHANNEL: //TODO: Add your teams slack channel, for example backpack
:REPOSITORY_URL: //TODO: Add your repository URL, for example https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK

```

```adoc
= {API_FRIENDLY_NAME}

## Step 2: Publishing the docs from your pipeline ⚙️

To publish the docs automatically from your CI/CD pipeline, follow these steps:

### Adding secrets

By default, we use a library called `NSDocs` to manage the required secrets. Add the following:
::: tip
The `ConfluenceUserName` and `ConfluenceApiKey` secrets are already created in the [`NSDocs` library in the NSAPP Azure DevOps environment](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/NSAPP/_library?itemType=VariableGroups\&view=VariableGroupView\&variableGroupId=5319\&path=NSDocs). You only need to add the SonarQube token there.
:::

| Secret              | Key                              | Value                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|---------------------|----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| SonarQube token     | `SonarQubeToken-<your-api-name>` | Retrieve via:`https://sonarqube.topaas.ns.nl/api/project_badges/token?project=<YOUR_PROJECT_ID>`Example:`https://sonarqube.topaas.ns.nl/api/project_badges/token?project=NSAPP_homepage-bff` |
| Confluence username | `ConfluenceUsername`             | NS e-mail address without the `@ns.nl` part. Preferably use a functional account.                                                                                                                        |
| Confluence API key  | `ConfluenceApiKey`               | Generate here:[Atlassian documentation](https://support.atlassian.com/confluence-cloud/docs/manage-api-tokens-for-your-atlassian-account/)                                                           |

### Integrating into your pipeline

* Reference the NSDocs variable group (library) in your main pipeline file like this:
  ```yaml [ci.yaml]
  variables:
    - group: NSDocs
  ```
* Add the [docs.yml](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/apps/docs/how-tos/docs-to-confluence/pipeline/docs.yml)```yml
  parameters:
    - name: confluenceUsername
      type: string
    - name: confluenceApiKey
      type: string
    - name: nsdocsVersion
      type: string
      default: latest
    - name: docDir
      type: string
      default: ./docs
    - name: registryServiceConnection
      type: string
      default: NSPAAS-HARBOR-PUSH-PULL-$(System.TeamProject)
    - name: sonarqubeToken
      type: string
      default: ''

  jobs:
    - job: DeployDocs
      displayName: "Deploy docs"
      steps:
        - task: Docker@2
          displayName: "Login to Harbor"
          inputs:
            command: login
            containerRegistry: ${{ parameters.registryServiceConnection }}
        - script: |
            echo "Replacing \${SONARQUBE_TOKEN} with pipeline secret"
            sed -i "s|\${SONARQUBE_TOKEN}|$SONARQUBE_TOKEN|g" ${{ parameters.docDir }}/_attributes.adoc
          displayName: "Inject SonarQube token"
          env:
            SONARQUBE_TOKEN: ${{ parameters.sonarqubeToken }}
        - script: |
            docker run --rm -i -e "CONFLUENCE_USERPASS=${{ parameters.confluenceUsername }}@ns.nl:${{ parameters.ConfluenceApiKey }}" \
              -e "WORKDIR=${{ parameters.docDir }}" \
              -v "$(Build.SourcesDirectory):/project" \
              container-registry.nspaas.ns.nl/qes-public/docs-as-code:${{ parameters.nsdocsVersion }} publish
          displayName: "nsdocs publish"

  ```
* Integrate the `PublishDocs` template inside your main pipeline file like this:
  ```yaml [ci.yaml]
      - stage: PublishDocs
        displayName: "Publish docs"
        dependsOn: [ ]
        condition: |
          eq(variables.isMain, true)
        jobs:
          - template: ./ci/docs.yml
            parameters:
              confluenceUsername: $(ConfluenceUsername) # Retrieved from the NSDocs secret
              confluenceApiKey: $(ConfluenceApiKey) # Retrieved from the NSDocs secret
              nsdocsVersion: 0.1.9
              sonarqubeToken: $(SonarQubeToken-bookstore-demo-api) #TODO: Reference your own token from the NSDocs secret here. 
              docDir: apps/bookstore-rest-api/docs #TODO: Reference your own docs directory here.
  ```

With this, every pipeline run can automatically publish your updated docs to Confluence.

## Examples 🔍

Want inspiration or a quick start? Check out these examples:

* [Example Pull Request](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK/pullrequest/372322)
* [Example published Confluence page](https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MLAB/pages/639763509/Homepage+BFF)
* [Homepage BFF repository](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/NSAPP/_git/homepage-bff)
* [Bookstore REST API repository](https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/apps/bookstore-rest-api)

These will give you a clear idea of the setup and outcome.

## More information 📚

This how-to guide is using NSDocs to publish Asciidoc documentation to Confluence.
For more details, check out the [NSDocs documentation](https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/QES/pages/158240951/nsdocs)

# NS Cloud AWS

[NS Cloud AWS] is the dedicated cloud platform that enables teams at NS to build and run applications on AWS
in a standardized, secure, and compliant way. It provides a shared foundation with strong guardrails, so product
teams can focus on delivering business value instead of reinventing cloud fundamentals.

This page gives a high-level summary of the most important features and services.

## Landing zone

The **NS Cloud AWS landing zone** is the standardized baseline configuration for AWS accounts at NS.
Each workload account is automatically provisioned with this baseline and already complies with NS
security, networking, and governance requirements out of the box.

In practice, the landing zone provides:

* A predefined AWS account setup for **development**, **staging**, and **production** workloads.
* Centralized account management using **AWS Organizations**, including service control policies (SCPs).
* Strong guardrails, such as:
  * Region restrictions (only `eu-west-1` by default, with `eu-central-1` for disaster recovery or multi-region setups).
  * Mandatory tagging (for example `ApplicationServiceID`).
  * Protection of landing zone–managed resources.
* A standardized network setup:
  * A preconfigured VPC with public and private subnets spread across availability zones.
  * Central control over connectivity between accounts, on-premise, and the internet.
* Baseline security services enabled by default, such as GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Inspector.
* Centralized logging and monitoring foundations.
* Shared configuration values (for example VPC and subnet identifiers) exposed via **AWS Parameter Store**, so teams can
  reference them directly in infrastructure code (for example when using CDK).

Accounts are provisioned through a ServiceNow request and come “batteries included”: access, roles, logging,
networking, and security services are already configured.

For full details, see the [landing zone documentation].

> \[!TIP]
> To access landing zone resources in your infrastructure code,
> you can use the [LandingZone] CDK construct from `@backpack/cdk-constructs`.

## AWS accounts and identity

Each application runs in its own set of AWS workload accounts (development, staging, production),
fully isolated from other teams.

Access to AWS accounts is managed centrally via **IAM Identity Center (SSO)** and Entra ID groups.
Standard permission sets are provided (for example Reader, Developer, and Elevated Teams), and access
changes are requested through ServiceNow.

For exceptional situations, a controlled **break-glass procedure** exists to temporarily elevate permissions.
All such actions are audited and monitored by the security team.

## Service catalog

The **NS Cloud AWS service catalog** defines which AWS services are approved for use within NS Cloud AWS.

Key characteristics:

* A curated list of AWS services that are allowed in **staging and production** accounts.
* Development accounts are more permissive, allowing teams to experiment.
* Approved services are assessed against NS security and compliance requirements.
* Guardrails are enforced using AWS Organizations and SCPs (for example blocking non-approved services).
* New services can be requested when there is a clear use case and they meet the acceptance criteria.

Check the [service catalog] for the current list of approved services and request procedures.

## Operations, security, and cost ownership

NS Cloud AWS follows a clear responsibility split:

* **NS Cloud AWS team** operates the platform: landing zone, shared services, networking, identity, security
  guardrails, and overall platform reliability.
* **Application teams** operate their workloads: deployments, scaling, monitoring, incident response,
  performance, and cost optimization.

This follows the principle: *you build it, you run it, you own it*.

The platform provides tooling such as CloudWatch, Datadog, Security Hub, and cost management tools to support
teams in operating their services effectively.

## Security baseline

Security within NS Cloud AWS is based on **[NSCF 11 Security Baseline – Applicatie teams]**. This baseline defines
a layered set of **preventive**, **detective**, and **proactive** controls to reduce risk and ensure compliance by
default.

Application teams are encouraged to use standardized building blocks (e.g. Backpack) to embed security
controls early in their CI/CD pipelines, with findings and incidents automatically tracked and followed up through
central security processes.

[NS Cloud AWS]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/NSCAWS/overview

[landing zone documentation]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/NSCAWS/pages/455770915/NS+Cloud+AWS+Landing+Zone

[service catalog]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/NSCAWS/pages/463831257/NS+AWS+Service+Catalogus

[NSCF 11 Security Baseline – Applicatie teams]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/NSCAWS/pages/1702331145/NSCF+11+Security+Baseline+-+Applicatie+teams

[LandingZone]: ../../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/classes/LandingZone.md

# CDK snippets

These examples demonstrate how to configure CDK constructs following our best practices.

## AWS Lambda

See [`@backpack/cdk-constructs`][cdk-constructs] for our recommended AWS Lambda construct.

## Amazon API Gateway

See [`@backpack/cdk-constructs`][cdk-constructs] for our recommended API Gateway construct.

## Amazon DynamoDB

The following function creates a DynamoDB table with point-in-time recovery enabled:

```ts twoslash
import { Stack, RemovalPolicy } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { Table, Attribute, AttributeType, BillingMode } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-dynamodb';
import { AccountPrincipal, Effect, PolicyStatement } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam';

function createDynamoDbTable(
  this: Stack,
  id: string,
  options: { partitionKey: Attribute; sortKey?: Attribute },
) {
  return new Table(this, id, {
    partitionKey: options.partitionKey,
    sortKey: options.sortKey,
    billingMode: BillingMode.PAY_PER_REQUEST,
    pointInTimeRecoverySpecification: {
      pointInTimeRecoveryEnabled: true,
    },
    removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.RETAIN // or RemovalPolicy.DESTROY for "DEV
  });
}
```

## Amazon SNS topic

The following function creates an SNS topic, and arranges permissions for other AWS accounts to subscribe to it:

```ts twoslash
import { Stack } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { Topic } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-sns';
import { SqsSubscription } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-sns-subscriptions';
import { AccountPrincipal, Effect, PolicyStatement } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam';
import { IFunction } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda';

function createSnsTopic(
  this: Stack,
  id: string,
  options: { grantAwsAccountIds: string[]; publishingFunctions: IFunction[] }
) {
  const topic = new Topic(this, id, {
    displayName: id,
    topicName: id,
  });

  topic.addToResourcePolicy(
    new PolicyStatement({
      effect: Effect.ALLOW,
      actions: ['SNS:Subscribe'],
      principals: options.grantAwsAccountIds.map((awsAccountId) => new AccountPrincipal(awsAccountId)),
      resources: [topic.topicArn],
    }),
  );

  options.publishingFunctions.forEach((lambdaFunction) => topic.grantPublish(lambdaFunction));

  return topic;
}
```

## Amazon SQS queue

This function creates an SQS queue and subscribes to an SNS topic:

```ts twoslash
import { Stack, Duration } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { ITopic } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-sns';
import { Queue } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-sqs';
import { SqsEventSource } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-event-sources';
import { SqsSubscription } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-sns-subscriptions';
import { IFunction } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda';

function createSqsQueue(
  this: Stack,
  id: string,
  options: { lambdaFunction: IFunction; topic: ITopic }
) {
  const deadLetterQueue = new Queue(this, `${id}Dlq`, {
    retentionPeriod: Duration.days(14),
  });

  const queue = new Queue(this, id, {
    visibilityTimeout: Duration.seconds(60),
    receiveMessageWaitTime: Duration.seconds(0),
    deadLetterQueue: {
      queue: deadLetterQueue,
      maxReceiveCount: 1, // Maximum number of times a message can be received before being sent to DLQ
    },
  });

  options.lambdaFunction.addEventSource(
    new SqsEventSource(queue, {
      maxBatchingWindow: Duration.seconds(15),
      reportBatchItemFailures: true,
    }),
  );

  options.topic.addSubscription(new SqsSubscription(queue));

  return queue;
}
```

[cdk-constructs]: ../../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/index.md
