# Resource tagging

To improve observability and transparency, we recommend tagging your CDK resources.

## Recommended tags

The following standardized tags are recommended to be used in Backpack projects.

| Tag                    | Example            | Note                                                 |
|------------------------|--------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| `ApplicationServiceID` | asid0006615        | As registered in the CMDB                            |
| `Service`              | homepage-bff       | Prevent spaces to make sure Datadog applies same tag |
| `Application`          | ns\_app\_core        |                                                      |
| `Team`                 | team\_fundamentals  | Name of your team                                    |
| `Cluster`              | it\_co\_reizigers    |                                                      |
| `Department`           | rg2                |                                                      |
| `Owner`                | name.of.ownerns.nl | Your product owner                                   |
| `C`                    | 2                  | Confidentiality (1–3)                                |
| `I`                    | 3                  | Integrity (1–3)                                      |
| `A`                    | 1                  | Availability (1–3)                                   |
| `MC`                   | true               | Mission-critical (true/false)                        |
| `Env`                  | production         | Environment (test/staging/production)                |
| `Version`              | 1.2.3              | Semver or commit hash                                |

More information on these tags can be found at [Tagging Strategy] on Confluence.

[Tagging Strategy]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/OBS/pages/569770004/Tagging+strategy

## Where can I find the correct values?

Most tags are based on how your application is registered in [CMDB/ServiceNow].

[CMDB/ServiceNow]: https://nsprod.service-now.com/nav_to.do?uri=%2Fcmdb_ci_business_app_list.do

To make life easier, you can also retrieve those values directly from the command line using the [Backpack CLI]:

```bash
npx @backpack/cli retrieve-tags asid0006615
```

[Backpack CLI]: ../../packages/@backpack/cli/index.md#retrieve-tags

## Implementation guidelines

In a typical Backpack project, we recommend the following implementation:

* Most tags are "fixed". Add those to your `generic.yaml` CDK config.
* Environment-specific tags (such as `Env`) can be added to your `dev.yaml`, `stg.yaml` and `prd.yaml` CDK config
  files.
* The `Version` tag can be put in your `generic.yaml` file and bumped manually, or you retrieve it dynamically using
  Git.

### Example

If you are using `@backpack/cdk-config`, this is how you can apply the recommended tags:

```typescript
import { execSync } from "node:child_process";

import { App, Stack } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { loadConfig, cdkLoader } from "@backpack/config";
import { BuildConfig } from "../config/BuildConfig";

const cdk = new App();

const buildConfig = await loadConfig({
  schema: BuildConfig,
  loaders: [
    cdkLoader(cdk, { configDirectory: "./cdk/config" })
  ],
});

// in this example, we use the current commit hash as version:
const gitHash = execSync("git rev-parse HEAD").toString().trim(); 
const tags = { ...buildConfig.tags, version: gitHash };

const myStack = new Stack(cdk, `my-stack`, {
  // ...
  tags: tags, // apply tags to all resources in this stack
});
```

### Validating tags

Backpack also provides a nice validation utility to ensure that your tags conform to the recommended tags:

```typescript

import { validateTags } from "@backpack/cdk-constructs";

// ... determine tags (see above)

// will only print warnings:
await validateTags(tags);

// will throw errors and block deployments:
await validateTags(tags, { failOnError: true });

// you can also pass a Stack instance, improving error messages:
await validateTags(yourStack);
```

### Automatically resolving tags

Backpack also provides a nice utility to automatically resolve tags from the CMDB:

```typescript
import { Stack } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { resolveAndApplyTags } from "@backpack/cdk-constructs";

const stack = new Stack();

await resolveAndApplyTags(stack, "asid0123456", {
  additionalTags: {
    Service: "my-service",
    Version: "1.2.0",
  },
  // optionally, you can cache the results to avoid unnecessary API calls:
  cache: {
    path: "./cdk/.tags-cache.json",
  }
});
```

# Optimizing your AWS Lambda

Here are some recommendations for optimizing your AWS Lambda.

## Choose the right memory and timeout

Memory size:

* In AWS Lambda functions, more memory leads to more CPU.
* Start with something like 512–1024 MB for typical Node.js APIs
* Measure with metrics:
  * If execution time is high, but memory usage is low: try more memory.
  * If memory usage is near 100%: increase memory as well.

Timeouts:

* Do not leave the timeout at 15 minutes "just in case".
* Set it close to the expected max runtime (e.g. 3 seconds for REST APIs, 30–60s for batch operations).
* Add alarms if it approaches the limit and on timeouts.

## Optimize cold starts and bundle size

A *cold start* is the initialization phase when a Lambda instance is created.

### Keep the init phase lean

* Code at the top level (outside the handler) runs on every cold start.
* Only put what truly needs to be global there: e.g. DI bootstrapping, retrieving config & secrets, etc.
* Put heavy work inside the handler if it’s not always needed.

### Optimize your bundle size

* Bundle your code in one small (minified) JS file.
* Tree-shake and remove unused dependencies.

> \[!TIP]
> To analyze the bundle size of an individual Lambda, you can pass `metafile: true` in the `bundling` options of your
> Lambda CDK construct.
>
> This will emit an `index.meta.json` file in your CDK output directory. You can upload this meta file into the
> esbuild [bundle size analyzer tool](https://esbuild.github.io/analyze/) for more insights of your bundle.

### More on cold start optimization

* https://medium.com/@adtanasa/size-is-almost-all-that-matters-for-optimizing-aws-lambda-cold-starts-cad54f65cbb

## Reuse connections and clients

Node.js Lambdas reuse the execution environment between invocations, so you can cache things.

Create these once on top level:

* Database clients (DynamoDB, RDS, Mongo, etc.)
* HTTP clients
* AWS SDK clients
* Configuration objects

Example:

```ts
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb";

const client = new DynamoDBClient(/* ... */); // or bootstrap with a DI framework

export const handler = async (event) => {
  // reuse `client`, no re-creation
};
```

## Write efficient async Node.js code

Avoid blocking the event loop:

* Don’t use sync functions from `fs`, `crypto`, `zlib`, etc. on large data. Use their async/promisified variants
  instead.
* Don’t do big CPU-heavy loops in JS if you can offload to:
  * Other services (e.g., Step Functions, separate batch Lambdas)
  * Native libraries / specialized services

Use async/await cleanly:

* Make sure you await all promises;
* When possible, await promises in parallel with `Promise.all()`:

```ts
// good:
const [user, orders] = await Promise.all([
  getUser(userId),
  getOrders(userId),
]);
```

# Configuration & secrets

This guide provides a pragmatic approach how to deal with configuration.

## Use structured configuration objects

Avoid reading `process.env` all over the codebase. Instead, define **one configuration object** that represents
everything your service needs in a structured way.

For example:

* `app`: name, stage, logging/telemetry
* `clients`: base URLs, timeouts, retries
* `features`: feature flags

This makes configuration discoverable, testable, and easier to reason about.

## Validate configuration at startup

TypeScript types don’t protect you at runtime. Always validate configuration when the Lambda starts, and fail fast if
something is missing or invalid.

Example with `@backpack/config` and `zod`:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

export const AppConfig = z.object({
  app: z.object({
    name: z.string(),
    env: z.enum(["dev", "stg", "prd"]),
  }),
  clients: z.object({
    foo: z.object({
      baseUrl: z.string().url(),
      timeoutMs: z.number().positive().default(500),
    }),
  }),
  secrets: z.object({
    dbCredentialsSecretId: z.string().min(1),
  }),
});

export type AppConfig = z.infer<typeof AppConfig>;
```

Load once at startup and reuse:

```ts
import { loadConfig } from "@backpack/config";

export const config = await loadConfig({
  schema: AppConfig,
  loaders: [/* ... */],
});
```

Check out the [API reference](../../packages/@backpack/config/index.md) of `@backpack/config`
for more examples.

## What about secrets?

Secrets can be modeled as **part of your config object**, even though their *values* are stored elsewhere.

Best practice:

* Secrets live in **AWS Secrets Manager**
* Resolve secrets once per execution environment (cold start) and cache them

Example pattern:

```ts
const secretId = config.secrets.dbCredentialsSecretId;
const dbCredentials = await secrets.getJsonSecret(secretId);
```

This keeps your configuration consistent and typed.

## Decide where to store what

A practical split:

* **Environment variables**: small values and (CDK) references (e.g. DynamoDB table ARNs)
* **Config files / defaults**: structured non-secret config
* **Secrets Manager**: credentials, tokens, private keys

## Keep configuration immutable and injectable

* Load config once; treat it as immutable
* Pass config into constructors/factories
* Avoid hidden reads from `process.env` deep inside modules

This greatly improves testability and predictability.

## Make failures obvious and early

* Validate config at startup
* Fail fast with clear error messages
* Never log secret values

# Project structure

How to organize your project, depends on your use case and architecture.

## Single npm workspace

A typical Backpack project currently has a single `package.json`, representing a single npm workspace.

Its directory structure may look like this:

* `app/` - contains the (TypeScript) source files of your serverless app
* `cdk/` - contains your infrastructure code for AWS CDK
  * `bin/` - contains the entry point(s) for AWS CDK
  * `config/` - environment-specific configuration for your infrastructure
  * `lib/` - contains (TypeScript) source files for your infrastructure-as-code
* `docs/` - any system documentation for your project
* `test/` - any acceptance/integration tests

## Using npm workspaces (experimental)

You can also choose for multiple separate npm workspaces. For example:

* Infrastructure code (CDK)
* Backend (REST API)
* Frontend (UI)

This pattern is useful when adopting a mono-repo approach as it allows for more fine-grained dependency management at
the package level.

> \[!TIP] Feedback requested!
> We are considering adopting npm workspaces into Backpack. If you have any feedback regarding this,
> we are happy to hear your thoughts.

## Hexagonal design

[Hexagonal architecture] separates your app’s core **domain logic** from the outside world using **ports** (interfaces)
and **adapters** (implementations). It makes your domain independent, so things like databases or REST endpoints can be
swapped without touching business logic.

Pros:

* Easy to test and maintain
* Swappable external parts (e.g., APIs, DBs)
* Clean separation of concerns

Cons:

* More boilerplate and mapping needed
* Can be overkill for small apps

[Hexagonal architecture]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexagonal_architecture_\(software\)

More information on this architecture, and how to apply it on AWS Lambda:

* [Hexagonal architecture pattern](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/hexagonal-architecture.html)
* [Developing evolutionary architecture with AWS Lambda](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/developing-evolutionary-architecture-with-aws-lambda/)

# Dependency injection

When your serverless app becomes bigger, it might be useful to adopt dependency injection principles.

## Benefits

* **Easier testing**: real dependencies can easily be replaced with mocks or fakes for isolated unit testing.
* **Loose coupling**: classes depend on abstractions (interfaces) rather than concrete implementations, making the code
  more flexible and maintainable.
* **Better organization**: encourages separation of concerns, leading to cleaner, modular code.
* **Reusability**: classes become more modular and can work with different dependencies in various contexts.
* **Improved maintainability**: dependencies can be swapped or updated with minimal code changes.

## Tips & tricks

For serverless projects, we have the following recommendations:

* Make sure to create and bootstrap your DI container during the cold start of your lambda, to utilize performance
  boosts;
* Reuse services by providing them as a "singleton": this will make sure instances are reused between separate
  lambda invocations;
* If using classes, use constructor injection as much as possible, to maximize type-safety and to easily see what
  dependencies a class needs;
* Using a single shared DI container for multiple lambdas may lead to bundles sizes that are larger than necessary. This
  can be solved by using tree-shakable tokens (if the chosen library allows it), or by using separate DI containers.
  Read more about [analyzing your bundle size](../infrastructure/lambda-optimization.md).

## Recommended libraries

* [Needle DI](https://needle-di.io/): features tree-shakable tokens, and uses native
  ECMAScript decorators, eliminating the need for decorator metadata.
* [InversifyJS](https://github.com/inversify/InversifyJS): an older but wider used library. Requires TypeScript decorator
  metadata. Make sure to configure it with `defaultScope: 'Singleton'`.

## Example with Needle DI

Here is a simple example using [`@needle-di/core`][Needle DI] as DI library:

::: code-group

```ts [add-book.handler.ts]
import { bootstrapAsync } from "@needle-di/core";
import { defineRestLambda } from "@backpack/aws-lambda";

// on cold start, bootstrap a new instance with dependency injection
const addBookLambda = await bootstrapAsync(AddBookLambda);

// AWS Lambda handler
export const handler = defineRestLambda((event) => {
  return addBookLambda.handle(event);
});
```

```ts [add-book.lambda.ts]
import { injectable, inject } from "@needle-di/core";
import type { APIGatewayProxyEvent, APIGatewayProxyResult } from "aws-lambda";

import { Book } from "../models";

@injectable()
export class AddBookLambda {
  constructor(private readonly bookStore = inject(BookStoreService)) {}

  public async handle(event: APIGatewayProxyEvent): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult> {
    const book = parseBody(event).json({ validated: Book });

    await this.bookStore.insertBook(book);

    return jsonOk(book);
  }
}
```

```ts [book-store.service.ts]
import { inject, injectable } from "@needle-di/core";

import type { Book } from "./models";

/**
 * The BookStore service. Example of a service that contains domain logic.
 */
@injectable()
export class BookStoreService {
  constructor(private readonly booksRepository = inject(BooksRepository)) {}

  /**
   * Inserts a book.
   */
  public async insertBook(book: Book): Promise<void> {
    // additional logic

    await this.booksRepository.insert(book);
  }

  // ...
}
```

:::

Check out the [documentation of Needle DI][Needle DI] to learn more.

[Needle DI]: https://needle-di.io/

---
# Schema validation with Zod

Runtime validation is an essential part of building robust Node.js applications. In modern TypeScript codebases, we
recommend using [Zod] to validate JSON payloads, API responses, and other external data exchange.

This guide explains **why** you need Zod, **when** to apply it, and **how** to use it.

[Zod]: https://zod.dev/

## Why strict type-safety is not enough

TypeScript prevents many errors through compile-time checks. However, as soon as you receive data from an external or
untrusted source — such as JSON from an API, user input, or a file — TypeScript can no longer guarantee its shape at
runtime.

Therefore:

* Use `unknown` for all untrusted input.
* Enforce a *runtime* check with Zod before using the data.

Avoid casting `unknown` data to a specific type without validation. Such casts can easily become single points of
failure, where an unexpected data structure leads to runtime errors or incorrect processing.

## When to use runtime validation

Use runtime validation whenever data enters your system from outside your trust boundary.

### Typical scenarios

* **AWS Lambda handlers**: e.g. after `JSON.parse(event.body)`
* **HTTP clients**: e.g. [Fetch API], [XMLHttpRequest], [Axios] or any other HTTP client
* **Message queues / events**: e.g. SNS/SQS, EventBridge, Kafka messages
* **Files and configuration**: e.g. reading JSON, YAML, or other structured content
* **Environment variables**: e.g. `process.env.*` in Node.js

[Fetch API]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API

[XMLHttpRequest]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest

[Axios]: https://axios-http.com/docs/intro

## Using Zod for schema-based validation

Zod is a schema-first validation library for TypeScript. It provides:

* Runtime validation
* Compile-time type inference
* Composable schemas
* Clear error information

### Basic example

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

// define your schema
const Person = z.object({
  name: z.string(),
  age: z.number().int().min(0),
});

// infer the TypeScript type from the schema
type Person = z.infer<typeof Person>;

function parsePerson(jsonData: unknown): Person {
  // parse will validate and either return a Person or throw a ZodError
  return Person.parse(jsonData);
}

const person = parsePerson(JSON.parse('{"name":"Ada Lovelace","age":36}'));
```

Pattern:

* All external data is initially typed as `unknown`.
* You pass it to a `parse*` function that uses a Zod schema.
* The returned value is fully type-safe to use in your application.

## Handling validation errors

When using Zod in a Node.js application, especially in REST APIs, you should follow a consistent strategy for handling
validation errors.

* **Fail fast**: validate as early as possible in the request flow.
* **Add context**: log where and why validation failed.
* **Respond appropriately**: return an HTTP 400 response for invalid HTTP requests.

## Example with HTTP 400 response

For REST APIs, it is recommended to respond with HTTP 400 on validation failures. Optionally, you can implement
[Problem Details for HTTP APIs][Problem Details] (RFC 9457) to standardize your error responses.

[Problem Details]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

type CreateUserRequest = z.infer<typeof CreateUserRequest>;
const CreateUserRequest = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(1),
  email: z.string().email(),
});

export async function handler(event: { body: string }) {
  try {
    const rawBody: unknown = JSON.parse(event.body);
    const body: CreateUserRequest = CreateUserRequest.parse(rawBody);

    // ... safe to use `body` here
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof z.ZodError) {
      return {
        statusCode: 400,
        body: JSON.stringify({
          title: "Invalid request",
          type: "/problems/invalid-request",
          status: 400,
          detail: "Request body does not match the expected format.",
          errors: error.errors,
        }),
      };
    }

    // unhandled error, rethrow or map to HTTP 500
    throw error;
  }
}
```

For more guidance and utilities on error handling, check out the [error handling guide](./error-handling.md).

## Practical patterns for Node.js projects

### Group schemas by feature or domain

Organise Zod schemas close to the code where they are used, for example:

```text
src/
  users/
    user.model.ts
    user.service.ts
    user.controller.ts
  orders/
    order.model.ts
    order.service.ts
```

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

export const User = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  name: z.string(),
  email: z.string().email(),
});

export type User = z.infer<typeof User>;
```

### Validate environment variables

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

type Env = z.infer<typeof Env>;
const Env = z.object({
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(3000),
  // ...
});

export const env: Env = Env.parse(process.env);
```

Even better is to use `@backpack/config` package for this.
Check out its [API reference](../../packages/@backpack/config/index.md).

### Use `.safeParse()` when you cannot throw

In some workflows you do not want to throw on validation errors but handle them explicitly:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

const Payload = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  value: z.number(),
});

function handleMessage(message: unknown) {
  const result = Payload.safeParse(message);

  if (!result.success) {
    // handle validation error (log, dead-letter queue, metrics, etc.)
    console.error("Invalid payload", result.error);
    return;
  }

  const payload = result.data;
  // safe to use `payload` here
}
```

### Compose schemas for nested data

Zod encourages composition and reuse:

```ts
type Address = z.infer<typeof Address>;
const Address = z.object({
  street: z.string(),
  city: z.string(),
  postalCode: z.string(),
});

type User = z.infer<typeof User>;
const User = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  name: z.string(),
  address: Address, // or z.lazy(() => Address) if it is declared later
});
```

## When not to use Zod

While Zod is useful, it does not need to be used everywhere.

Validation is typically recommended when:

* Handling untrusted input (external JSON, HTTP, queues, files, env vars).
* Dealing with complex object structures.
* Maintaining contracts between services or teams.
* Building public-facing APIs or libraries.

Validation is optional when:

* Working with purely internal data where all producers and consumers are under your control.
* Writing small internal scripts with well-known inputs.
* Optimizing extremely performance-critical code paths where validation overhead is a concern (and input is already
  guaranteed safe).

In those internal and performance-critical cases, you may rely more on TypeScript’s static type system and direct object
construction, as long as the trust boundary is clear.

# Error handling

Error handling in JavaScript can be challenging. On this page, you’ll find some practical guidelines and design patterns
to help you handle errors more reliably in your code.

## Common design patterns

The most common way to handle errors in JavaScript is with a `try`/`catch` block.

However, this approach can become messy in larger codebases, especially with asynchronous code. Depending on your style
and context, consider one of the following patterns:

* **`Result` union type** – a simple way to make success and failure explicit, useful for local or synchronous error
  handling.
* **`AsyncResult` monad** – an extension of `Promise` that works well for asynchronous flows and functional-style
  programming.

You can read more about these approaches on the [design patterns](./error-handling/design-patterns.md) page.

## Best practices

* Recover from errors as close to the source as possible — or let them propagate to a global error handler.
* Centralize logging in one place, using appropriate log levels. Avoid logging the same error multiple times.
* Always throw instances of `Error` (or subclasses), include a `cause` when rethrowing, and provide clear and actionable
  messages.
* Be careful not to log or expose sensitive data such as tokens, credentials, or personal information.

## Error handling in REST APIs

For guidance on handling errors in REST APIs, we wrote [a dedicated in-depth guide](./error-handling/rest-apis.md).

---

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/development/error-handling/design-patterns.md'
---
# Design patterns for error handling

On this page, we’ll take a deeper look at different design patterns for error handling in JavaScript/TypeScript.

## Why error handling?

There are two main reasons to add explicit control flow around errors:

1. **Consuming the error** – when you want to act on the error (e.g. logging, metrics, or side effects).
2. **Recovering from the error** – when you want to recover gracefully and provide a fallback value.

## Common issues with try/catch

Using JavaScript’s built-in `try`/`catch` flow is straightforward, but can lead to several problems.

Consider the following example:

```typescript{1,5,8}
let value: number; // issue #1
try {
  value = mightFail();
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof MyError) { // issue #2
    value = 10;
  } else {
    throw error; // issue #3
  }
}

console.log('Got value', value);
```

1. **No try/catch expressions** – JavaScript doesn’t support `try`/`catch` as an expression.
   This forces you to declare variables outside the block and use `let` instead of `const`.

2. **Type uncertainty** – since `catch` can receive anything, you need explicit type checks
   or assertions to handle specific error types.

3. **Awkward rethrowing** – when catching only certain errors, you often need to rethrow others,
   which can make control flow harder to follow.

## Using Promises

JavaScript already includes a great mechanism for handling both success and failure: the `Promise`.

Although promises are often associated with asynchronous code, they can also simplify error handling in synchronous
functions by wrapping them.

```typescript
import { promiseTry } from "@backpack/error-handling/promises";

const value = await promiseTry(() => mightFail()) // ES2023 alternative to Promise.try()
  .then((r) => r * 2) // success path
  .catch(() => 10);   // fallback value

console.log("Got value", value);
```

An additional benefit: if your code later becomes asynchronous, no refactoring will be needed.

::: warning Common pitfall
When using Promises, it’s tempting to combine `async/await` with a `try/catch` block.
However, this reintroduces the issues discussed earlier:

```typescript
let value: string;
try {
  value = await myPromise();
} catch {
  value = "fallback value";
}
```

Instead, you can handle the error directly with .catch():

```typescript
const value = await myPromise().catch(() => "fallback value");
```

:::

## `AsyncResult` — Promise on steroids

The [`@backpack/error-handling`] package provides several utilities to make error handling cleaner and more expressive.

One of them is the `AsyncResult` class — an enhanced version of `Promise` that offers higher-order
methods for handling results and errors in a more declarative way:

```typescript
import { AsyncResult } from "@backpack/error-handling/async-result";

const value = await AsyncResult
  .try(() => mightFail())
  .map((r) => r * 2)
  .onFailure(() => console.log("Something went wrong"))
  .recoverIfInstanceOf(MyCustomError, () => "fallback-1")
  .orElse("fallback-2");

console.log("Got value", value);
```

We recommend this approach for most cases, especially in asynchronous or API-driven contexts
(e.g. global error handling in REST APIs).

Check out [`@backpack/error-handling`] for the full API reference and examples.

## Embracing the `Result` type

Another approach is to use a `Result` type (sometimes called a *monad* in functional programming).

[Many languages][Result] provide this construct — it’s a simple wrapper that represents either a successful result
or an error. It allows explicit and type-safe error handling without exceptions.

In TypeScript, a `Result` can be modeled as a union type:

```ts
type Result<TValue, TError> = Success<TValue> | Failure<TError>;

export interface Success<T> {
  value: T;
}

export interface Failure<E> {
  error: E;
}
```

The [`@backpack/error-handling`] package provides a ready-to-use implementation.

You can create a `Result` using the `runCatching()` helper:

```ts twoslash
import { runCatching } from "@backpack/error-handling/result";

function mightFail(): number {
  /* ... */
  return 42;
}

class MyCustomError extends Error { /* ... */ }

const result = runCatching(() => mightFail(), MyCustomError);

if (result.failed) {
  console.warn("Got custom error", result.error);
  //                                      ^?
} else {
  console.log("Got value", result.value);
}
```

This approach is ideal for synchronous code or situations where exceptions are undesirable.

Learn more in the [`@backpack/error-handling`] API reference.

[Result]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Result_type

[`@backpack/error-handling`]: ../../../packages/@backpack/error-handling/index.md

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/development/error-handling/rest-apis.md'

# Error handling in REST APIs

Backpack provides several utilities and guidelines to help you handle errors consistently in REST APIs.

## RFC-9457 Problem details

Just returning a generic HTTP 500 error to the client is often not enough, you might want to provide more information.

That’s where the [RFC 9457 Problem][Problem] standard comes in. It defines a consistent JSON format for
communicating detailed error information:

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
 "type": "/problems/out-of-credit",
 "status": 403,
 "title": "You do not have enough credit.",
 "detail": "Your current balance is 30, but that costs 50.",
 "balance": 30
}
```

Backpack includes a `ProblemError` class to make creating such responses easy:

```ts twoslash
import { ProblemError } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

throw new ProblemError({
  type: "/problems/out-of-credit",
  status: 403,
  title: "You do not have enough credit.",
  detail: "Your current balance is 30, but that costs 50.",
  balance: 30
});
```

Or you can create your own custom subclass, so you can parametrize it and reuse it across your application:

```ts twoslash
import { ProblemError } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

class OutOfCreditProblem extends ProblemError {
  constructor(balance: number, message: string) {
    super({
      type: "/problems/out-of-credit",
      status: 403,
      title: "You do not have enough credit.",
      detail: message,
      balance: balance
    });
  }
}
```

Additionally, you can use one of the pre-defined subclasses such as `UnauthorizedProblem` or `NotFoundProblem`. Check
out the [API reference](../../../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/rest/index.md#rfc-9457-problem-details) for the full list.

## Global error handling

When errors are not explicitly handled, your Lambda function will return a generic 500 error. It’s often better to
centralize logging and convert errors into standardized responses using a global error-handling chain.

Here is an example how you can achieve this with `AsyncResult`:

```ts twoslash
import { parseRequest, ProblemError, problemErrorConverter, problemResult, jsonResult } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import type { APIGatewayProxyEvent, APIGatewayProxyResult } from "aws-lambda";
import { z } from "zod";
import { AsyncResult } from "@backpack/error-handling/async-result";

export class GetBookLambda {
  public async handle(event: APIGatewayProxyEvent): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult> {
    return (
      AsyncResult
        // wrap your logic that may fail
        .try(() => this.getBook(event))

        // if successful, return a success response
        .map((book) => jsonResult(book, { statusCode: 200 }))

        // apply centralized logging
        .onFailure(yourErrorLogger())

        // convert known errors into structured responses
        .recoverIfInstanceOf(YourCustomError, yourErrorConverter()) // custom
        .recoverIfInstanceOf(ProblemError, problemErrorConverter()) // default from Backpack

        // for unhandled errors, return a generic problem response
        .orElse(
          problemResult({
            type: "/problems/internal-server-error",
            title: "Internal Server Error",
            detail: "An unknown error occurred.",
            status: 500,
          }),
        )
    );
  }

  /** The actual logic that may fail. */
  private async getBook(event: APIGatewayProxyEvent) {
    const request = parseRequest(event);
    const isbnSchema = z.string().length(13);
    
    // any validation error here is handled automatically
    // by the "problemErrorConverter":
    const isbn = request.getPathParameter("isbn", { validated: isbnSchema });

    const book = undefined; /* ... imagine actual logic here */

    if (book === undefined) {
      // will be handled automatically by "problemErrorConverter":
      throw new BookNotFoundError(isbn);
    }

    return book;
  }
}

/** Example of an RFC-9457 compliant problem error. */
class BookNotFoundError extends ProblemError {
  constructor(isbn: string) {
    super({
      type: "/problems/book-not-found",
      status: 404,
      title: "Book not found",
      detail: `Book ${isbn} was not found.`,
    });
  }
}

/** Example of a centralized logger. */
function yourErrorLogger() {
  return (error: unknown) => {
    // apply logging here...
    console.error("Got unhandled error", error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error));
  };
}

class YourCustomError extends Error {
  /* ... */
}

/** Example of a custom error handler that converts a specific error into a problem response. */
function yourErrorConverter() {
  return (error: YourCustomError) => {
    // handle the error here and return a proper response...

    return problemResult({
      type: "/problems/custom-error",
      title: "Custom Error",
      detail: error.message,
      status: 418,
    });
  };
}
```

[Problem]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html#name-the-problem-details-json-ob

## Reusing your error handlers

When implementing multiple endpoints, you’ll likely want to reuse your error-handling chain to avoid duplication.

A simple (and recommended) way is to extract it into a base handler class:

```ts
export abstract class DefaultRestHandler {
  public async handle(event: APIGatewayProxyEvent): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult> {
    const request = parseRequest(event);

    return AsyncResult
      .try(() => this.handleRequest(request))
      // your reusable error-handling chain:
      //.onFailure(...)
      //.orElseGet(...)
      // etc
  }

  public abstract handleRequest(request: Request): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult>;
}
```

Alternatively, for a more functional approach, you can express your error-handling pipeline as a reusable function using
`@backpack/error-handling/promises`:

```ts
import { ProblemError, problemErrorConverter, problemResult } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import { catchAll, onFailure, orElse, recoverIfInstanceOf } from "@backpack/error-handling/promises";

export function yourErrorHandler() {
  return catchAll(
    onFailure(yourErrorLogger()),

    recoverIfInstanceOf(YourCustomError, yourErrorConverter()), // custom
    recoverIfInstanceOf(ProblemError, problemErrorConverter()), // default from Backpack

    orElse(
      problemResult({
        type: "/problems/internal-server-error",
        title: "Internal Server Error",
        detail: "An unknown error occurred.",
        status: 500,
      }),
    ),
  );
}
```

You can now apply this error handling simply with:

```ts
AsyncResult
  .try(() => yourLogic())
  .recover(yourErrorHandler())
```

# Working with date and time ⏱️

This page explains how Backpack recommends working with date and time, and clarifies the differences between **UTC,
offsets, and time zones**.

## Recommendation: use Temporal

Backpack **strongly recommends using the [Temporal API]** for all new date and time logic.

[Temporal API]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Temporal

Temporal provides a clear, explicit model for:

* absolute moments in time
* local calendar values
* time zones and DST rules
* safe and predictable arithmetic

### Using Temporal in Node.js

At the time of writing, Temporal is not yet available natively in Node.js. Until then, we recommend using [
`temporal-polyfill`][temporal-polyfill], which follows the official Temporal specification and is
forward-compatible with the native implementation:

```bash
npm install temporal-polyfill
```

Usage:

```ts
import { Temporal } from "temporal-polyfill";

console.log(`It is now ${Temporal.Now.instant()}`);
```

[temporal-polyfill]: https://www.npmjs.com/package/temporal-polyfill

### Why Temporal?

Temporal is the recommended way to work with date and time in Backpack.

Compared to the built-in `Date`, Temporal is **explicit, immutable, and DST-safe by design**.\
There are no implicit time zones, no surprising conversions, and no silent arithmetic bugs.

Compared to libraries like [Luxon], [date-fns], or [Day.js], Temporal goes one step further:
those libraries improve ergonomics, but they are still built on top of `Date` and inherit its limitations.

Temporal is different because it is:

* a **language-level standard**, not a wrapper
* based on **explicit types** (`Instant`, `PlainDateTime`, `ZonedDateTime`)
* designed to make **invalid or ambiguous states hard to represent**

[Luxon]: https://moment.github.io/luxon/

[date-fns]: https://date-fns.org/

[Day.js]: https://day.js.org/

## Important concepts

* `Instant` represents an exact moment on the global timeline.
* An **offset** (`+01:00`, `+02:00`) is just a numeric difference from UTC at a specific moment.
* A **time zone** (`Europe/Amsterdam`) is a *rule set* that determines which offset applies at which time (including
  DST).

## Why offsets are not time zones

Offsets represent a moment accurately, but lack the contextual rules required for planning or business logic.

An offset only answers:

> “How far from UTC is this moment?”

A time zone answers:

> “Which offset applies here, now and in the future?”

Example:

* `Europe/Amsterdam`
  * Winter → `+01:00`
  * Summer → `+02:00`

Using only offsets loses:

* DST transitions
* historical rule changes
* correct "tomorrow at 09:00" semantics

## Temporal types overview

| Concept            | Temporal type            | Represents                 |
|--------------------|--------------------------|----------------------------|
| Moment on timeline | `Temporal.Instant`       | Exact point in time        |
| Moment + zone      | `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` | Moment interpreted locally |
| Local date + time  | `Temporal.PlainDateTime` | Calendar + clock           |
| Date only          | `Temporal.PlainDate`     | Calendar date              |
| Time only          | `Temporal.PlainTime`     | Clock time                 |
| Duration           | `Temporal.Duration`      | Time interval              |

## String formats & typical usage

| Example string                                | Represents                  | Typical use               |
|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|---------------------------|
| `2026-01-14T08:00:00Z`                        | Exact moment                | Events, storage, ordering |
| `2026-01-14T09:00:00+01:00`                   | Exact moment (offset-based) | Interchange format        |
| `2026-01-14T09:00:00+01:00[Europe/Amsterdam]` | Moment + zone rules         | Appointments              |
| `2026-01-14T09:00:00`                         | Local date + time           | UI input                  |
| `2026-01-14`                                  | Local date                  | Travel dates              |
| `09:00:00`                                    | Local time                  | Opening hours             |

## Arithmetic rules

| Operation                      | Use this             | Reason                  |
|--------------------------------|----------------------|-------------------------|
| “Exactly 24 hours later”       | `Instant + Duration` | Always exact seconds    |
| “Tomorrow at 09:00 local time” | `ZonedDateTime`      | DST-safe calendar logic |

DST reality:

* `+1 day` ≠ `+24 hours`
* A local day can be **23, 24, or 25 hours**

## Example

The following function checks whether a ticket is still valid:

```ts
import { Temporal } from "temporal-polyfill";

function isTicketExpired(
  ticketDate: Temporal.PlainDate,
  referenceDate: Temporal.Instant = Temporal.Now.instant()
) {
  // ticket expires:
  const expirationDateTime = ticketDate
    .add({ days: 1 }) // ...the next day
    .toPlainDateTime({ hour: 4 }) // ...at 4 AM
    .toZonedDateTime("Europe/Amsterdam"); // ...at Dutch local time (to apply DST)
  
  return referenceDate.epochMilliseconds <= expirationDateTime.epochMilliseconds;
}
```

## API guidelines

If your API represents **a moment in time**:

* Accept: UTC (`Z`) **or** offset-based ISO strings
* Normalize to: `Temporal.Instant`
* Store: as an ISO-8601 UTC string (`"2026-01-14T08:00:00Z"`) or epoch milliseconds.

Example:

```ts
Temporal.Instant.from("2026-01-14T09:00:00+01:00");
```

UTC and offset inputs representing the same moment are equivalent.

Without a time zone, DST-correct interpretation is impossible.

## JSON serialization notes

* `Temporal.Instant` **always** serializes as UTC via `JSON.stringify()`
* This cannot be configured
* If you need offsets or zones in JSON, convert explicitly before serializing

Rule of thumb: if you care about the offset, you didn’t actually want a `Temporal.Instant`.

# Using Vitest

Here you can find some tips and tricks for using Vitest in your project.

For more information, check out the [official Vitest documentation](https://vitest.dev/).

## Installation

Using Vitest is very straightforward. Install:

```sh
npm i -D vitest @vitest/coverage-v8
```

And run it using the following npm scripts:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "vitest run",
    "test:watch": "vitest",
    "test:coverage": "vitest run --coverage"
  }
}
```

## Using test projects

As of Vitest 3.2, you can use separate test projects:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // ...
    projects: [
      {
        test: {
          name: "unit",
          include: ["app/**/*.test.ts"],
        },
        extends: true,
      },
      {
        test: {
          name: "integration",
          include: ["test/integration/**/*.test.ts"],
          // specific configuration overrides, e.g.:
          fileParallelism: false,
        },
        extends: true,
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

This allows you to use different configurations for different test projects. To run a specific project:

```bash
vitest run --project unit
vitest run --project integration
```

## Naming conventions

* Use `*.test.ts` for test files;
* Keep unit tests close to the code (e.g. `app/foo/bar.test.ts` next to `app/foo/bar.ts`).
* For acceptance/integration tests, you can organize them separately (e.g. `integration-tests/**/*.test.ts` or similar).

## The basics

Prefer intention-revealing [matchers and assertions]:

```ts
import { expect, it } from "vitest";

it("returns 3 items", () => {
  const items = ["a", "b", "c"];
  expect(items).toHaveLength(3);
});

it("formats an id", () => {
  const user = {
    id: "user123",
    name: "John",
  };

  expect(user).toEqual({
    id: expect.stringMatching(/^user\d+$/),
    name: "John",
  });
});
```

[matchers and assertions]: https://vitest.dev/api/expect.html

## Mocking

Mocking is an essential part of testing. Here are some recipes for common use cases.

### Mocking date and time

Mocking the current time in Vitest is effortless:

```ts
import { afterEach, beforeEach, expect, it, vi } from "vitest";

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  vi.setSystemTime("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

it("uses the current time", () => {
  expect(new Date().toISOString()).toBe("2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z");

  // also works with Temporal:
  expect(Temporal.Now.instant().toString()).toBe("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
});
```

Check out the official [Mocking section](https://vitest.dev/guide/mocking/dates.html) for more details.

### Mocking AWS SDK calls

To mock interactions with the AWS SDK, we recommend using [aws-sdk-client-mock] with [aws-sdk-client-mock-vitest].

```ts
import { afterEach, beforeEach, it } from "vitest";
import { mockClient } from "aws-sdk-client-mock";
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, GetCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb";

// to install the Vitest matchers:
import "aws-sdk-client-mock-vitest/extend";

const dynamoDbDocumentMock = mockClient(DynamoDBDocumentClient);

beforeEach(() => {
  dynamoDbDocumentMock.reset()
});

it("GET item", () => {
  givenItemExists({ id: "item123", foo: "Foo" });

  // test logic...
  
  expect(dynamoDbDocumentMock).toHaveReceivedCommandTimes(GetCommand, 1);
});

function givenItemExists(item: Item) {
  dynamoDbDocumentMock
    .on(GetCommand, { Key: { id: item.id } })
    .resolves({ Item: item });
}
```

[aws-sdk-client-mock]: https://www.npmjs.com/package/aws-sdk-client-mock

[aws-sdk-client-mock-vitest]: https://www.npmjs.com/package/aws-sdk-client-mock-vitest

### Mocking HTTP requests

To mock HTTP requests, we recommend using `@backpack/mockserver-client`:

```ts
import { afterEach, beforeEach, it, vi } from "vitest";
import { useMockServer } from "@backpack/mockserver-client/vitest";

const mockServer = useMockServer({ type: "in-memory" }).setup();

it("GET book", async () => {
  await givenBookPresent({ isbn: "9781234567897", title: "The Man in the Mist" });

  // test logic...
});

async function givenBookPresent(book: Book) {
  await mockServer.whenGet("/api/v1/books").respondJSON(book);
}
```

Check out the [API reference](../../packages/@backpack/mockserver-client/index.md) to learn more.

## Writing readable tests

### Test structure

When unit testing, use (nested) `describe` suites to indicate which public methods are being tested:

```ts
import { describe } from "vitest";

describe("BookService", () => {
  describe("getBook()", () => {
    it(`should return a book with ISBN `, () => {
      /* ... */
    });

    it(`should return undefined when book is not found`, () => {
      /* ... */
    });
  });

  describe("deleteBook()", () => {
    it(`should delete an existing ISBN `, () => {
      /* ... */
    });

    it(`should gracefully handle non-existing ISBN`, () => {
      /* ... */
    });
  });
});
```

### Focus on behavior

Keep integration/acceptence tests functional — focus on behavior. Hide the technical details in helper
functions or methods.

Function-style:

```ts
import { describe, it } from "vitest";

describe("GET /books/:isbn", () => {
  it(`should return a book with ISBN `, async () => {
    // given:
    const bookEntity = givenBookPresent({
      isbn: "9781234567897" // (hide unnessacary details)
    });

    // when:
    const bookResponse = await getBook();

    // then:
    expect(bookResponse.status).toBe(200);
    expect(bookResponse.body).toEqual({
      id: "9781234567897", // express reference matching
      title: bookEntity.title, // express testing for equality
    });
  });

  // ...
});
```

### Organize test fixtures

Either with local test fixtures:

```ts
import { describe } from "vitest";
import { mockClient } from "aws-sdk-client-mock";
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/testing";

describe("GET /books/:isbn", () => {
  // ...

  // @backpack/rest-client, or any other test client
  const testClient = createRestClient(/* ... */);

  // using aws-sdk-client-mock
  const dynamoDbDocument = mockClient(DynamoDBDocumentClient);

  function givenBookPresent(book: BookEntity) {
    return dynamoDbDocument
      .on(GetCommand, { Key: { id: item.id } })
      .resolves({ Item: item });
  }

  function getBook(): v1.Book {
    return testClient
      .url("/api/v1/books/9781234567897")
      .get()
      .json<v1.Book>();
  }
});
```

Or even better — with your test fixtures into classes. For example:

```ts
import { mockClient } from "aws-sdk-client-mock";
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb";
import { GetCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb";

class BookTableFixture {
  private readonly dynamoDbClientMock = mockClient(DynamoDBDocumentClient);

  public givenBookPresent(book: BookEntity) {
    this.dynamoDbClientMock
      .on(GetCommand)
      .resolvesOnce({ Item: book });
  }

  public givenNoBookPresent() {
    this.dynamoDbClientMock
      .on(GetCommand)
      .resolvesOnce({ Item: undefined });
  }

  public reset() {
    this.dynamoDbClientMock.reset();
  }
}
```

## Other practical tips

* focus on a clear "arrange / act / assert" (or "given / when / then") structure;
* assert on observable output (return values, emitted events, calls) rather than internal implementation.
* To prepare data for a test, you can use partial objects or implement builder patterns;
* Keep tests small: one reason to fail per test.

## Publishing results and coverage in CI/CD

To publish test results and coverage in Azure DevOps, you can use the following tasks:

```yaml
- task: PublishTestResults@2
  displayName: "Publish Vitest Test Results"
  condition: succeededOrFailed()
  inputs:
    testRunner: JUnit
    testResultsFiles: "junit-report.xml"

- task: PublishCodeCoverageResults@2
  displayName: "Publish Vitest Coverage Report"
  condition: succeededOrFailed()
  inputs:
    summaryFileLocation: "**/coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml"
```

To make this work, you need to have the following `vitest.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // ...
    reporters: ["default", "junit"],
    outputFile: {
      junit: "./junit-report.xml",
    },
    coverage: {
      provider: "v8",
      reporter: ["text", "lcov", "html", "cobertura"],
      include: ["app/**"],
    },
  },
});
```

# Testing strategies for Backpack projects

This guide describes the recommended testing strategy for Backpack projects.
It is based on practical experience with serverless applications running on AWS,
and aims to balance **developer speed**, **confidence**, and **operational simplicity**.

## Test types

Backpack distinguishes **three test types**, each with a clear responsibility and scope:

* **Unit tests** — isolated logic
* **Acceptance tests** — in-memory, behavior-focused
* **Integration tests** — deployed on AWS

These test types are complementary and intentionally scoped. There is no single “perfect”
test layer — instead, each type answers a different question.

## Overview

| Test type   | Where it runs | What it validates                           |
|-------------|---------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Unit        | Local         | Isolated logic                              |
| Acceptance  | Local         | Service behavior and flows                  |
| Integration | AWS           | Infrastructure wiring and real AWS behavior |

## 1. Unit tests

Unit tests validate **small, isolated units of functionality**, such as individual functions
or classes. They are intentionally narrow in scope and avoid I/O, infrastructure, or framework concerns.

**Typical characteristics**

* No network calls
* No AWS SDK calls
* No framework/DI wiring
* Fast execution

**What to test**

* Pure logic
* Edge cases
* Error handling
* Algorithms or calculations

**Benefits**

* Very fast feedback
* Easy to reason about
* Ideal for complex logic

**Trade-offs**

* Limited confidence about real-world behavior
* Do not validate wiring or integration

**Advice**

* Use unit tests where isolation adds value (e.g. very algorithmic logic)
* Prefer higher-level tests for most business behavior
* Avoid mocking deeply nested dependencies just to “unit test everything”

## 2. Acceptance tests (in-memory)

Acceptance tests validate **the behavior of your service** by exercising complete
application flows, such as REST APIs or asynchronous message processing. These tests run **locally and in memory**, with
all external boundaries mocked.

Acceptance tests form the **backbone of the test suite**.

Sometimes also referred to as:

* component tests
* sociable tests
* behavior tests

**Typical setup**

* Run application code directly (no deployment)
* Mock HTTP boundaries
* Mock AWS SDK boundaries
* Use fixtures for external state

**Typical tools**

* Vitest (test runner + assertions)
* In-memory fixtures for persistence
* Backpack mockserver or `vitest-fetch-mock` (for HTTP mocking)

**What this tests**

* End-to-end behavior *within the service boundary*
* API contracts
* Error scenarios
* Business flows

**Benefits**

* Very fast and deterministic
* No AWS access required
* Easy to run locally and in CI
* Highly readable tests

**Trade-offs**

* Relies on contracts instead of real infrastructure
* Does not validate IAM, networking, or CDK configuration

**Recommended practices**

* Organize tests by **feature or flow**, not by file
* Abstract implementation details into fixtures
* Keep tests expressive and intent-driven
* Design tests so they can later be reused for integration testing

## 3. Integration tests (AWS)

Integration tests validate **the integration between application code and real AWS
infrastructure**. These tests run against a **deployed stack on AWS**, typically using a dedicated
integration environment.

Integration tests focus on **infrastructure correctness**, not exhaustive behavior.

**Typical setup**

* Stack deployed using CDK
* Real AWS services (Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, IAM)
* External services outside your system boundary may still be mocked

**What this tests**

* IAM permissions
* Resource configuration
* Networking and routing
* Real AWS service behavior

**Benefits**

* High confidence that the service works in AWS
* Catches misconfigurations early
* Complements acceptance tests

**Trade-offs**

* Slower feedback
* Requires deployment
* Needs CI/CD coordination and environment locking

**Recommended practices**

* Use a **dedicated integration stack** (e.g. via suffix/prefix on development)
* Keep the stack persistent to allow fast incremental deployments
* Limit integration tests to **happy paths**
* Rely on acceptance tests for detailed behavior coverage
* Use environment locking to prevent parallel interference

## Recommended setup

Backpack recommends running integration tests against a **dedicated stack** alongside the regular
development environment, rather than against staging or production.

Example:

```bash
npx cdk deploy -c config=dev -c envSuffix=int
```

This provides:

* Isolated DynamoDB tables
* A dedicated API Gateway base path
* Fast incremental deployments
* No interference with developers

The integration environment is typically **pipeline-owned**, not developer-owned.

# Using Datadog

Here are some instructions to set up monitoring with [Datadog]. For more information, please check out
the [official guide][Datadog guide].

[Datadog]: https://docs.datadoghq.com

[Datadog guide]: https://docs.datadoghq.com/serverless/libraries_integrations/cdk/?site=eu

## Adding Datadog to your AWS Lambda

The Datadog integration with AWS Lambda is pretty straightforward. It just adds additional layers to your Lambda
functions to instrument it and forward logs and metrics to Datadog.

Our recommended approach is to use the `DatadogLambda` CDK construct from [@backpack/cdk-constructs]:

```ts
import { DatadogLambda } from "@backpack/cdk-constructs";

new DatadogLambda(this, "DatadogLambda", {
  lambdaFunctions: [/* ... pass your lambda functions here ... */],
  service: "bookstore",
  environment: "staging", // pass your environment here
  version: "1.0.0", // a semantic version or a commit hash
});
```

This construct works the same as the [official one][datadog-cdk-construct], with a few differences:

* The API key is automatically retrieved from the NS Cloud LandingZone;
* Backpack keeps the layer versions up to date for you.

[datadog-cdk-construct]: https://docs.datadoghq.com/serverless/libraries_integrations/cdk/#typescript

[@backpack/cdk-constructs]: ../../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/index.md

## Adding Datadog monitors

A useful library to add Datadog monitors to your CDK code is  [GoodNotes/cdk-datadog-resources].

```ts
import { DatadogMonitor } from "@goodnotes-oss/cdk-datadog-resources";

new DatadogMonitor(this, "LambdaErrorsMonitor", {
  type: "query alert",
  name: `Bookstore - Lambda Errors`,
  query: `sum(last_5m):sum:aws.lambda.errors{service:bookstore, env:production} by {functionname}.as_count() >= 10`,
  message: `Lambda has {{value}} error(s) on {{functionname.name}} where threshold is {{threshold}}!`,
  priority: 2,
  tags: [`env:production`, `service:bookstore`],
});
```

Please check out [Monitoring and alerts](./monitoring-and-alerts.md) for more information.

[GoodNotes/cdk-datadog-resources]: https://github.com/GoodNotes/cdk-datadog-resources

## Examples

Check out our [Bookstore REST API] for examples.

## Best practices

Please read the [dedicated Confluence page] about Datadog monitoring best practices.

[Bookstore REST API]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/apps/bookstore-rest-api

[dedicated Confluence page]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MLAB/pages/1225196369/Monitoring+guidelines

# Logging and metrics

## When to use what?

* Use **logging** for detailed, contextual information about individual events, mainly for debugging and understanding
  *why* something happened. Logs are verbose and high-cardinality, so use them selectively.

* Use **metrics** for numerical signals over time, such as counts, rates, and latency. Metrics are ideal for monitoring,
  alerting, and spotting trends in system health.

## Recommended logging libraries

Currently, Backpack does not enforce a specific logging implementation. As long as you have
[set up Datadog](./using-datadog.md), all output will be collected in Datadog.

However, it is recommended to use a library that supports structured logging. For example:

* [AWS Lambda Powertools]
* [Pino]
* [Winston]

## Logging best practices

Here are some general guidelines for logging in Backpack projects:

* **Use logging levels deliberately**: reserve `error` for unexpected situations that require fixing; use `warn` for
  recoverable anomalies, `info` for normal business events, and `debug` or `trace` for diagnostic detail.

* **Log once**: either handle and log an error locally, or propagate it and log it in a central error handler — never
  both.

* **Prefer structured logging over strings**: log objects with stable, meaningful keys instead of concatenated or
  interpolated strings.

* **Include relevant context intentionally**: add identifiers such as request IDs or business IDs that help diagnose
  issues, but avoid unnecessary or noisy data.

* **Never log secrets or personal data**: do not log credentials, tokens, or PII.

* **Treat errors as exceptional, not control flow**: expected or common scenarios should not be logged as errors.

* **Write logs that answer a clear question**: each log entry should explain what happened, why it matters, or what
  action is required.

## Persistent keys

Most logging libraries allow you to define a set of persistent keys that are added to every log entry.

For example, for [AWS Lambda Powertools]:

```ts
import { parseHeaders } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import { Logger } from "@aws-lambda-powertools/logger";
import type { APIGatewayProxyEvent, Context } from "aws-lambda";

export const logger = new Logger({
  persistentKeys: {
    logger: {
      name: "@aws-lambda-powertools/logger",
    },
  },
});

/**
 * Configures the logger to include the context of an AWS Lambda invocation.
 */
export function configureLoggingContext(event: APIGatewayProxyEvent, context: Context) {
  const headers = parseHeaders(event);

  logger.addContext(context);
  logger.appendKeys({
    caller: headers.get("X-Caller-ID"),
    caller_version: headers.get("X-Caller-Version"),
    request_id: headers.get("X-Request-ID"),
    user_agent: headers.get("User-Agent"),
  });
}

```

## Publishing custom metrics

The `datadog-lambda-js` library allows you to publish custom metrics directly from your AWS Lambda functions by using
the provided `sendDistributionMetric`, `sendGaugeMetric`, or `sendCountMetric` helpers.

```ts
import { sendDistributionMetric } from "datadog-lambda-js";

export const handler = async (): Promise<void> => {
  const start = Date.now();

  // your business logic here

  sendDistributionMetric(
    "orders.processing_time_ms",
    Date.now() - start,
    "category:foo", // additional tags
  );
};
```

Make sure `datadog-lambda-js` is excluded from your production bundle:

* If you are using the CDK construct from Backpack, it will automatically exclude it for you.
* Otherwise, add `datadog-lambda-js` to the `bundling.externalModules` option of your `NodejsFunction` construct.

These metrics are emitted asynchronously via the Datadog Lambda Extension and automatically tagged with useful metadata
such as function name, region, and version.

> \[!WARNING]
> When publishing custom metrics, be careful with including dynamic tags. Prevent high cardinality metrics — in other
> words, don't publish too many different values. This may incur a lot of costs.

[AWS Lambda Powertools]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/powertools/typescript/latest/

[Pino]: https://github.com/pinojs/pino

[Winston]: https://github.com/winstonjs/winston

# Monitoring and alerts

## Creating a monitor

Monitors can be created manually in the Datadog UI, but the recommended approach is to include them
as CDK construct in your infrastructure code:

```ts
import { DatadogMonitor } from "@goodnotes-oss/cdk-datadog-resources";

new DatadogMonitor(this, "LambdaErrorsMonitor", {
  type: "query alert",
  name: `Bookstore - Lambda Errors`,
  query: `sum(last_5m):sum:aws.lambda.errors{service:bookstore, env:production} by {functionname}.as_count() >= 10`,
  message: `Lambda has {{value}} error(s) on {{functionname.name}} where threshold is {{threshold}}!`,
  priority: 2,
  tags: [`env:production`, `service:bookstore`],
});
```

A few tips and tricks:

* Only create the monitors in your preferred environments (e.g., only production).
* Use the Datadog [Metrics explorer] to verify your query.
* Instead of hard-coding the thresholds, you can organize them in config files. See [@backpack/config].

[Metrics explorer]: https://app.datadoghq.eu/metric/explorer

[@backpack/config]: ../../packages/@backpack/config/index.md

## Setting up alerting

To set up alerting, there are a few options.

### Jira Service Management / Opsgenie (recommended)

This integrates Datadog monitors into Jira/Opsgenie, giving you a full alerting toolkit: on-call schedules/shifts,
escalations, routing rules, deduplication, acknowledgements, incident workflows, etc. This is the recommended option for
most teams.

To use it, you can refer to the [Opsgenie integration] documentation. Basically, you need to:

* configure the OpsGenie integration in Datadog and register your project or team;
* include a `@opsgenie-{service-name}` in your monitor message body.
* Jira/Opsgenie has its own [Slack integration][Jira Slack integration]; make sure to configure it as well.

### Direct Datadog Slack integration

This option sends monitor notifications straight from Datadog to Slack channels, bypassing Jira/Opsgenie entirely. This
is simpler to set up, but usually means you lose things like structured on-call, escalation policies, and
audit-friendly alert lifecycle management.

[Opsgenie integration]: https://docs.datadoghq.com/integrations/opsgenie/#example-usage

[Jira Slack integration]: https://ns-topaas.atlassian.net/jira/ops/teams/og-59494a86-9207-43ac-b1f0-bc88a6887374/integrations

# `@backpack/cli` ⚡

A command-line interface tool designed to support development of Backpack projects.

## Generating projects

The `generate-project` command allows you to generate a new project.

::: tip Tip: looking for example projects?
If you are looking for examples of real life Backpack projects, you can also have a look at
our [demo projects](/introduction/demo-projects.md).
:::

### Prerequisites

First, make sure to [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed for Backpack.

Optionally, make sure you have your default AWS profile configured with SSO:

::: code-group

```text [~/.aws/config]
[sso-session NS]
sso_start_url = https://ns-sso.awsapps.com/start
sso_region = eu-west-1
sso_registration_scopes = sso:account:access

[default]
sso_session = NS
```

:::

### Getting started

To generate a new project, you can run the Backpack CLI using [`npx`](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v8/commands/npx):

```shell
npx @backpack/cli generate-project [targetDirectory]
```

Replace `[targetDirectory]` with the desired directory name for your new project.

### What's included?

Depending on the options you choose during the process, it allows you to create a fully working project, containing:

* An initial CDK project skeleton;
* A fully working CI/CD pipeline;
* DataDog monitoring;
* REST API using AWS Lambda with API Gateway;
* Proper setup of tooling like Vitest, ESLint and TypeScript
* Some example code, so you can directly get started.

After pushing your code to an Azure DevOps environment and running the CI/CD pipeline, you should be able to run your
app in production in no time!

### CLI options

The CLI is primarily designed for interactive use, but you can use the following options to change its behavior.

| Option                 | Type      | Description                                               | Default |
|------------------------|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------------|---------|
| `--interactive`        | `boolean` | Run in interactive mode                                   | `true`  |
| `--help`               | `boolean` | Show help                                                 |         |
| `--service`            | `string`  | The name of the service                                   |         |
| `--minimal`            | `boolean` | Render a very minimal project                             | `false` |
| `--ci`                 | `boolean` | Include a CI/CD pipeline                                  | `true`  |
| `--datadog-monitoring` | `boolean` | Add monitoring with Datadog                               | `true`  |
| `--app-config`         | `boolean` | Easily use different configurations for every environment | `true`  |
| `--app-secrets`        | `boolean` | App secrets from AWS Secret Manager                       | `true`  |
| `--rest-api`           | `boolean` | API Gateway with Lambda proxy integration                 | `false` |
| `--dynamo-db`          | `boolean` | Include a DynamoDB table                                  | `false` |
| `--only-dev`           | `boolean` | Generate only resources for AWS DEV environment           | `true`  |
| `--aws-account-dev`    | `string`  | The AWS account id for DEV environment                    |         |
| `--aws-account-stg`    | `string`  | The AWS account id for STG environment                    |         |
| `--aws-account-prd`    | `string`  | The AWS account id for PRD environment                    |         |
| `--install`            | `boolean` | Whether to run npm install on the project                 | `true`  |
| `--git`                | `boolean` | Whether to init a Git repo on the project                 | `true`  |
| `--profile`            | `string`  | The AWS profile id for the DEV environment                |         |

## Generating a CI/CD pipeline

The `generate-pipeline` command allows you to generate a new CI/CD pipeline for your existing Backpack project.

### Getting started

To generate a new pipeline, just run the following command from the root of your existing project:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli generate-pipeline
```

Additionally, you can pass a different project directory as first argument:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli generate-pipeline path/to/your/project
```

### CLI options

The CLI is primarily designed for interactive use, but you can use the following options to change its behavior.

| Option          | Type      | Description                                   | Default |
|-----------------|-----------|-----------------------------------------------|---------|
| `--interactive` | `boolean` | Run in interactive mode                       | `true`  |
| `--help`        | `boolean` | Show help                                     |         |
| `--service`     | `string`  | The name of the service                       |         |
| `--main-branch` | `string`  | The name of the main branch                   | `main`  |
| `--only-dev`    | `boolean` | Only include a deploy job for DEV environment | `false` |

## Installing AI agent instructions

The `agents init` command adds Backpack-specific instructions for AI coding agents to an existing
project.

It creates or updates an `AGENTS.md` file in the project root. This file points agents to the
current Backpack documentation, including `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, and the AI agent guidance.

### Getting started

To install Backpack agent instructions, run the command from the root of your project:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli agents init
```

By default, the command only continues when the project uses one or more `@backpack/*` packages.
This prevents accidentally adding Backpack-specific instructions to unrelated projects.

If the project does not contain any `@backpack/*` dependencies yet, but you still want to add the
instructions, use `--force`:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli agents init --force
```

### Existing AGENTS.md files

If an `AGENTS.md` file already exists, the command will not overwrite it. Instead, it prints a
conservative patch suggestion.

To merge a marked Backpack section into an existing `AGENTS.md`, run:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli agents init --merge
```

Existing local instructions are preserved.

### Checking existing instructions

To check whether a project already contains Backpack agent guidance without changing files, run:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli agents init --check
```

### CLI options

| Option    | Type      | Description                                                               | Default |
|-----------|-----------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------|
| `--force` | `boolean` | Continue even when no `@backpack/*` dependencies are detected             | `false` |
| `--merge` | `boolean` | Add a marked Backpack section to an existing `AGENTS.md` file             | `false` |
| `--check` | `boolean` | Check whether `AGENTS.md` is present and contains Backpack agent guidance | `false` |

## Retrieving tags

Retrieves all recommended resource tags for a given ASID. See [Resource Tagging] for more
information.

[Resource Tagging]: /guides/infrastructure/resource-tagging.md

```bash
npx @backpack/cli retrieve-tags your-asid-here
```

## Running a mockserver

The Backpack CLI can also be used to run a **local mockserver** for development and testing.

This starts a standalone instance of `@backpack/hono-mockserver`, which can be used by tests,
tools, or applications via HTTP.

### Getting started

To start a local mockserver, run:

```bash
npx @backpack/cli mock-server start
```

By default, this starts a mockserver on port `3001`.

Once running, you can:

* connect to it using `useMockServer({ type: "remote" })`
* configure it via the mockserver admin API
* inspect received requests and mappings manually

For more details on mocking and verification, see the documentation for
[`@backpack/mockserver-client`][client-docs] and [`@backpack/hono-mockserver`][server-docs].

[client-docs]: /packages/@backpack/mockserver-client/index.md

[server-docs]: /packages/@backpack/hono-mockserver/index.md

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/config

# `@backpack/config` ⚙️️

Type-safe configuration management using [Zod].

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm (along with Zod):

```bash
npm install @backpack/config zod
```

## Usage

### Step 1: define your config schema

First, create a schema using [Zod]. You can use any of Zods features (such as transforms and default values), as
long as the top-level data structure is an object.

Example:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

export const Config = z.object({
  service: z.string(),
  clients: z.object({
    foo: z.object({
      baseUrl: z.string().url(),
      timeoutMilliseconds: z.number().default(200),
    }),
    bar: z.object({
      baseUrl: z.string().url(),
      timeoutMilliseconds: z.number().default(200),
    }),
  })
});
```

### Step 2: load your config

To load your actual config, you can use one or more loaders.

If multiple loaders are provided, it will deep-merge the data from all loaders, with the last loader taking precedence.
If any loader fails, it will still return the data from other loaders.

```ts
import { loadConfig, envLoader, yamlLoader, importLoader } from "@backpack/config";

const myConfig = await loadConfig({
  schema: Config,
  loaders: [
    // loads from environment variables
    envLoader(),

    // loads from a YAML file
    yamlLoader("path/to/config.yaml"),

    // you need to implement your own environment/profile detection 
    //  to load from a specific source:
    yamlLoader(`path/to/config-${profile}.yaml`),

    // loads from a TypeScript file, using a dynamic import:
    importLoader(() => import("./path/to/config.ts")),
  ],
});
```

### Step 3: specify your actual config files

Make sure the sources of your loaders are provided according to your schema:

Example using YAML:

```yaml
service: My Bookstore
clients:
  foo:
    baseUrl: https://path.to/foo
    timeoutMilliseconds: 500
# ...
```

Example using TypeScript:

```ts
// (make sure to use a default export)
export default {
  service: "My Bookstore",
  clients: {
    foo: {
      baseUrl: "https://path.to/foo",
      timeoutMilliseconds: 500,
    }
    // ...
  }
} 
```

## Advanced

### Type-safety

You can leverage your Zod-schema for additional type-safety.

First, use the `z.infer<>` [helper](https://zod.dev/basics?id=inferring-types) to create a type-alias:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

export type Config = z.infer<typeof Config>;
export const Config = z.object({
  // ...
});
```

Next, use the `satisfies` operator to get additional type-checking.

```ts
import type { Config } from "path/to/config.ts";

export default {
  service: "My Bookstore",
  clients: {
    foo: {
      baseUrl: "https://path.to/foo",
      timeoutMilliseconds: 500,
    }
    // ...
  }
} satisfies Config;
```

If you are using multiple loaders to combine several partial configs, you can use `DeepPartial<Config>` to make all
properties optional. Alternatively, you can use the `defineConfig()` helper - which accepts partial configs by default:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "@backpack/config";
import type { Config } from "path/to/config.ts";

export default defineConfig<Config>({
  // app name is defined in a different config file.

  clients: {
    foo: {
      baseUrl: "https://path.to/foo",
      timeoutMilliseconds: 500,
    }
    // ...
  }
});
```

### Passing context

In some cases, you may want to pass additional context to your config file. For example, to access certain things from
your application context, such as an injection container.

To do this, you can use the `importLoader()` like this:

```ts
import { loadConfig, envLoader, yamlLoader, importLoader } from "@backpack/config";

export type Context = { /* ... */ }

const myConfig = await loadConfig({
  schema: Config,
  loaders: [
    importLoader({
      read: () => import("./path/to/config.ts"),
      context: { /* ... */ }
    }),
  ],
});
```

Now, you can specify your TypeScript config as an arrow function:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "@backpack/config";
import type { Config } from "path/to/config.ts";

export default defineConfig<Config, Context>((context) => ({
  // ...
}));
```

[Zod]: https://zod.dev/

[CDK context]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/context.html

[CDK tags]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/tagging.html

## Loaders
