[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/error-handling

# `@backpack/error-handling` 🚩

A package with various utilities to simplify error handling.

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/error-handling
```

## `Result<T, E>`

A small utility type representing either a success or a failure. Inspired by [many other programming languages][Result]
that offer similar monads.

```typescript
type Result<T, E> = Success<T> | Failure<E>;
```

This object contains:

* either a `value: T` with `success: true` and `failed: false`
* or an `error: E` with `success: false` and `failed: true`

[Result]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Result_type

The recommended way to use this monad is by using the `runCatching()` function:

```typescript
import { runCatching } from "@backpack/error-handling/result";

const result = runCatching(() => mightFail(), MyCustomError);

if (result.failed) {
  console.warn("Got custom error", result.error);
  return;
}

console.log("Got value", result.value);
```

[See the full API reference](./result/index.md)

## `AsyncResult<T>`

An extension of `Promise<T>`, adding more operators to it, to state your intentions more explicitly.

Example usage:

```typescript
import { AsyncResult } from "@backpack/error-handling/async-result";

const value = await AsyncResult.try(() => mightFail())
  .map((r) => r * 2)
  .onFailure((error) => console.warn("Got error", error))
  .recoverIfInstanceOf(MyCustomError, () => "fallback-1")
  .orElse("fallback-2");

console.log("Got value", value);
```

[See the full API reference](./async-result/classes/AsyncResult)

## Promise utilities

Most methods on `AsyncResult` also exist as higher-order functions, so they can be applied on regular
`Promise` chains.

For example:

```typescript
const value = await promiseTry(() => mightFail())
  .then(map((r) => r * 2))
  .catch(onFailure((error) => console.warn("Got error", error)))
  .catch(recoverIfInstanceOf(MyCustomError, () => "fallback-1"))
  .catch(orElse("fallback-2"));
```

[See the full API reference](./promises/index.md)

## `@catchErrors()` decorator

Backpack also offers a decorator which can be applied on methods that return a `Promise<T>`.
This decorator accepts one or more `.catch()` callbacks, which will be applied in the provided order.

Example:

```typescript
import { catchErrors } from "@backpack/error-handling/promises";

class MyService {
  @catchErrors((error) => "fallback")
  public async mightFail(): Promise<string> {
    // ...

    return "foo";
  }
}
```

All the higher-order functions [mentioned above](#promise-utilities), which are supposed to be used with `.catch()`, can
also be used in combination with the `@catchErrors()` decorator:

```typescript
class MyService {
  @catchErrors(
    onFailure((error) => console.error("Got error", error)),
    recoverIfInstanceOf(MyError, () => "fallback 1"),
    orElse("fallback-2"),
  )
  public async mightFail(): Promise<string> {
    // ...

    return "foo";
  }
}
```

This also allows us to use Lambda error handlers, such as provided by `@backpack/aws-lambda`, or by easily
creating one yourself:

```typescript
export class MyLambda {
  @catchErrors(myErrorHandler())
  public async handle(): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult> {
    // ...
  }
}

const myErrorHandler = () =>
  catchAll(
    recoverIfInstanceOf(MyCustomError, myCustomErrorConverter()),
    recoverIfInstanceOf(ProblemError, problemErrorConverter()),
    orElseGet((error) =>
      problemResult({
        type: "/problems/internal-server-error",
        title: "Internal Server Error",
        detail: "Something went wrong. 😼",
        status: 500,
      }),
    ),
  );
```

> \[!NOTE] About decorators
>
> Native [ECMAScript decorators](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-decorators)
> are currently in [stage 3](https://github.com/tc39/proposals#stage-3) of the TC39 standardization process,
> and are [not yet implemented][implementation status] in Node.js.
>
> However, this is not a problem if your code is transpiled. By using Amazon Lambda Node.js CDK construct
> which uses [esbuild] under the hood, this is already taken care of.

[TypeScript]: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-5-0/#decorators

[esbuild]: https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/releases/v0.21.0

[implementation status]: https://github.com/tc39/proposal-decorators/issues/476

## Modules

* [async-result](async-result/index.md)
* [index](index/index.md)
* [promises](promises/index.md)
* [result](result/index.md)

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/http

# @backpack/http

Generic HTTP-related utilities.

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/http
```

## Cache utilities

> \[!TIP]
> For usage patterns with AWS Lambda, check out the full caching guide in [`@backpack/aws-lambda`](../aws-lambda/index.html#http-caching).

### `cacheControl()` — Cache-Control header builder

Fluent builder for constructing `Cache-Control` header values.

```ts
import { cacheControl } from "@backpack/http";

cacheControl().maxAge(300).mustRevalidate().build();
// → "max-age=300, must-revalidate"

cacheControl().noStore().build();
// → "no-store"

cacheControl().public().maxAge(31_536_000).immutable().build();
// → "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"

cacheControl().maxAge(60).staleWhileRevalidate(30).staleIfError(300).build();
// → "max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30, stale-if-error=300"
```

### `durableCacheStorage()` — X-Cache-Storage header

Builds the `X-Cache-Storage` header value that instructs the mobile cache client to persist a
response in durable storage — surviving OS cache pressure and user-initiated cache clears.

```ts
import { durableCacheStorage } from "@backpack/http";

durableCacheStorage();
// → "durable; max-stale=604800"  (one-week retention)

durableCacheStorage({ maxStale: 86_400 });
// → "durable; max-stale=86400"   (24-hour retention)
```

### `generateETag()`

Generates weak ETags from response bodies.

> Add an `ETag` whenever the team is able to calculate one. It allows clients to revalidate cheaply
> — the server sends back `304 Not Modified` without a body when the resource has not changed.

Example for AWS Lambda:

```ts
import { defineRestLambda } from "@backpack/aws-lambda";
import { handleConditionalRequest, jsonOk } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import { generateETag } from "@backpack/http";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  const etag = generateETag("..."); // e.g. based on response body
  // → W/"a1b2c3d4…"

  const notModified = handleConditionalRequest(event, etag);
  if (notModified) return notModified; // 304 — client already has this version

  return jsonOk(/* ...*/)
});
```

ETags are weak (`W/"…"`) because the same logical resource may produce different byte sequences
across deployments. Weak ETags are sufficient for `If-None-Match` / `304 Not Modified` revalidation.

## Classes

* [CacheControlBuilder](classes/CacheControlBuilder.md)

## Interfaces

* [DurableCacheStorageOptions](interfaces/DurableCacheStorageOptions.md)

## Variables

* [X\_CACHE\_STORAGE\_HEADER](variables/X_CACHE_STORAGE_HEADER.md)

## Functions

* [cacheControl](functions/cacheControl.md)
* [durableCacheStorage](functions/durableCacheStorage.md)
* [generateETag](functions/generateETag.md)

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/i18n

# `@backpack/i18n` 🌐

A lightweight, type-safe i18n toolkit for Backpack projects.

## Overview

This package helps you:

* define translations for multiple languages with **identical keys**
* create a **fully type-safe** `translate()` function (including interpolation)
* use small, composable selectors like `message`, `pluralize`, and `timeSelect`
* format numbers and dates consistently using a lightweight `createFormatter()` wrapper around `Intl`

No runtime magic, no loaders, no surprise side quests. Just the power of TypeScript.

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/i18n
```

## Quick start

### 1) Define translations

Use `defineTranslations()` to enforce that all language dictionaries have the **exact same keys**.

```ts
import { defineTranslations } from "@backpack/i18n";

export const translations = defineTranslations({
  en: {
    "app.title": "Backpack application",
    "cart.items": (i: { count: number }) => `Cart (${i.count})` as const,
    "time.status": (i: { instant: Temporal.Instant }) =>
      `Timestamp: ${i.instant.epochMilliseconds}` as const,
  },
  nl: {
    "app.title": "Backpack applicatie",
    "cart.items": (i: { count: number }) => `Winkelwagen (${i.count})` as const,
    "time.status": (i: { instant: Temporal.Instant }) =>
      `Tijdstip: ${i.instant.epochMilliseconds}` as const,
  },
});
```

### 2) Create a translate function

Use `createTranslateFn()` to get a translate function that is:

* type-safe on keys (supports nested keys via dot paths)
* type-safe on interpolation (function translations infer parameters)

```ts
import { createTranslateFn } from "@backpack/i18n";

const t = createTranslateFn(translations);

t("nl", "app.title"); // "Backpack applicatie"
t("en", "cart.items", { count: 3 }); // "Cart (3)"
```

### 3) Bind to a language

Use `t.forLanguage()` to create a language-bound function. You can pass:

* a static language (`"nl"`)
* or a getter (`() => currentLanguage`)

```ts
const tn = t.forLanguage("nl");

tn("app.title"); // "Backpack applicatie"
tn("cart.items", { count: 2 }); // "Winkelwagen (2)"
```

```ts
let currentLanguage: "nl" | "en" = "nl";
const tl = t.forLanguage(() => currentLanguage);

tl("app.title"); // "Backpack applicatie"
currentLanguage = "en";
tl("app.title"); // "Backpack application"
```

## Translation values

Translation values can be:

* plain values (string/number/etc)
* functions for interpolation

```ts
export const translations = defineTranslations({
  en: {
    "greeting": (i: { name: string }) => `Hi ${i.name}!` as const,
    "cta.buy": "Buy",
  },
  nl: {
    "greeting": (i: { name: string }) => `Hoi ${i.name}!` as const,
    "cta.buy": "Kopen",
  },
});

const t = createTranslateFn(translations);
t("nl", "greeting", { name: "John" }); // "Hoi John!"
```

## Selectors

Selectors are small helpers that return translation functions. They are useful to keep translation files readable and consistent.

### `message()`

`message()` helps TypeScript keep literal strings inferred precisely or keeps function signatures clean.

```ts
import { message } from "@backpack/i18n/selectors";

export const translations = defineTranslations({
  en: {
    "welcome": message((i: { name: string }) => `Welcome ${i.name}!`),
    "logout": message("Logout"),
  },
  nl: {
    "welcome": message((i: { name: string }) => `Welkom ${i.name}!`),
    "logout": message("Uitloggen"),
  },
});
```

### `pluralize()`

`pluralize()` uses `Intl.PluralRules` to select the correct plural form.

```ts
import { pluralize } from "@backpack/i18n/selectors";

export const translations = defineTranslations({
  en: {
    "files.count": pluralize((i: { count: number }) => ({
      one: `${i.count} file`,
      other: `${i.count} files`,
    })),
  },
  nl: {
    "files.count": pluralize((i: { count: number }) => ({
      one: `${i.count} bestand`,
      other: `${i.count} bestanden`,
    })),
  },
});
```

Notes:

* If a plural rule is missing, it falls back to `other`.
* The `locale` argument is optional; if omitted, the runtime default locale is used.

### `timeSelect()`

`timeSelect()` selects a message based on whether an instant is in the past or future.

It compares using `Temporal.Instant` (absolute time), so it does not require a timezone.

```ts
import { timeSelect } from "@backpack/i18n/selectors";
import { Temporal } from "temporal-polyfill";

export const translations = defineTranslations({
  en: {
    "event.when": timeSelect((i: { instant: Temporal.Instant }) => ({
      past: "Already happened",
      future: "Still coming",
    })),
  },
  nl: {
    "event.when": timeSelect((i: { instant: Temporal.Instant }) => ({
      past: "Dit was al gebeurd",
      future: "Dit komt nog",
    })),
  },
});
```

## Type definitions

The library also exports utility types to strongly type `translate` in classes and services.

### Infer supported languages

```ts
import type { InferLanguage } from "@backpack/i18n";

type Language = InferLanguage<typeof translations>;
// "en" | "nl"
```

### Typing a translate function

```ts
import { createTranslateFn, type TranslateFn } from "@backpack/i18n";
import { translations } from "./i18n";

export class TripMapper {
  private readonly translate: TranslateFn<typeof translations>;

  constructor() {
    this.translate = createTranslateFn(translations);
  }
}
```

`TranslateFn<typeof translations>` automatically derives:

* allowed languages
* valid dot-path keys
* interpolation parameters
* return types

Providing the second generic parameter is optional and only needed if you want to restrict the language union.

### Typing a language-bound function

```ts
import { createTranslateFn, type TranslateForLanguageFn } from "@backpack/i18n";
import { translations } from "./i18n";

export class TripMapper {
    private readonly translate: TranslateForLanguageFn<typeof translations>;

    constructor() {
        this.translate = createTranslateFn(translations).forLanguage(() => "nl"); // or some dynamic language
    }
}
```

## Formatter utilities

`createFormatter()` provides a small, consistent wrapper around `Intl` for:

* `number()`
* `currency()`
* `date()`
* `time()`
* `datetime()`

It supports locale resolution and a default time zone (defaults to `Europe/Amsterdam`).

```ts
import { createFormatter } from "@backpack/i18n/formatters";

const fmt = createFormatter(() => "nl", {
  defaultTimeZone: "Europe/Amsterdam",
  defaultCurrency: "EUR",
  enforce24Hour: true,
});

fmt.number(12.345);
fmt.currency(19.99);
fmt.date(new Date(), "narrow");
fmt.time(new Date(), "short");
fmt.datetime(new Date(), "medium");
```

### Formatting presets overview

| Helper   | Preset    | nl-NL example                     | en-GB example                       |
| -------- | --------- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| number   | `integer` | 12                                | 12                                  |
| number   | `decimal` | 12,35                             | 12.35                               |
| currency | `symbol`  | € 19,99                           | €19.99                              |
| currency | `name`    | 19,99 euro                        | 19.99 euros                         |
| date     | `short`   | 14-01-2026                        | 14/01/2026                          |
| date     | `medium`  | 14 jan 2026                       | 14 Jan 2026                         |
| date     | `narrow`  | wo 14 jan 2026                    | Wed, 14 Jan 2026                    |
| date     | `long`    | 14 januari 2026                   | 14 January 2026                     |
| date     | `full`    | woensdag 14 januari 2026          | Wednesday, 14 January 2026          |
| time     | `short`   | 14:05                             | 14:05                               |
| time     | `medium`  | 14:05:26                          | 14:05:26                            |
| time     | `long`    | 14:05:26 CET                      | 14:05:26 CET                        |
| datetime | `short`   | 14-01-2026, 15:40                 | 14/01/2026, 15:40                   |
| datetime | `narrow`  | wo 14 jan 2026, 15:40             | Wed, 14 Jan 2026, 15:40             |
| datetime | `medium`  | 14 jan 2026, 15:40                | 14 Jan 2026, 15:40                  |
| datetime | `full`    | woensdag 14 januari 2026 om 15:40 | Wednesday, 14 January 2026 at 15:40 |

### Date and time inputs

The formatter accepts:

* `Date`
* Temporal types that implement `toDate()`
* Temporal types that can be converted to a ZonedDateTime using a timezone
* fallback objects that implement `toLocaleString()`

If you pass a `Temporal.PlainDate` or `Temporal.PlainDateTime`, the formatter will try to convert it using the configured `defaultTimeZone`.

## Temporal support

Since Node.js hasn't yet implemented Temporal, use the polyfill:

```bash
npm install temporal-polyfill
```

And import it like this:

```ts
import { Temporal } from "temporal-polyfill";
```

## When to use this library

Use `@backpack/i18n` when:

* your translations live **entirely inside your codebase**
* you want **maximum type safety** with minimal runtime overhead
* you do not need runtime-loaded translation files or CMS-backed content
* you prefer simple functions over string-based ICU message formats

This is **not a silver bullet**. If you need:

* dynamic translation loading
* editor tooling for translators
* ICU message syntax
* external localization platforms

then a heavier i18n solution may be a better fit.

## Tips & best practices

1. **Avoid enums for translation keys**\
   Enums add indirection and runtime output without providing additional safety here.\
   Let the translation object itself be the single source of truth.

2. **Group translations by domain**\
   Split large translation objects by feature (e.g. `booking`, `payment`, `errors`) and compose them before calling `defineTranslations()`.

## API overview

### `defineTranslations(translations)`

Defines and returns a translations object for multiple languages while enforcing that all languages have the same keys.

### `createTranslateFn(translations)`

Creates a translate function.

* Key types are derived using dot-paths (e.g. `"a.b.c"`).
* If the translation value is a function, args are inferred from its parameters.

## Modules

* [index](index/index.md)
* [selectors](selectors/index.md)

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/packages/@backpack/testing.md'

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/testing

# `@backpack/testing` 📋

This package provides testing utilities to use with Vitest.

## Installing

First, ensure you have set up Nexus as private registry needed to use
Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install -D @backpack/testing
```

## Utilities

This package currently provides the following testing utilities:

* `createMockedObject()` for creating type-safe mocked objects
* `createBuilder()` for building test data with composable defaults

## `createMockedObject()`

`createMockedObject()` creates a type-safe mock object for a dependency.

It can be used in two ways:

* pass a class reference to mock a class-based dependency
* pass a generic type to mock an interface, type alias or other object-shaped
  dependency

Both modes return a `MockedObject<T>`. Methods are Vitest-compatible mock
functions, so they can be configured with helpers like `mockReturnValue()`,
`mockResolvedValue()` and `mockImplementation()`.

### Mock a class dependency

When a class reference is provided, `createMockedObject()` patches all prototype
methods with Vitest-compatible spy functions.

```ts
import { describe, it } from "vitest";
import { createMockedObject } from "@backpack/testing";

import { MyService } from "./my-service";
import { MyRepository } from "./my-repository";

describe("MyService", () => {
  const repositoryMock = createMockedObject(MyRepository);
  const myService = new MyService(repositoryMock);

  afterEach(() => {
    repositoryMock.resetAll();
  });

  it("should invoke the repository only once", () => {
    myService.doSomething();
    expect(repositoryMock.save).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });

  it("should handle value returned by repository", () => {
    repositoryMock.save.mockReturnValue("some value");
    const result = myService.doSomething();
    expect(result.value).toBe("some value");
  });
});
```

You can also provide a template to override methods or properties.

```ts
const repositoryMock = createMockedObject(MyRepository, {
  save: () => "some value",
});
```

### Mock an interface or type alias

When no class reference is provided, `createMockedObject()` uses a `Proxy` to
create mock functions lazily when they are accessed. This is useful for
interfaces and type aliases, because they do not exist at runtime.

```ts
import { describe, it } from "vitest";
import { createMockedObject } from "@backpack/testing";

interface MyRepository {
  save(item: Item): Promise<void>;
  findById(id: string): Promise<Item | undefined>;
}

describe("MyService", () => {
  const repositoryMock = createMockedObject<MyRepository>();
  const myService = new MyService(repositoryMock);

  afterEach(() => {
    repositoryMock.resetAll();
  });

  it("should invoke the repository only once", async () => {
    await myService.doSomething();

    expect(repositoryMock.save).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });

  it("should handle value returned by repository", async () => {
    const item = { id: "item-1" };

    repositoryMock.findById.mockResolvedValue(item);

    await expect(myService.findItem("item-1")).resolves.toBe(item);
  });
});
```

For non-function properties, provide a template value explicitly.

```ts
interface ServiceConfig {
  baseUrl: string;
  timeoutInMs: number;
}

const configMock = createMockedObject<ServiceConfig>({
  baseUrl: "https://example.com",
  timeoutInMs: 1000,
});
```

## `createBuilder()`

`createBuilder()` helps you create test data with reusable defaults.

In many tests, most of the object is just setup noise. You usually only care
about one or two fields that are relevant for that specific test. Builders let
you define a valid default object once, and then override only the parts that
matter in each test.

The builder uses deep merge semantics, so nested objects can be overridden
without repeating the full object shape.

### Features

* inference-first builders with minimal boilerplate
* optional typed mode for domain-shaped validation
* deep merge of defaults and overrides
* explicit support for `undefined` and `REMOVE`
* `extend()` for composing builders
* `.tap()` and `.map()` for additional workflows
* `lazy()` for dynamic defaults such as UUIDs

### Quick example

```ts
import { createBuilder } from "@backpack/testing";

interface Device {
  deviceId: string;
  installationId: string;
  os: {
    name: "IOS" | "ANDROID";
  };
  messaging?: {
    pushToken?: string;
  };
  preferences: {
    language: "NL" | "EN";
  };
  nsrId: string;
}

const createDevice = createBuilder()
  .typed<Device>()
  .withDefaults({
    deviceId: "device-1",
    installationId: "installation-1",
    os: { name: "IOS" },
    preferences: { language: "NL" },
    nsrId: "nsr-1",
  });

const device = createDevice({
  messaging: { pushToken: "abc" },
});
```

In this example, `createDevice()` always returns a valid `Device`. Individual
tests can override only the fields they care about, while the builder keeps the
rest of the object stable and predictable.

### Typed builders

Use `.typed<T>()` when the builder should produce objects that conform to a
domain type.

```ts
const createDevice = createBuilder()
  .typed<Device>()
  .withDefaults({
    deviceId: "device-1",
    installationId: "installation-1",
    os: { name: "IOS" },
    preferences: { language: "NL" },
    nsrId: "nsr-1",
  });
```

Typed builders validate the defaults, extensions and overrides against the
target shape. This catches typos and extra keys close to the test setup, instead
of letting invalid test data drift through the test suite.

Required fields must be present in the final result. Optional fields may be
omitted, set to `undefined`, or removed with `REMOVE`.

### Mental model

Overrides behave like partial object assignments.

```ts
const device = createDevice({
  os: { name: "ANDROID" },
});
```

This keeps the default device, but replaces `os.name` with `"ANDROID"`.

For nested objects, only the provided keys are changed. Other nested keys are
kept from the defaults.

```ts
const device = createDevice({
  messaging: { pushToken: "abc" },
});
```

This adds or updates `messaging.pushToken` without requiring the test to repeat
the rest of the device object.

### Merge semantics

| Input            | Behavior                                   |
|------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| key omitted      | leave the default value unchanged          |
| `key: value`     | assign the value or deep merge object      |
| `key: undefined` | explicitly set the property to `undefined` |
| `key: REMOVE`    | delete the property                        |
| arrays           | replace the array                          |

### Optional properties: `undefined` vs `REMOVE`

For optional properties, setting a property to `undefined` and removing the
property are not the same thing.

```ts
import { createTypedBuilder, REMOVE } from "@backpack/testing";

interface Person {
  name: string;
  age?: number;
}

const createPersonWithAge = createTypedBuilder<Person>().withDefaults({
  name: "Vera",
  age: 31,
});

const a = createPersonWithAge();
const b = createPersonWithAge({ age: undefined });
const c = createPersonWithAge({ age: REMOVE });

console.log(a); // { name: "Vera", age: 31 }
console.log(b); // { name: "Vera", age: undefined }
console.log(c); // { name: "Vera" }
```

In this example:

* omitting `age` keeps the default value
* setting `age` to `undefined` keeps the property, but assigns `undefined`
* setting `age` to `REMOVE` removes the property from the resulting object

Use `undefined` when the property should still be present with an explicit
`undefined` value. Use `REMOVE` when the property should not be present at all.

### Lazy defaults

Use `lazy()` when a default value should be generated for each build call.

```ts
import { createBuilder, lazy } from "@backpack/testing";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const createDevice = createBuilder()
  .typed<Device>()
  .withDefaults({
    deviceId: lazy(() => randomUUID()),
    installationId: "installation-1",
    os: { name: "IOS" },
    preferences: { language: "NL" },
    nsrId: "nsr-1",
  });

const firstDevice = createDevice();
const secondDevice = createDevice();
```

Without `lazy()`, a value such as `randomUUID()` would be evaluated once when the
builder is defined. With `lazy()`, it is evaluated every time the builder is
called.

Lazy values work recursively and are preserved when builders are extended.

### Builder composition

Use `extend()` to create a more specific builder from an existing one.

```ts
const createDeviceWithPushToken = createDevice.extend({
  messaging: { pushToken: "123" },
});
```

This is useful when multiple tests share the same variation of an object. Instead
of repeating the same override in every test, define a specialized builder once
and keep the individual tests focused on what they actually verify.

```ts
const iosDevice = createDevice();

const androidDevice = createDevice({
  os: { name: "ANDROID" },
});

const deviceWithPushToken = createDeviceWithPushToken();
```

Extensions are merged with the previous defaults. When a test calls the extended
builder, it can still apply additional overrides.

```ts
const androidDeviceWithPushToken = createDeviceWithPushToken({
  os: { name: "ANDROID" },
});
```

### Effects and mapping

Builders can also be wrapped with `.tap()` or `.map()` when test setup needs an
extra step.

Use `.tap()` for side effects. The original built value is returned.

```ts
const givenDevice = createDevice.tap(async (device) => {
  await deviceServiceFixture.givenDevice(device);
});

const device = await givenDevice({
  os: { name: "ANDROID" },
});
```

This pattern is useful for fixtures: build the object, store it somewhere, and
continue using the same object in the test.

Use `.map()` when the built value should be transformed into something else.

```ts
const whenMessagePublished = createEvent.map((event) =>
  client.process(event),
);

const result = await whenMessagePublished({});
```

### tap vs map

* `tap()` performs a side effect and returns the original value
* `map()` transforms the value and returns the mapped result

### Advanced patterns

Most builders should stay small and boring. When a builder starts to model more
complex setup logic, prefer patterns that preserve the builder's own type
inference instead of wrapping everything in broad `DeepPartial<T>` helper
functions.

#### Discriminated unions

Typed builders can be used with discriminated unions, but deep merge does not
understand mutually exclusive branches. It merges object shapes structurally:
omitted keys are kept, provided keys are overwritten or merged.

For discriminated unions, prefer dedicated builders for each subtype.

Considering:

```ts
type Animal = Cat | Dog;

interface Cat {
  type: "cat";
  name: string;
  meow: string;
}

interface Dog {
  type: "dog";
  name: string;
  bark: string;
}
```

Don't do:

```ts
const createAnimal = createBuilder()
  .typed<Animal>()
  .withDefaults({
    type: "dog",
    name: "Buddy",
    bark: "Woof!",
  });

const cat = createAnimal({
  type: "cat",
  name: "Some cat",
  meow: "Meow!",
});

// Runtime result:
// {
//   type: "cat",
//   name: "Some cat",
//   bark: "Woof!",
//   meow: "Meow!",
// }
```

This is valid structurally, because the result still satisfies `Animal`, but the
`Dog`-specific `bark` field is not removed automatically.

But do instead:

```ts
const createDog = createBuilder()
  .typed<Dog>()
  .withDefaults({
    type: "dog",
    name: "Buddy",
    bark: "Woof!",
  });

const createCat = createBuilder()
  .typed<Cat>()
  .withDefaults({
    type: "cat",
    name: "Minoes",
    meow: "Meow!",
  });

const dog = createDog({ name: "Max" });
const cat = createCat({ name: "Some cat" });
```

Use a union builder only when you explicitly want deep merge behavior across
branches and are okay with branch-specific fields being flattened into the final
object.

#### Wrapping builders with extra logic

When you want to add extra setup logic, prefer `.tap()` or `.map()`. This keeps
the builder call signature intact, so overrides stay inference-driven.

Don't do:

```ts
import type { DeepPartial } from "@backpack/testing";

async function givenDevice(overrides?: DeepPartial<Device>) {
  const device = createDevice(overrides);

  await deviceServiceFixture.givenDevice(device);

  return device;
}
```

This works, but the broad `DeepPartial<Device>` parameter loses the precise
literal inference from each call site.

But do instead:

```ts
const givenDevice = createDevice.tap(async (device) => {
  await deviceServiceFixture.givenDevice(device);
});

const device = await givenDevice({
  os: { name: "ANDROID" },
});
```

Use `.map()` when the wrapper should return another value.

```ts
const whenMessagePublished = createEvent.map((event) =>
  messageClient.publish(event),
);

const result = await whenMessagePublished({
  payload: { title: "Hello" },
});
```

#### Parameterized builders

When a helper needs parameters and still needs builder overrides, prefer
currying with `.extend()`. This lets the parameter create a specialized builder,
and keeps the final overrides fully inferred.

Don't do:

```ts
import type { DeepPartial } from "@backpack/testing";

function createDeviceForInstallation(
  installationId: string,
  overrides?: DeepPartial<Device>,
) {
  return createDevice({
    installationId,
    ...overrides,
  });
}
```

This mixes builder configuration and per-test overrides in one broad function
argument.

But do instead:

```ts
function createDeviceForInstallation(installationId: string) {
  return createDevice.extend({ installationId });
}

const createDeviceForInstallation1 = createDeviceForInstallation(
  "installation-1",
);

const androidDevice = createDeviceForInstallation1({
  os: { name: "ANDROID" },
});
```

This pattern is useful for fixtures such as `createDeviceForCustomer(customerId)`,
`createOrderForUser(userId)` or `createMessageForChannel(channel)`.

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/hono

# `@backpack/hono`

Utilities for running and testing Backpack applications with Hono.

> \[!INFO]
> Currently, this package focuses on local development and testing.
> Runtime utilities for Hono-based applications will be added in later releases.

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/hono
```

## `fromAwsLambdaHandler()` adapter

Use the `fromAwsLambdaHandler()` adapter to integrate your existing API Gateway Lambda handler in a Hono application.

For example:

```ts
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { fromAwsLambdaHandler } from "@backpack/hono";

import { handler as helloWorld } from "./app/hello-world.lambda";
import { handler as updateBook } from "./app/update-book.lambda";

const app = new Hono();

app.get("/api/v1/hello", fromAwsLambdaHandler(helloWorld));
```

Integrating your AWS Lambda handlers in a Hono application provides the following benefits:

* Local development: Hono provides several dev servers to enable local development, such as `@hono/vite-dev-server`.
  Check out our dedicated [how-to guide](/guides/tooling/local-development.md) on local development
* Testing: since Hono provides a Fetch-like API, it allows a more ergonomic way to test your AWS handlers.

> \[!WARNING]
> This adapter is intended for local development and tests. It provides a minimal local API Gateway event and Lambda
> context, but does not fully emulate API Gateway.
>
> Binary/base64 encoded request and response bodies are currently out of scope.

## `createTestRestClient()`

Creates a Backpack REST client for testing a Hono app.

The returned client uses `@backpack/rest-client`, but delegates requests directly to the provided Hono app instead of
performing real network calls. This is useful for in-memory integration tests.

Before:

```ts
import app from "../server.ts";

it("should update a book", async () => {
  const response = await app.request("/api/v1/books/978-6-2270-9353-7", {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ title: "Man in the Mist" }),
  });

  const updatedBook = await response.json();

  expect(updatedBook).toEqual({
    isbn: "978-6-2270-9353-7",
    title: "Man in the Mist",
  });
});
```

After:

```ts
import { createTestRestClient } from "@backpack/hono";
import app from "../server.ts";

const restClient = createTestRestClient(app);

it("should update a book", async () => {
  const updatedBook = await restClient
    .url("/api/v1/books/978-6-2270-9353-7")
    .put({ title: "Man in the Mist" })
    .json();

  expect(updatedBook).toEqual({
    isbn: "978-6-2270-9353-7",
    title: "Man in the Mist",
  });
});
```

## Functions

* [createTestRestClient](functions/createTestRestClient.md)
* [fromAwsLambdaHandler](functions/fromAwsLambdaHandler.md)

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/rest-client

# `@backpack/rest-client` 🌍

A pre-configured REST client built on top of [Wretch], enhanced with additional middleware for extended functionality.

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/rest-client
```

## Example usage

Wretch is basically a thin wrapper around the Fetch API:

```ts
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";

const books = await createRestClient({ baseUrl: "https://my-book-store.com" })
  .url("/api/v1/books")
  .get()
  .json();
```

You can check out the [Wretch documentation][Wretch] to learn more.

## Advanced usage

```ts
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";

const restClient = createRestClient({
  // additional options:
  baseUrl: "https://api.bookstore.com/",
  timeoutMilliseconds: 2_000,
  apiManagementSubscriptionKey: "...",
  userAgent: "my-app/v2",
});

// additional methods:
const result = await restClient

  // set or override subscription key:
  .apiManagementSubscriptionKey("...")

  // set or override user agent header
  // shorthand for `.headers({ "User-Agent", "..." })`:
  .userAgent("my-app")

  // set or override timeout:
  .setTimeout(2_000)

  // shorthand for `.headers({ "Accept-Language", "..." })`:
  .acceptLanguage("my-app")

  .url("/api/v1/books")
  .get()

  // shorthand for `.json().then(it => MyZodSchema.parse(it)`
  .validatedJson(MyZodSchema);
```

## Handling HTTP errors

Unlike the raw [Fetch API], Wretch rejects HTTP error responses. That means methods such as `.res()` or `.json()` throw
for statuses like `400` or `404`, instead of returning a `Response` directly.

This is useful for regular API calls, because consumers do not have to manually check `response.ok`.

When you do want to handle a specific HTTP status yourself, use the matching Wretch hook and return the value that
should continue through the chain:

```ts
const response = await restClient
  .url("/api/v1/books")
  .get()
  .badRequest((error) => error.response)
  .res();

expect(response.status).toBe(400);
```

Wretch exposes specific hooks such as `.badRequest()` and `.notFound()` for this. The returned value from the callback
becomes the value for the next step in the chain, so returning `error.response` maps the error back to the raw
`Response`.

## Middleware

The Backpack REST client supports optional middleware that can be executed before and after each request.

Middleware can be added via the `middlewares` option when creating the client:

```ts
import { createRestClient, type Middleware } from "@backpack/rest-client";

const restClient = createRestClient({
  middlewares: [yourMiddleware()],
});

export const yourMiddleware = (): Middleware => {
  return (next) => async (url, requestInit) => {
    // (do something before the request is sent)

    const response = await next(url, requestInit);

    // (do something after the response is received)

    return response;
  };
};
```

Multiple middleware can be combined and are executed in the order they are provided.

## OAuth bearer tokens

You can add OAuth bearer tokens to outgoing requests with the `bearerToken()` middleware. Token providers are async, so
they can call an identity provider, read secrets lazily, and cache token responses.

### OAuth 2.0 client credentials

The `clientCredentials()` provider supports the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow for any token endpoint that accepts
`grant_type=client_credentials`, `client_id`, `client_secret`, and an optional `scope`.

```ts
import { SecretsManagerClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-secrets-manager";
import { CachedSecretsManagerService } from "@backpack/aws-secrets-manager";
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";
import {
  bearerToken,
  clientCredentials,
  fromAwsSecretsManager,
} from "@backpack/rest-client/middleware";

const secretsManager = new CachedSecretsManagerService(
  new SecretsManagerClient(),
);

const restClient = createRestClient({
  baseUrl: "https://api.bookstore.com",
  middlewares: [
    bearerToken(
      clientCredentials({
        tokenUrl: "https://identity.example.com/oauth2/token",
        clientId: "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
        clientSecret: fromAwsSecretsManager<{ clientSecret: string }>({
          secretsManager,
          secretId: "/bookstore/oauth/client-credentials",
          select: (secret) => secret.clientSecret,
        }),
        scope: "api://bookstore/.default",
      }),
    ),
  ],
});
```

For local development you can load the same values from environment variables:

```ts
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";
import {
  bearerToken,
  clientCredentials,
  fromEnv,
} from "@backpack/rest-client/middleware";

const restClient = createRestClient({
  baseUrl: "https://api.bookstore.com",
  middlewares: [
    bearerToken(
      clientCredentials({
        tokenUrl: fromEnv("OAUTH_TOKEN_URL"),
        clientId: fromEnv("OAUTH_CLIENT_ID"),
        clientSecret: fromEnv("OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET"),
        scope: fromEnv("OAUTH_SCOPE"),
      }),
    ),
  ],
});
```

For Azure Entra ID v2, use `azureClientCredentials()` as a small convenience wrapper. It derives the v2 token endpoint
from `tenantId`, sends `scope`, and intentionally does not support legacy `resource` based token requests.

```ts
import {
  azureClientCredentials,
  bearerToken,
  fromEnv,
} from "@backpack/rest-client/middleware";

const azureMiddleware = bearerToken(
  azureClientCredentials({
    tenantId: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000",
    clientId: "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
    clientSecret: fromEnv("AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET"),
    scope: "api://bookstore/.default",
  }),
);
```

For tests or custom team logic, use `staticToken()` or `callbackToken()`:

```ts
import {
  bearerToken,
  callbackToken,
  staticToken,
} from "@backpack/rest-client/middleware";

const testMiddleware = bearerToken(staticToken("test-token"));
const customMiddleware = bearerToken(callbackToken(() => tokenStore.get()));
```

## Adding additional logging

You can add logging using the `powertoolsLogging()` middleware.

This middleware uses [Powertools Logger] to add structured logging for outgoing requests and incoming responses.

```ts
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";
import { powertoolsLogging } from "@backpack/rest-client/middleware";
import { Logger } from "@aws-lambda-powertools/logger";

const restClient = createRestClient({
  middlewares: [
    powertoolsLogging({
      logger: new Logger({
        /* ... */
      }),
      requestLogging: {
        enabled: true,
        includeRequestBody: false,
      },
      responseLogging: {
        enabled: true,
      },
    }),
  ],
});
```

## Circuit breaker

You can protect your application against failing downstream services by adding a **circuit breaker**.

A circuit breaker prevents repeated calls to a failing service by temporarily failing fast once a failure threshold is exceeded. This reduces latency during incidents and gives the downstream service time to recover.

### Basic usage

```ts
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";
import { circuitBreaker } from "@backpack/rest-client/middleware";

const restClient = createRestClient({
  baseUrl: "https://api.bookstore.com",
  middlewares: [
    circuitBreaker({
      key: "bookstore-api",
    }),
  ],
});
```

### Configuration options

```ts
circuitBreaker({
  // unique identifier for the downstream dependency
  key: "bookstore-api",

  // minimum number of requests before evaluating failure rate
  volumeThreshold: 20,

  // percentage of failures required to open the circuit
  errorThresholdPercentage: 50,

  // time (in ms) the circuit remains open before allowing a probe request
  resetTimeoutMs: 10_000,

  // rolling time window (in ms) used to calculate failure rate
  rollingWindowMs: 30_000,

  // maximum number of concurrent probe requests while half-open
  halfOpenMaxCalls: 1,
});
```

### Failure semantics

By default, the circuit breaker treats the following as failures:

* network errors (e.g. timeouts, aborted requests)
* HTTP 5xx responses

HTTP 4xx responses are **not** considered failures by default, since they typically indicate client-side issues.

This behavior can be customized using the `isFailure` option.

### Error handling

When the circuit is open, requests fail fast by throwing a `CircuitBreakerOpenError`.

You can catch this error explicitly if you want to handle it differently.

> \[!NOTE]
> The circuit breaker state is kept in-memory per execution environment.
> This provides a simple and low-overhead default that works well in serverless environments.

> \[!TIP]
> Do you have ideas for additional middleware (retry, rate limiting)?
> Please consider making a contribution by submitting [a pull request][repo].

[repo]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK

[Wretch]: https://github.com/elbywan/wretch

[Fetch API]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch

[Powertools Logger]: https://docs.powertools.aws.dev/lambda/typescript/latest/core/logger/

* [index](index/index.md)
* [middleware](middleware/index.md)

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/vite-plugin-lambda

# `@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda`️ 🚀

> \[!WARNING]
> `@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda` is deprecated. For local development, use a setup based on [Hono](https://hono.dev/)
> instead. Check out the [Local Development](/guides/tooling/local-development.html#local-development) how-to guide for
> more information.

Inspired by [Vite Plugin Node](https://www.npmjs.com/package/vite-plugin-node), this package contains a plugin
for [Vite] that enables you to run your lambdas locally in a dev server.

## Features

* Runs on [Vite], so all the good stuff like Hot Module Replacement (HMR), programmatic API and tons of
  configuration options, is automatically available.
* Emulates the AWS API Gateway proxy integration locally:
  * converts every HTTP request into a `APIGatewayProxyEvent` to invoke your lambda;
  * converts the `APIGatewayProxyResult` returned by your lambda back into an HTTP response;
* Easily extendable with custom [Express] handlers, like serving a Swagger UI based on your OpenAPI spec
* Allows easy debugging of your REST lambdas

## Getting started

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install -D @backpack/vite-plugin-lambda
```

You also need to install `vite` itself, as well as `express` as web framework for Node.js:

```bash
npm install -D vite express @types/express
```

Next, set up your `vite.config.ts` in the root of your project:

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import { VitePluginLambda } from "@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda";

export default defineConfig({
  // Vite server config, for details see: https://vitejs.dev/config/#server-host
  server: {
    port: 3000,
  },
  // to support stage-3 decorators:
  esbuild: {
    target: "es2022"
  },
  // add VitePluginLambda as plugin:
  plugins: [
    VitePluginLambda({
      appPath: "./server.ts",
      /* other options are optional: */
      // exportName: "app",
      // appName: "My awesome app",
    }),
  ],
});
```

Now create a `server.ts`, and register your lambda handler function(s) using the `lambdaHandlers` helper function:

```typescript
import express from "express";
import { lambdaHandlers } from "@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda";

export const app = express();

app.use(
  lambdaHandlers({
    handlers: {
      // example:
      "/api/v1/persons": {
        get: {
          handler: () => import("./app/lambdas/get-persons.handler").then((it) => it.handler),
        },
        post: {
          handler: () => import("./app/lambdas/add-person.lambda").then((it) => it.handler),
        },
      },
    },
  }),
);

export default app;
```

Run it! 🚀 Just run `npx vite` to start Vite. You may want to add this as an npm script in your `package.json`:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite"
  }
}
```

Now you can just run `npm run dev`.

> Tip: Vite supports [tons of options](https://vitejs.dev/guide/cli). For example, to automatically open your browser,
> you can specify the script as `vite --open`.

## Rendering Swagger UI

You can include a Swagger UI based on your OpenAPI specs. You can easily achieve this
with [swagger-ui-express](https://www.npmjs.com/package/swagger-ui-express):

```bash
npm install -D swagger-ui-express @types/swagger-ui-express yaml
```

In `server.ts`, add the following code:

```typescript
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

import swaggerUi from "swagger-ui-express";
import YAML from "yaml";

const swaggerDocument = YAML.parse(file);
const file = await readFile("./path/to/openapi.yaml", "utf8");

export const app = express()
  .get("/", (_, res) => res.redirect("/swagger-ui"))
  .use("/swagger-ui", swaggerUi.serve, swaggerUi.setup(swaggerDocument))
  .use(
    lambdaHandlers({
      /* ... */
    }),
  );

export default app;
```

Make sure that `./path/to/openapi.yaml` points to your OpenAPI YAML specs.

## Loading environment variables

You can use `@dotenvx/dotenvx` to load dotenv files for your environment variables.

This allows you even to load different variables, for example using
the [Vite mode](https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode#modes):

```ts
import { config } from "@dotenvx/dotenvx";

// load environment variables
const VITE_MODE = import.meta.env.MODE;

config({
  quiet: true,
  path: [`.env.${VITE_MODE}.local`, `.env.${VITE_MODE}`, ".env.local", ".env"],
  ignore: ["MISSING_ENV_FILE"],
});
```

## Limitations

* This plugin is only intended for AWS lambdas that handle HTTP requests through the
  [AWS API Gateway for REST APIs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/set-up-lambda-integrations.html),
  see [Lambda proxy integrations in API Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/set-up-lambda-proxy-integrations.html).
  This means that if your AWS lambda handles events
  from [a different kind of service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-services.html),
  this plugin might not be suitable for your case. Note
  that [callback-based](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/nodejs-handler.html#nodejs-handler-callback)
  handlers are also not supported.

* When you run your project locally, it won't automatically pick up your environment variables as `process.env`
  variable.
  Please consider using [Vite Plugin Environment](https://www.npmjs.com/package/vite-plugin-environment) for that, which
  is able to expose environment variables to your
  Node.js lambda, and also [supports `.env` files](https://vitejs.dev/guide/env-and-mode.html#env-files). Alternatively,
  you can use [dotenvx](https://github.com/dotenvx/dotenvx) to manually load environment variables in your `server.ts`.

[Vite]: https://vitejs.dev/

[Express]: https://expressjs.com/

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/hono-mockserver

# `@backpack/hono-mockserver` 🧪

A lightweight mock server built on **Hono**, designed for **Node.js and serverless** environments.
Inspired by [WireMock](https://wiremock.org/).

## Overview

This package provides the **core runtime** of the Backpack mockserver:

* a Hono app that behaves like a mock HTTP server
* a REST-based **admin API** to configure mocks and verify requests
* a single, predictable **matching engine** for routing and verification
* pluggable storage (in-memory and DynamoDB)

It is designed to work:

* locally
* in CI
* in AWS Lambda behind API Gateway
* as the runtime behind the Backpack Vitest DX

No Docker, no JVM. Just TypeScript and HTTP.

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md).

Then install:

```bash
npm install @backpack/hono-mockserver
```

## Quick start (local / Node)

Create a mockserver as a plain Hono app:

```ts
import { createMockServer, inMemoryStore } from "@backpack/hono-mockserver";

const app = createMockServer({
  store: inMemoryStore(),
});
```

Mount it on any HTTP server you like:

```ts
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";

serve({
  fetch: app.fetch,
  port: 3001,
});
```

Your mockserver is now running 🎉

The admin API is available under `/__mockserver`.

## Using it in AWS Lambda

The Hono app can be wrapped in a Lambda handler:

```ts
import { handle } from "hono/aws-lambda";
import { createMockServer, inMemoryStore } from "@backpack/hono-mockserver";

export const handler = handle(
  createMockServer({
    store: inMemoryStore(),
  }),
);
```

This works behind API Gateway (REST or HTTP) without special configuration.

## Admin API

The admin API allows you to configure mocks and verify traffic.

### Endpoints

| Method | Path            | Purpose                         |
| -----: | --------------- | ------------------------------- |
|    GET | `/mappings`     | list all mappings               |
|    PUT | `/mappings/:id` | create or update a mapping      |
| DELETE | `/mappings/:id` | delete a mapping                |
|   POST | `/reset`        | clear mappings & recorded calls |
|    GET | `/requests`     | list received requests          |
|   POST | `/verify`       | verify request patterns         |

### Debugging

You can debug your mappings and requests in several ways:

1. **Swagger UI**: Visit `/__mockserver` in your browser to see the interactive API documentation and test the admin endpoints.
2. **Admin API**: Use `curl` or any HTTP client to inspect `/__mockserver/mappings` and `/__mockserver/requests`.
3. **Client**: If you are using `@backpack/mockserver-client`, you can use the client's built-in methods to inspect the state (see its documentation).

## Request matching

### RequestPattern

```ts
type RequestPattern = {
  method: "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "PATCH" | "DELETE" | "HEAD" | "OPTIONS";
  pathMatcher: PathMatcher;
  headers?: MatcherMap;
  query?: MatcherMap;
  body?: BodyMatcher;
};
```

### PathMatcher

```ts
type PathMatcher =
  | { type: "exact"; value: string }
  | { type: "glob"; value: string }
  | { type: "contains"; value: string }
  | { type: "regex"; value: string; flags?: string };
```

Glob matching supports `**` for zero or more path segments.

### Header & query matchers

```ts
type Matcher =
  | { type: "equals"; value: string }
  | { type: "contains"; value: string }
  | { type: "regex"; value: string; flags?: string }
  | { type: "exists" }
  | { type: "absent" };
```

### Body matching

* **text** → string matcher
* **json** →
  * `equals` (deep exact match)
  * `subset` (deep partial match, objects + arrays)

## Priority

Mappings can define a `priority` (lower = wins):

```ts
const mapping = {
  id: "fallback",
  priority: 10,
  // ...
}
```

Useful for default routes vs. more specific mocks.

## What this package does *not* do

* no fetch interception
* no Vitest helpers
* no DSL like `whenGet()`

Those live in `@backpack/mockserver-client`.

## When to use this package directly

Use `@backpack/hono-mockserver` if you:

* want a mockserver as a standalone service
* deploy mocks centrally (shared test environment)
* run it in Lambda or behind API Gateway
* need full control over routing and lifecycle

If you’re writing tests → you probably want the client package instead: `@backpack/mockserver-client`.

## Modules

* [admin](admin/index.md)
* [index](index/index.md)

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/mockserver-client

# `@backpack/mockserver-client` 🧩

This package provides the developer-facing API for working with the Backpack mockserver, with a strong focus on
**testing** and **local development**.

## Overview

* `useMockServer()` — the default, test-first entry point;
* a fluent DSL for defining mocks (`when`, `whenGet`, …);
* expressive **Vitest matchers** (including asymmetric matchers) for verification;
* support for both **in-memory** and **remote** mockservers.

## Installing

```bash
npm install @backpack/mockserver-client
```

## Quick start

The fastest way to get started is with `useMockServer()`.

```ts
import { useMockServer } from "@backpack/mockserver-client/vitest";

const mockServer = useMockServer({ type: "in-memory" }).setup();

it("returns a greeting", async () => {
  await mockServer.whenGet("/hello").respondText("Hi!");

  const res = await fetch("/hello");
  const text = await res.text();

  expect(text).toBe("Hi!");

  await expect(mockServer).toHaveReceivedRequest({
    method: "GET",
    path: "/hello",
  });
});
```

That’s it.

Behind the scenes, this spins up an in-memory mockserver and intercepts all `fetch()` calls —
without starting an actual HTTP server. However, you can also run it against a remote mockserver.

## When to use this package

Use `@backpack/mockserver-client` if you:

* write integration or contract tests;
* want fast, isolated tests without Docker/WireMock;
* prefer a fluent mocking DSL;
* want expressive Vitest matchers instead of manual assertions;
* if you also intend to run your tests against a deployed app — you won't have to change your test code.

If you need to **run** the mockserver itself, combine this with
`@backpack/hono-mockserver` (directly or via the Backpack CLI).

## `useMockServer()`

`useMockServer()` is the **recommended entry point** for most users.

### In-memory mode

This is the recommended mode for local integration tests. It does not spin up an actual HTTP server, resulting in
superfast tests.

```ts
const mockServer = useMockServer({ type: "in-memory" }).setup();
```

This will:

* spin up a Hono mockserver with an in-memory store
* intercept **all global `fetch()` calls**
* auto-register cleanup in `afterAll()`
* register custom Vitest matchers

Your application code does not need to know it’s being mocked.

### Remote mode (shared or local server)

```ts
const mockServer = useMockServer({
  type: "remote",
  baseUrl: "http://localhost:3001",
}).setup();
```

Use this when:

* running against a shared mockserver
* testing against a locally running instance
* debugging mocks manually via HTTP

### The `.setup()` method

The `.setup()` method is required to initialize the Vitest integration. It performs the following actions:

* **Registers Vitest matchers**: Enables the use of `expect(mockServer).toHaveReceivedRequest(...)`.
* **Registers `beforeEach`**: Automatically resets the mock server (clears mappings and recorded requests) before each
  test.
* **Registers `afterAll`**: Ensures the mock server is properly disposed of after all tests in the file have finished,
  restoring the global `fetch` if necessary.

You can customize the behavior of `setup()`:

```ts
mockServer.setup({
  reset: "manual", // Disable automatic beforeEach reset
  matchers: false, // Disable automatic matcher registration
});
```

## Running a mockserver

### Running locally

You can also run a mockserver as a **standalone local service** using the Backpack CLI:

```bash
npx @backpack/cli mock-server start
```

This starts a `@backpack/hono-mockserver` instance locally, typically on port `3001`.

You can then connect to it using `useMockServer({ type: "remote" })` or via the client API.

This is useful for:

* manual testing
* debugging mappings
* sharing a mockserver between tools or test suites

This allows you to run the exact same tests locally and against a running mockserver
without changing your test code.

### Running in AWS

To deploy it in your AWS account, you can use the `MockServer` construct from `@backpack/cdk-constructs`:

```ts
import { MockServer, AccountDomainName } from "@backpack/cdk-constructs";

new MockServer(this, "MockServer", {
  domainName: new AccountDomainName(this, "MockServerAccountDomainName", {
    subDomain: "mockserver.bookstore",
  }),
});
```

This will deploy it to https://mockserver.bookstore.your-aws-account.cla.ns.nl.

## Mocking requests (DSL)

### Basic examples

```ts
await mockServer.whenGet("/hello").respondText("Hoi!");

await mockServer.when("GET", "/api/**").respondJson({ ok: true });
```

### Partial path matching (glob or contains)

If you don't want to match the full path, you can use **glob wildcards** or a **contains** matcher.

#### Glob wildcards

When a string contains `*` or `?`, it is automatically treated as a glob:

* `*` matches any characters except `/` (single segment);
* `**` matches any characters including `/` (multiple segments);
* `?` matches a single character.

```ts
await mockServer.whenGet("/api/*/users").respondJson([]);
await mockServer.whenGet("/api/**").respondJson({ ok: true });
```

#### Contains matcher

If you want to match any path that contains a specific substring:

```ts
await mockServer
  .when("GET", { type: "contains", value: "checkout" })
  .respondText("matched");
```

### Regex path

```ts
await mockServer
  .when("GET", { type: "regex", value: "^/items/\\d+$" })
  .respondText("matched");
```

### Matching headers

```ts
await mockServer
  .whenGet("/secure")
  .withHeader("authorization", { type: "contains", value: "Bearer " })
  .withHeader("x-env", "test") // equals
  .respondText("ok");
```

Header names are matched **case-insensitively**.

### Matching query parameters

Use `withQuery()` for multiple parameters:

```ts
await mockServer
  .whenGet("/search")
  .withQuery({
    q: "pizza",
    page: { type: "regex", value: "^[0-9]+$" },
  })
  .respondJson({ hits: 3 });
```

Or `withQueryParam()` as a convenience helper:

```ts
await mockServer
  .whenGet("/search")
  .withQueryParam("lang", "nl-NL")
  .respondEmpty({ status: 204 });
```

Additional query parameters in the request are ignored.

### Matching on request body (text)

```ts
await mockServer
  .whenPost("/echo")
  .withBodyText({ type: "contains", value: "hello" })
  .respondText("matched");
```

### Matching on request body (JSON)

Exact match:

```ts
await mockServer
  .whenPost("/submit")
  .withBodyJsonEquals({ a: 1, b: 2 })
  .respondJson({ stored: "exact" });
```

Subset match (allows extra fields in the request body):

```ts
await mockServer
  .whenPost("/submit")
  .withBodyJsonSubset({ a: 1 })
  .respondJson({ stored: "subset" });
```

### Explicit mock with options

Use `.respond()` when you want to provide the full response definition yourself, instead of using one of the convenience
helpers such as `.respondJson()`, `.respondText()`, or `.respondEmpty()`.

Pass mapping options, such as `id` or `priority`, as the second argument.

```ts
await mockServer
  .whenGet("/health")
  .respond({ contentType: "json", json: { status: "ok" } }, { priority: 1 });
```

### Mapping priority

If multiple mappings match, the one with the **lowest priority value wins**.

```ts
await mockServer
  .whenPost("/submit")
  .withBodyJsonEquals({ a: 1 })
  .respondJson({ exact: true }, { priority: 0 });

await mockServer
  .whenPost("/submit")
  .withBodyJsonSubset({ a: 1 })
  .respondJson({ subset: true }, { priority: 10 });
```

## Path matching heuristics

When using strings for paths:

* if it contains `*` or `?`, it is automatically treated as **glob**;
* otherwise, it performs an **exact** match;
* regex and contains matchers must be **specified explicitly**.

## Verifying requests

### Using Vitest matchers

```ts
await expect(mockServer).toHaveReceivedRequest({
  method: "GET",
  path: "/hello",
});

await expect(mockServer).toHaveReceivedRequestsTimes(
  { method: "GET", path: "/hello" },
  2,
);
```

Note: don't forget to `await` the expectation.

### Using the verify API directly

```ts
const result = await mockServer.verify({
  method: "GET",
  path: "/hello",
});

// { matched: true, count: 1 }
```

Verification supports the same matching model as mappings,
including headers, query parameters and body matchers.

In addition, verification also supports **Vitest asymmetric matchers**,
such as `expect.stringContaining`, `expect.stringMatching` and `expect.objectContaining`.

> Note: Vitest matchers are supported **for verification only**.\
> The mocking DSL (`when`, `withHeader`, etc.) continues to use the built-in matcher model.

### Using Vitest matchers (advanced)

In addition to the built-in DSL, you can use **Vitest asymmetric matchers**
for more flexible verification.

```ts
await expect(mockServer).toHaveReceivedRequest({
  method: "POST",
  path: expect.stringMatching(/^\/messages/),
  headers: {
    authorization: expect.stringContaining("Bearer "),
  },
  body: {
    contentType: "json",
    matcher: expect.objectContaining({
      notification: expect.objectContaining({
        title: expect.stringContaining("Hoi"),
      }),
    }),
  },
});
```

This allows you to write more expressive and flexible assertions,
especially for dynamic values such as IDs, tokens, or partially matching JSON payloads.

## Debugging

If you need to inspect the state of the mock server during a test, you can use the following methods:

### List recorded requests

To get a simple list of received requests (method and path):

```ts
const requests = await mockServer.listRequests();
// [{ method: "GET", path: "/hello" }]
```

For full request details (headers, body, etc.), use the underlying client:

```ts
const fullRequests = await mockServer.client.requests.list();
// [{ id: "...", method: "GET", path: "/hello", headers: { ... }, bodyText: "..." }]
```

### List mappings

To see all currently registered mappings:

```ts
const mappings = await mockServer.client.mappings.list();
```

### Manual inspection

When using a remote mockserver, you can also visit the Swagger UI at `/__mockserver` to inspect mappings and requests in
your browser.

## Advanced: creating a client directly

If you need lower-level access, you can create a client manually.

### Remote client

```ts
import { createMockServerClient } from "@backpack/mockserver-client";

const mockServer = createMockServerClient({
  baseUrl: "http://localhost:3001",
});
```

### In-memory client

```ts
import { createMockServer, inMemoryStore } from "@backpack/hono-mockserver";
import { createMockServerClient } from "@backpack/mockserver-client";

const app = createMockServer({
  store: inMemoryStore(),
});

const mockServer = createMockServerClient({
  fetch: (url, init) => app.request(url, init),
});
```

Most users won’t need this — `useMockServer()` already covers the common cases.

# `@backpack/eslint-config`️ 🛠

This package contains presets for ESLint.

## What's included?

This package provides two presets:

* **recommended**: includes type-aware (type-checked) rules from `typescript-eslint`.
  This is the default and preferred preset.
* **legacy**: a previous preset without type-aware rules.
  Use this if you are not ready for type-checked linting or run into issues.

Both presets contain recommended rules from:

* [eslint](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/)
* [typescript-eslint](https://typescript-eslint.io/users/configs#recommended)
* [eslint-plugin-import-x](https://www.npmjs.com/package/eslint-plugin-import-x), including dependencies
  * Pre-configured settings for [`import-x/no-extraneous-dependencies`][no-extraneous-dependencies] matching the
    [recommended project structure](/guides/development/project-structure.md)
* [eslint-plugin-vitest](https://github.com/vitest-dev/eslint-plugin-vitest?tab=readme-ov-file#recommended)

***

> \[!TIP] Feedback requested!
> Would you like to share your thoughts on ESLint presets?
> Please consider making a contribution by submitting [a pull request][repo].

[repo]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK

## Getting started

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.
Also, make sure you are using ESLint 9.0 or higher. If that is not the case, you need to upgrade it first.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install -D @backpack/eslint-config
```

Now, set up your `eslint.config.ts`:

```javascript
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";
import backpack from "@backpack/eslint-config";

export default defineConfig(...backpack.configs.recommended, { // or backpack.configs.legacy
  rules: {
    // additional overrides here...
  },
});
```

If you are migrating from an existing setup, you can remove some unnecessary dependencies:

```bash
npm uninstall @eslint/js @typescript-eslint/parser @vitest/eslint-plugin eslint-import-resolver-typescript eslint-plugin-import eslint-plugin-import-x
```

[no-extraneous-dependencies]: https://github.com/un-ts/eslint-plugin-import-x/blob/HEAD/docs/rules/no-extraneous-dependencies.md

## Interfaces

* [BackpackEslintConfigs](interfaces/BackpackEslintConfigs.md)

## Variables

* [configs](variables/configs.md)
* [default](variables/default.md)

# `@backpack/typescript-config`️ 🛠

This package contains some useful presets for your TypeScript configuration.

## Background

The `tsconfig.json` file can seem a bit scary, with all the different (and sometimes confusing) options.
This package makes this easier by providing a preset.

Most of the decisions are based on this [TSConfig Cheat Sheet](https://www.totaltypescript.com/tsconfig-cheat-sheet).
However, if you encounter a weird default in any of the presets, please raise an issue.

## Requirements

You are using TypeScript 5.4 or higher. If that is not the case, you might need to tweak a few settings.

## Getting started

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install -D @backpack/typescript-config
```

Set up your `tsconfig.json`:

```jsonc
{
  "extends": "@backpack/typescript-config/bundler",
  "include": ["**/*.ts"],

  // If you still need to override certain options, you can do so.
  "compilerOptions": {
    // ...
  },
}
```

## List of presets

* `bundler`: if you are using a bundler (recommended for most Backpack projects)
* `tsc/app`: if you are using `tsc` to transpile code for an app
* `tsc/library`: if you are using `tsc` to transpile code for a library
* `tsc/library-monorepo`: if you are using `tsc` to transpile code for a mono-repo

# `@backpack/cdk-constructs`️ 🏗️

A collection of [L3 constructs] for [AWS CDK].

## Why?

This package aims to provide opinionated high-level constructs, reducing the amount of boilerplate in your
infrastructure code.

* Offers sensible defaults and optimizations for your existing L2 constructs.
* Integrates with resources provisioned by the NS Cloud Landing Zone (LZ).
* Includes additional utilities that can benefit your project.

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/cdk-constructs
```

[L3 Constructs]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/constructs.html

[AWS CDK]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/home.html

# `@backpack/amazon-dynamodb`️ 🗃

A lightweight utility package for working with [Amazon DynamoDB].

[Amazon DynamoDB]: https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/amazon-dynamodb
```

Make sure to also install the following AWS SDK libraries:

```bash
npm install @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb
```

## `DynamoDbRepository`

An implementation of the repository pattern, designed to abstract away direct DynamoDB interactions in your codebase.

### Creating a repository

```ts
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb";
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb";
import { DynamoDbRepository } from "@backpack/amazon-dynamodb";

const client = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient());
const booksRepository = new DynamoDbRepository<Book>(
  client,
  {
    tableName: 'Books', // required

    // optionally, pass your Powertools Logger instance:
    logger: MyLogger,

    // optionally, pass a mapper to add read/write mapping functions:
    itemMapper: {
      // e.g. use Zod to validate data coming from DynamoDB
      readItem: (item) => Book.parse(item),

      // you can also use Zod for writing the data,
      // to strip unknown fields, to have another validation guard,
      // or when you want to use Zod codecs
      writeItem: (item) => Book.encode(item),
    }
  }
);
```

### Usage patterns

You can use `DynamoDbRepository` in multiple ways depending on your application structure:

* **Direct usage**: use the repository directly in your domain layer for simple use cases.
* **Composition**: wrap the repository in your own repository class to customize or limit access to certain methods.
* **Inheritance**: extend the repository to add custom queries or override default behavior.

## Classes

* [DynamoDbRepository](classes/DynamoDbRepository.md)
* [TransactWriteCancelledError](classes/TransactWriteCancelledError.md)

## Interfaces

* [ConditionParts](interfaces/ConditionParts.md)

* [ItemMapper](interfaces/ItemMapper.md)

* [TransactWriteCancellationReason](interfaces/TransactWriteCancellationReason.md)
* [TransactWriteConditionCheckAction](interfaces/TransactWriteConditionCheckAction.md)
* [TransactWriteDeleteAction](interfaces/TransactWriteDeleteAction.md)
* [TransactWritePutAction](interfaces/TransactWritePutAction.md)
* [TransactWriteUpdateAction](interfaces/TransactWriteUpdateAction.md)

# `@backpack/amazon-s3`️ 📦

Utilities for interacting with [Amazon S3].

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/amazon-s3
```

Make sure to also install the following AWS SDK client:

