# `@backpack/aws-lambda`️ 👩‍💻

A package containing all sorts of utilities for writing AWS Lambda functions.

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/aws-lambda
```

## `defineLambda()` helpers

Helps to define correct AWS Lambda function handlers, by enabling type inference and enforcing the correct type
definitions for your specific Lambda integration.

For example:

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda } from "@backpack/aws-lambda";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event, context) => {
  //                                           ^?
  // ...

  return { statusCode: 200, body: "OK" };
  // ^ should return a `APIGatewayProxyResult`
});
```

The following helper functions are currently provided by Backpack:

| Helper function            | Lambda integration      |
|----------------------------|-------------------------|
| `defineLambda()`           | (none or irrelevant)    |
| `defineRestLambda()`       | [API Gateway (REST)]    |
| `defineSnsLambda()`        | [SNS]                   |
| `defineSqsLambda()`        | [SQS]                   |
| `defineS3Lambda()`         | [S3]                    |
| `defineS3BatchLambda()`    | [S3 Batch]              |
| `defineScheduledLambda()`  | [EventBridge scheduler] |
| `defineAuthorizerLambda()` | [Lambda authorizer]     |

[repo]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK

[API Gateway (REST)]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-apigateway.html

[SNS]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sns.html

[SQS]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html

[S3]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-s3.html

[S3 Batch]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-s3-batch.html

[EventBridge scheduler]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-eventbridge-scheduler.html

[Lambda authorizer]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-use-lambda-authorizer.html

## REST event utilities

If your AWS Lambda integrates with [API Gateway for REST APIs], you can use the following utilities for your
`APIGatewayProxyEvent` event.

[API Gateway for REST APIs]: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-rest-api.html

### `parseHeaders()`

Parses request headers. Provides type-completion, performs normalization, and includes some validation utilities.

```ts twoslash
import { APIGatewayProxyResult, APIGatewayProxyEvent } from "aws-lambda";
import { z } from "zod";
import { defineRestLambda, parseHeaders, jsonOk } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  const headers = parseHeaders(event);

  // returns an optional header by default:
  const callerId = headers.get("X-Caller-Id");
  //    ^?

  // specifying `required: true` will always return a `string`,
  //   and throws a `RequestValidationError` if not present
  const contentType = headers.get("Content-Type", { required: true });
  //    ^?

  // specifying `multi: true` will return an array instead
  const acceptHeaders = headers.get("Accept", { multi: true });
  //    ^?

  // specifying the `validated` option, it will validate the value against a Zod schema,
  //  and throws a `RequestValidationError` if invalid
  const Locale = z.enum(["nl", "en"]);
  const locale = headers.get("Accept-Language", { validated: Locale });
  //    ^?

  return jsonOk("OK")
})
```

### `parsePathParameters()` and `parseQueryParameters()`

Both helper functions improve type-safety and include some validation utilities for parsing parameters.

```ts twoslash
import { APIGatewayProxyResult } from "aws-lambda";
import { z } from "zod";
import {
  defineRestLambda,
  parsePathParameters,
  parseQueryParameters,
  jsonOk,
} from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  const pathParameters = parsePathParameters(event);
  const queryParameters = parseQueryParameters(event);

  // returns an required header by default,
  //   and throws a `RequestValidationError` if not present
  const artistId = pathParameters.get("artistId");
  //    ^?

  // specifying `required: false` will return a `string | undefined` instead
  const departmentId = pathParameters.get("departmentId", { required: false });
  //     ^?

  // specifying the `validated` option, it will validate the value against a Zod schema,
  //  and throws a `RequestValidationError` if invalid
  const SortDirection = z.enum(["asc", "desc"]);
  const sortDirection = queryParameters.get("sort", { validated: SortDirection });
  //    ^?

  return jsonOk("OK")
});
```

### `parseBody()`

Parses a request body. Supports both plain text and JSON, and provides built-in validation utilities.

```ts twoslash
import { APIGatewayProxyResult } from "aws-lambda";
import { z } from "zod";
import { defineRestLambda, parseBody, jsonOk } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  const body = parseBody(event);

  const text = body.text();
  //    ^?

  const json = body.json();
  //    ^?

  // you can also type-cast a JSON object (unsafe)
  const unsafeJson = body.json<MySchema>();
  //    ^?

  // you can also validate your JSON against a Zod schema (safe)
  //  throws a `RequestValidationError` if invalid
  const MySchema = z.object({ foo: z.string(), bar: z.string().optional() })
  const safeJson = body.json({ validated: MySchema });
  //    ^?

  return jsonOk("OK")
});

type MySchema = {
  foo: string;
  bar?: string;
}
```

### `parseRequest()` - all of the above

The function `parseRequest()` returns an object that include all utilities mentioned above:

* `getHeader()`
* `getQueryParameter()`
* `getPathParameter()`
* `getBody()`

### Accept-Language helpers

When working with REST APIs, many endpoints need to determine the preferred
language of a client based on the `Accept-Language` header.

Backpack provides a small set of utilities to make this easy and type-safe.

#### `parseHeaders()` – language helpers

The object returned by `parseHeaders()` includes the following helpers:

* `parseAcceptLanguage()`
* `resolveAcceptLanguage()`

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, parseHeaders, jsonOk } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  const headers = parseHeaders(event);

  const parsed = headers.parseAcceptLanguage();
  //    ^ `LanguageCode[]`

  const language = headers.resolveAcceptLanguage();
  //    ^ `LanguageCode.nl | LanguageCode.en`

  return jsonOk({ language });
});
```

By default, `resolveAcceptLanguage()` uses Backpack defaults:

* allowed languages: `nl`, `en`
* fallback language: `nl`

#### Custom allowed languages

You can override the allowed languages:

```ts
import { LanguageCode } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

const language = headers.resolveAcceptLanguage({
  allowed: [LanguageCode.de, LanguageCode.en],
});

language;
// ^ `LanguageCode.de | LanguageCode.en | undefined`
```

And also pass an explicit fallback language:

```ts
import { LanguageCode } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

const language = headers.resolveAcceptLanguage({
  allowed: [LanguageCode.de, LanguageCode.en],
  default: LanguageCode.en,
});

language;
// ^ `LanguageCode.de | LanguageCode.en`
```

#### Allowing all languages

If you want to accept any language code, you can use the provided constant:

```ts
import { ALL_LANGUAGE_CODES } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

const language = headers.resolveAcceptLanguage({ allowed: ALL_LANGUAGE_CODES });
//    ^ LanguageCode | undefined
```

These helpers are completely optional and build on top of the lower-level
language parsing and resolving utilities provided by this package.

## REST result utilities

If your AWS Lambda integrates with [API Gateway for REST APIs], you can use the following utilities for returning
an `APIGatewayProxyResult` object.

### `result()`

This function can be used to wrap your result object, adding additional type-completion.

For example: it hints to use the `HttpStatus` enum from Backpack:

![aws-lambda-http-status.png](/screenshots/aws-lambda-http-status.png)

it also adds type-completion for HTTP headers:

![aws-lambda-http-headers.png](/screenshots/aws-lambda-http-headers.png)

### `jsonResult()`

Creates a result with a JSON body. Accepts any object, and converts it to JSON. It also sets the `Content-Type` header
to `application/json`.

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, jsonResult, HttpStatus } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  // ...
  return jsonResult({ /* ... */ }, { statusCode: HttpStatus.OK });
});
```

### `jsonOk()`

Same as `jsonResult()`, but with the status code set to HTTP 200 (OK).

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, jsonOk } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  // ...
  return jsonOk({ /* ... */ });
});
```

Pass explicit `cache` options to control caching. See the [HTTP caching](#http-caching) section below for the full list
of presets and real-world usage patterns.

### `problemResult()`

Creates an [RFC-9457 compliant][Problem] problem result, to return an explicitly documented error.

```ts twoslash
import {
  defineRestLambda,
  jsonOk,
  problemResult,
  RequestValidationError,
} from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import { AsyncResult } from "@backpack/error-handling/async-result";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async () =>
  AsyncResult
    .try(() => {
      /* ... */
    })
    .map((it) => jsonOk(it))
    .recoverIfInstanceOf(RequestValidationError, () =>
      problemResult({
        type: "/problems/validation-error",
        title: "Validation error",
        status: 400,
      }),
    )
);
```

[Problem]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html#name-the-problem-details-json-ob

## HTTP caching

Backpack provides first-class support for HTTP caching across two complementary mechanisms:

1. **`Cache-Control` headers** — via the `cache` option on `jsonResult()` and `jsonOk()`, including some presets.
2. **ETag / conditional requests** — via `handleConditionalRequest()` and the `generateETag()` utility from
   `@backpack/http`.

### Caching with `jsonResult()` and `jsonOk()`

Use one of the `CachePresets` values and pass it as the `cache` option:

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, jsonOk, CachePresets } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const data = { /* ... */ };
  return jsonOk(data, { cache: CachePresets.FIVE_MINUTES });
  // Cache-Control: max-age=300
});
```

### Caching presets

All presets include `Vary: Accept-Language` automatically.

| Preset                        | `Cache-Control`            | Use case                                  |
|-------------------------------|----------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| `CachePresets.NO_CACHE`       | `no-cache`                 | Force revalidation on every request       |
| `CachePresets.THIRTY_SECONDS` | `max-age=30`               | Frequently-changing data (e.g. planner)   |
| `CachePresets.FIVE_MINUTES`   | `max-age=300`              | Semi-dynamic data                         |
| `CachePresets.ONE_HOUR`       | `max-age=3600`             | Data changing a few times a day           |
| `CachePresets.ONE_DAY`        | `max-age=86400`            | Daily-refreshed data                      |
| `CachePresets.ONE_WEEK`       | `max-age=604800`           | Stable, infrequently-changing data        |

#### Real-world examples

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, jsonOk, CachePresets } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

// ── Homepage BFF widgets ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Cached for one hour, separate copy per language.
export const getWidgetsHandler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const widgets = { /* ... */ };
  return jsonOk(widgets, { cache: CachePresets.ONE_HOUR });
  // Cache-Control: max-age=3600
  // Vary: Accept-Language
});

// ── Planner ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Results change frequently — 30-second window to avoid overwhelming the API.
export const getPlannerHandler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const plannerResults = { /* ... */ };
  return jsonOk(plannerResults, { cache: CachePresets.THIRTY_SECONDS });
  // Cache-Control: max-age=30
  // Vary: Accept-Language
});

// ── Saved trips ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Refreshed once a day.
export const getSavedTripsHandler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const savedTrips = { /* ... */ };
  return jsonOk(savedTrips, { cache: CachePresets.ONE_DAY });
  // Cache-Control: max-age=86400
  // Vary: Accept-Language
});

// ── MijnNS ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Personalised content — refreshed every hour.
export const getMijnNsHandler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const mijnNsData = { /* ... */ };
  return jsonOk(mijnNsData, { cache: CachePresets.ONE_HOUR });
  // Cache-Control: max-age=3600
  // Vary: Accept-Language
});

// ── Products tab ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Language-dependent catalogue — daily cache, separate copy per language.
export const getProductsHandler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const products = { /* ... */ };
  return jsonOk(products, { cache: CachePresets.ONE_DAY });
  // Cache-Control: max-age=86400
  // Vary: Accept-Language
});

// ── Active train ticket ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Must be accessible offline — durable cache persists it on the device even
// after OS cache pressure or a user-initiated cache clear.
export const getTicketHandler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
   const ticket = { /* ... */ };
   return jsonOk(ticket, {
      cache: {
         maxAge: 604_800,
         vary: ["Accept-Language"],
         durable: { maxStale: 604_800 },
      }
   });
   // Cache-Control: max-age=604800
   // Vary: Accept-Language
   // X-Cache-Storage: durable; max-stale=604800
});
```

#### Opt out

Use `CachePresets.NO_CACHE` to force revalidation on every request — the response may still be stored by caches,
but it must be revalidated with the server before being served.

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, jsonOk, CachePresets } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const liveStatus = { /* ... */ };
  return jsonOk(liveStatus, { cache: CachePresets.NO_CACHE });
  // Cache-Control: no-cache
  // Vary: Accept-Language
});
```

To suppress all caching headers entirely (e.g. for sensitive data that must never be stored), pass
`cache: false` directly:

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, jsonOk } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const sensitiveResponse = { /* ... */ };
  return jsonOk(sensitiveResponse, { cache: false });
  // No Cache-Control header emitted
});
```

### ETag and conditional requests

For resources that change infrequently, ETags allow clients to revalidate cached responses efficiently.

When a client sends `If-None-Match` with a previously received ETag, the server can determine whether the
resource has changed. If not, it returns `304 Not Modified` without a response body.

This avoids unnecessary data transfer and reduces latency. Depending on how the ETag is generated (for example,
based on a version or last-modified timestamp), it can also help avoid expensive recomputation or data fetching
on the server.

You can use `handleConditionalRequest()` to validate an ETag against the incoming request. To generate the ETag, you can
use the `generateETag()` from `@backpack/http` or implement your own ETag generation logic.

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, jsonOk, handleConditionalRequest } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import { generateETag } from "@backpack/http";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  const books = await fetchBooks();

  const etag = generateETag(books);

  // Returns 304 Not Modified when the client's ETag matches
  const notModified = handleConditionalRequest(event, etag);
  if (notModified) return notModified;

  // Cache-Control: max-age=300  +  ETag: W/"…"
  return jsonOk(books, {
    cache: { maxAge: 300 },
    headers: { ETag: etag },
  });
});

async function fetchBooks() {
  return [{ id: 1, title: "Book" }];
}
```

ETags are *weak* (`W/"…"`) because the same logical resource may produce different byte sequences
across deployments. Weak ETags are sufficient for `If-None-Match` / `304 Not Modified` revalidation.

### Advanced: custom `Cache-Control` builder

When the shorthand `cache` options do not cover your needs, supply a pre-built
[`CacheControlBuilder`][CacheControlBuilder] from `@backpack/http` to `cache.cacheControl`.

This bypasses `maxAge`, `sMaxAge` and `mustRevalidate`, giving you full control over the header.

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, jsonOk } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import { cacheControl } from "@backpack/http";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const asset = { /* versioned asset */ };
  // Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
  return jsonOk(asset, {
    cache: {
      cacheControl: cacheControl().public().maxAge(31_536_000).immutable(),
    },
  });
});
```

`staleWhileRevalidate` and `staleIfError` are also available on the builder:

```ts twoslash
import { defineRestLambda, jsonOk } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";
import { cacheControl } from "@backpack/http";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const feed = { /* ... */ };
  // Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30, stale-if-error=300
  return jsonOk(feed, {
    cache: {
      cacheControl: cacheControl()
        .public()
        .maxAge(60)
        .staleWhileRevalidate(30)
        .staleIfError(300),
    },
  });
});
```

[CacheControlBuilder]: #cache-control-builder

### `CacheOptions` reference

| Option           | Type                   | Description                                                                                             |
|------------------|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `maxAge`         | `number`               | Freshness duration in seconds — maps to `max-age=N`.                                                    |
| `sMaxAge`        | `number`               | Freshness duration for shared caches — maps to `s-maxage=N`.                                            |
| `mustRevalidate` | `boolean`              | Adds `must-revalidate` to require revalidation once stale.                                              |
| `vary`           | `string[]`             | Sets the `Vary` header (e.g. `["Accept-Language"]`).                                                    |
| `durable`        | `{ maxStale: number }` | Adds `X-Cache-Storage: durable; max-stale=N` for mobile offline storage.                                |
| `cacheControl`   | `CacheControlBuilder`  | Advanced override — replaces `maxAge`, `sMaxAge` and `mustRevalidate` with a fully custom header value. |

Use `CachePresets.NO_CACHE` to force revalidation, or pass `cache: false` to suppress caching headers entirely.

## Error handling

Combining the error handling utilities from `@backpack/error-handling` with the default error handler
from `@backpack/aws-lambda/rest` allows you to easily set up proper error handling for REST endpoints.

The example below demonstrates three ways to set it up:

1. Using `AsyncResult<T>`
2. Using `Promise<T>`
3. Using the `@catchErrors()` decorator

::: code-group

```ts{11-13} twoslash [using AsyncResult]
import type { APIGatewayProxyResult } from "aws-lambda";
import { AsyncResult } from "@backpack/error-handling/async-result";
import { jsonOk, jsonResult, defaultErrorHandler, ProblemError } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export class MyLambda {

  public handle(): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult> {
    return AsyncResult
      .try(() => this.someOperation())
      .map(() => jsonOk("Done!"))
      .onFailure(myErrorLogger())
      .recoverIfInstanceOf(MyCustomError, myErrorConverter())
      .orElseGet(defaultErrorHandler());
  }

  private async someOperation(): Promise<void> {
    // ...
    throw new ProblemError({
      type: "/problems/foo-not-found",
      status: 404,
      title: "Foo not found!",
      detail: "Foo 123 could not be found!",
    });
    // ...
  }
}

class MyCustomError extends Error { /* ... */ }

function myErrorLogger() {
  return (error: unknown) => console.error(error);
}

function myErrorConverter() {
  return (error: MyCustomError) =>
    jsonResult(
      { message: `My custom error ${error.message}!` },
      { statusCode: 500 },
    );
}
```

```ts{10-12} twoslash [using Promise]
import type { APIGatewayProxyResult } from "aws-lambda";
import { promiseTry, map, onFailure, recoverIfInstanceOf } from "@backpack/error-handling/promises";
import { jsonOk, jsonResult, defaultErrorHandler, ProblemError } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export class MyLambda {

  public handle(): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult> {
    return promiseTry(() => this.someOperation())
      .then(map(() => jsonOk("Done!")))
      .catch(onFailure(myErrorLogger()))
      .catch(recoverIfInstanceOf(MyCustomError, myErrorConverter()))
      .catch(defaultErrorHandler());
  }

  private async someOperation(): Promise<void> {
    // ...
    throw new ProblemError({
      type: "/problems/foo-not-found",
      status: 404,
      title: "Foo not found!",
      detail: "Foo 123 could not be found!",
    });
    // ...
  }
}

class MyCustomError extends Error { /* ... */ }

function myErrorLogger() {
  return (error: unknown) => console.error(error);
}

function myErrorConverter() {
  return (error: MyCustomError) =>
    jsonResult(
      { message: `My custom error ${error.message}!` },
      { statusCode: 500 },
    );
}
```

```ts{10-12} twoslash [using @catchErrors()]
import type { APIGatewayProxyResult } from "aws-lambda";
import { catchErrors, onFailure, recoverIfInstanceOf, orElseGet } from "@backpack/error-handling/promises";
import { jsonOk, jsonResult, defaultErrorHandler, ProblemError } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

class MyCustomError extends Error { /* ... */ }

export class MyLambda {

  @catchErrors(
    onFailure(myErrorLogger()),
    recoverIfInstanceOf(MyCustomError, myErrorConverter()),
    orElseGet(defaultErrorHandler()),
  )
  public async handle(): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResult> {
    await this.someOperation();
    return jsonOk("Done!");
  }

  private async someOperation(): Promise<void> {
    // ...
  }
}

function myErrorLogger() {
  return async (error: unknown) => console.error(error);
}

function myErrorConverter() {
  return (error: MyCustomError) =>
    jsonResult(
      { message: `My custom error ${error.message}!` },
      { statusCode: 500 },
    );
}
```

***

Check the [full API reference](/packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/rest/#rfc-9457-problem-details) for more information.

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/aws-secrets-manager

# `@backpack/aws-secrets-manager`️ 🔐

Contains some utility classes for [AWS Secrets Manager].

## Installing

First, ensure you have [set up Nexus as private registry](/guides/tooling/using-nexus.md) needed to use Backpack.

Then, install the package using npm:

```bash
npm install @backpack/aws-secrets-manager
```

Make sure to also install the following AWS SDK client:

```bash
npm install @aws-sdk/client-secrets-manager
```

## Example usage

Create a `SecretsManagerService` with the AWS SDK client:

```ts
import { SecretsManagerClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-secrets-manager";
import { SecretsManagerService } from "@backpack/aws-secrets-manager";

const service = new SecretsManagerService(new SecretsManagerClient());
```

Use `getJsonSecret()` when the secret value is stored as JSON:

```ts
type OAuthSecret = {
  clientSecret: string;
};

const oauthSecret = await service.getJsonSecret<OAuthSecret>("/bookstore/oauth/client-credentials");

console.log(oauthSecret.clientSecret);
```

Use `getSecretString()` when the secret value should be returned as a raw string:

```ts
const apiKey = await service.getSecretString("/bookstore/api-key");
```

Both methods throw when the secret is missing by default. Pass `required: false` when a missing secret should return
`undefined` instead:

```ts
const optionalApiKey = await service.getSecretString("/bookstore/api-key", {
  required: false,
});
```

[AWS Secrets Manager]: https://aws.amazon.com/secrets-manager/

## Classes

* [CachedSecretsManagerService](classes/CachedSecretsManagerService.md)
* [SecretsManagerService](classes/SecretsManagerService.md)

## Interfaces

* [CachedSecretsManagerOptions](interfaces/CachedSecretsManagerOptions.md)

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/contributing/project-governance.md'
---
# Project governance

This document defines how Backpack is governed, evolved, and maintained.

## Purpose

Backpack is maintained as a **platform**, not a loose collection of libraries.
Governance exists to:

* provide predictable evolution for teams
* balance innovation with stability
* make decisions explicit instead of implicit
* reduce long-term maintenance and upgrade cost

## Scope

Governance applies to:

* all `@backpack/*` npm packages
* the Backpack CLI and project templates
* Backpack documentation and upgrade guides
* the supported runtime and tooling ecosystem

Backpack is versioned and released as **one platform**.

## Guiding principles

* **Stability over churn**\
  Avoid unnecessary breaking changes and release noise.
* **User impact over internal convenience**\
  Decisions are based on consumer impact, not implementation effort.
* **Automation over memory**\
  Rules should be enforced by tooling where possible.
* **Explicit trade-offs**\
  Breaking changes must be intentional and clearly communicated.

## Ownership and responsibilities

* The Backpack core team owns the platform direction and releases.
* Contributors are responsible for following governance and policies.
* Maintainers enforce governance during code review.
* CI/CD pipelines act as automated enforcement.

## Decision-making

* Small, isolated changes are decided via pull request review.
* Cross-cutting or breaking changes require explicit discussion.
* When impact is unclear, the safer option applies
  (for example: treat a change as breaking).

## Policies

The following policies are part of Backpack governance:

* [Release and versioning policy](./release-policy.md)\
  Defines how changes are classified, released, and supported.

---

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/contributing/release-policy.md'
---
# Release and versioning policy

This document defines how Backpack is versioned and released.

Backpack follows semantic versioning with a pragmatic,
platform-oriented interpretation.

## Scope

This policy applies to:

* all `@backpack/*` npm packages
* the Backpack CLI and project templates
* Backpack documentation and upgrade guides
* Backpack’s supported runtime and tooling ecosystem

Backpack is versioned as **one platform**.
All packages share the same version number.

## Supported versions

Backpack supports **only the latest released version**.

* no LTS branches
* no parallel release tracks
* no bug fixes or security updates for older versions

This keeps the platform predictable and easy to maintain.

## Release cadence

* **Major releases**: at most once per year\
  Typically aligned with a new Node.js LTS becoming available in AWS Lambda.
* **Minor releases**: periodically (target cadence: 2-3 months)\
  Released when sufficient value has accumulated.
* **Patch releases**: as needed\
  Released for bug fixes and maintenance.

There is no fixed calendar schedule.
Releases are intentionally batched to minimize upgrade noise and operational overhead.

## Semantic versioning model

Backpack uses semantic versioning:

```
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
```

Version numbers reflect **user impact**, not the size of internal changes.

## Major releases (X.0.0)

A major release indicates **breaking changes** that require user action.

A release MUST be major if one or more of the following apply.

### Runtime and platform

* support for a Node.js major version is dropped
* a new Node.js major version becomes the required runtime
* AWS Lambda runtime requirements change in a way that affects consumers

Node.js major upgrades are the primary driver for Backpack major releases.

### Public APIs

* removal of deprecated functions, classes, or packages
* incompatible changes to public APIs
* changes in default behavior that break existing applications

### Dependency policy

* dropping support for a previously supported major version
* increasing the minimum required version of a core dependency
  in a way that forces upgrades

### Templates and generators

* structural changes to generated project layouts
* changes that require migration for existing projects

**Rule of thumb:**\
If many teams must update code, configuration, or infrastructure to upgrade,
the release is major.

## Minor releases (X.Y.0)

A minor release introduces **new capabilities** or **non-breaking changes**.

Typical reasons:

* new features or new Backpack packages
* backward-compatible API extensions
* tooling upgrades with limited user impact
* compatible dependency upgrades
* widening peer dependency ranges

Minor releases may require attention but should not block upgrades.

## Patch releases (X.Y.Z)

Patch releases contain **safe, low-risk changes**.

Used for:

* bug fixes
* documentation updates
* internal refactoring
* dependency updates that do not affect public APIs or templates
* security fixes

Patch releases should be safe to apply at any time.

## Core dependencies

Backpack defines a small set of **core dependencies**
that strongly influence release classification.

### Runtime and platform

* Node.js
* AWS Lambda Node.js runtime

Node.js major upgrades are treated as breaking changes.

### Infrastructure and deployment

* `aws-cdk-lib`
* `constructs`
* `datadog-cdk-constructs-v2`

Dropping support for a major version is breaking.

### Language and tooling

* `typescript`
* `eslint`
* `vitest`
* `vite`

These usually result in minor releases,
unless they cause widespread failures or required migrations.

### Runtime and API behavior

* `zod`
* `@aws-lambda-powertools/*`
* AWS SDK v3 clients (`@aws-sdk/*`)

Major version upgrades are evaluated case by case
based on API and behavioral impact.

## Dependency upgrade guidelines

Dependency upgrades are classified by **consumer impact**, not version numbers.

* widening a peer dependency range is non-breaking
* increasing minimum supported versions may be breaking
* dropping support for a major version is breaking
* internal implementation upgrades are non-breaking
  unless behavior changes

## Deprecations

* APIs may be deprecated in any release
* deprecations must be documented and announced in release notes
* deprecated APIs are removed only in major releases

Deprecation periods must be reasonable and clearly communicated.

## Release notes and upgrade guides

Every release includes release notes.

* major releases include a dedicated upgrade guide
* minor releases highlight relevant changes and attention points
* patch releases focus on fixes and maintenance

Release notes are part of the contract between Backpack and its users.

---

---
url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/contributing/how-to-contribute.md'
---
# How to contribute

This page describes the practical workflow for contributing code, documentation,
and packages.

## Getting started

Backpack is developed as a single platform. Contributions typically fall into
one of these categories:

* documentation improvements
* bug fixes
* new features or packages
* tooling or infrastructure changes

If you are unsure about scope or impact, start with a small pull request or
discuss the idea first.

## Local development

The repository provides a set of standard scripts for local development.

### Preview documentation

```bash
npm run dev:docs
```

### Lint/format/type-check all packages

```bash
npm run check
```

### Run tests

```bash
npm run test
```

All scripts should pass locally before opening a pull request.

## Pull request guidelines

* Use [conventional commits] for the **pull request title**
* Keep pull requests focused and reasonably small
* Do not update the changelog manually; this is handled automatically
* If a change affects public behavior, update documentation accordingly

Pull requests are reviewed against the governance and release policies.

## Adding a new package

To generate a new package, run:

```bash
npm run generate-package <packageName>
```

After generating the package:

* add a reference to the new `package.json` in `.versionrc.json`
* ensure the package follows existing structure and conventions
* document public APIs if applicable
* add a `README.md` — it will be automatically included in the docs API Reference

New packages are considered part of the Backpack platform and follow the same
versioning and release rules as existing packages.

## Branching and releases

Backpack uses a simple branching model.

### Main branch

* `main` is the default and stable branch
* all stable releases are created from `main`
* changes should be merged into `main` as soon as they are ready

Every commit to `main` automatically publishes updated documentation through a
[dedicated pipeline][docs pipeline].

### Stable releases

Releases are created manually by running the release pipeline.

When the release pipeline is executed, it will:

* bump the versions of all packages
* publish artifacts to Nexus
* create a release commit and tag

Release classification (major, minor, patch) follows the Release and versioning
policy.

Example stable release flow:

```text
o C0 [v2.1.0]
|
o C1 fix
|
o C2 [v2.1.1]
|
o C3 fix
|
o C4 feature
|
o C5 [v2.2.0] (main)
```

### Pre-releases

In some cases, features or breaking changes need to be tested before merging
into `main`.

In those situations:

* do not block `main`
* create a dedicated release branch (for example: `releases/next`)
* continue releasing stable fixes from `main` if needed

When the release pipeline is run on a branch other than `main`, it automatically
creates a pre-release.

Supported pre-release types:

* `alpha`: active development and experimentation
* `beta`: stabilization and bug fixing
* `rc`: release preparation

Documentation for pre-release branches is published under `/next/index.html`.

Example pre-release flow:

```text
o C5 [v2.2.0]
|\
| \
|  | diverging from `main`
|  | to work on the next release
|  |
|  o C6 feature with breaking change
|  |
|  o C7 fix for the new feature
|  |
|  o C8 [v3.0.0-rc] (next)
|
 \
  o C9 hotfix
  |
  o C10 [v2.2.1] (main)
```

## Preparing a major release

Major releases require additional care.

Before cutting a major release:

* review and update important peer dependencies
  (for example: TypeScript, ESLint, Vitest, Vite)
* update documented supported versions in the docs
  (search for `peer-deps:` comments)
* prepare release notes and migration guides
* remove prerelease entries from the changelog

Major release requirements are defined in the Release and versioning policy.

## Cutting a new release

1. Determine the correct version according to [semantic versioning rules][semver rules]
2. Verify that all relevant changes are merged
3. Run the [release pipeline][release pipeline] with the chosen version
4. Test the release on an existing project
5. Publish upgrade or migration guides if required
6. Announce the release in the appropriate Slack channels

[docs pipeline]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/BACKPACK/_build?definitionId=20388

[release pipeline]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/BACKPACK/_build?definitionId=20390

[conventional commits]: https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/

[semver rules]: https://semver.org/

url: 'https://backpack.ns.nl/contributing/coding-standards.md'
---
# Coding standards

This document describes the coding standards used in Backpack.
The focus is consistency, clarity, and long-term maintainability.

These standards apply to all `@backpack/*` packages, tooling, templates,
and documentation where relevant.

## Principles

* Prefer readability over cleverness
* Optimize for long-term maintenance
* Make behavior explicit
* Strong typing is a feature

If code is surprising, it should be documented or simplified.

## TypeScript

* Avoid `any`; prefer `unknown` with explicit narrowing
* Model public APIs with precise types
* Treat exported symbols as stable contracts
* Prefer named exports over default exports

Breaking changes to public APIs follow the Release and versioning policy.

## Runtime and Node.js

* Use ECMAScript modules consistently
* Prefer `node:`-prefixed imports
* Avoid hidden global state
* Document runtime assumptions when they exist

## Project structure

* Group code by domain or feature
* Keep files small and focused
* Avoid deep or unclear nesting
* Keep public entry points obvious

Barrel files are allowed when they are intentional and curated.

## Formatting and linting

* Formatting is enforced by tooling
* Do not manually reformat code
* Fix linting issues instead of disabling rules

Suppressions require a clear justification.

## Testing

* Prefer fast, deterministic tests
* Avoid timing-based assertions
* Keep tests isolated and repeatable

Flaky tests should be fixed or removed.

## Dependencies

* Minimize dependencies where possible
* Prefer platform or standard APIs
* Introduce new dependencies deliberately

## Documentation

* Public APIs must be documented
* Examples should be minimal and realistic
* Documentation is part of the user experience

## Enforcement

Coding standards are enforced through:

* code review
* linting and formatting
* automated tests

# AI agent instructions

Backpack is the internal developer platform for building TypeScript services at NS.

Use this document when working with AI coding agents in projects that depend on Backpack packages, or when working inside the Backpack repository itself.

## Documentation sources

When working on Backpack-related code, always verify against current Backpack documentation.

Prefer current documentation over assumptions from memory.

### Projects that use Backpack

When working in a project that depends on Backpack packages, use the public Backpack documentation as the source of truth:

* [llms.txt](/llms.txt) for a compact index of important Backpack documentation
* [llms-full.txt](/llms-full.txt) for the full AI-readable documentation bundle
* Package documentation linked from the Backpack documentation
* Upgrade and migration guides linked from the Backpack documentation
* Examples linked from the Backpack documentation

For external agents, use the absolute URLs:

* https://backpack.ns.nl/llms.txt
* https://backpack.ns.nl/llms-full.txt

Before changing code, verify package names, imports, APIs, examples, and migration steps against these sources.

### The Backpack repository itself

When working inside the Backpack repository, also use the local documentation and source files:

* VitePress docs under `/apps/docs`
* Package docs under `/packages/*/README.md`
* Generated package documentation under `/apps/docs/packages`
* Upgrade and migration guides under `/apps/docs/guides/upgrading` and `/apps/docs/guides/migrating`
* Demo/examples in `/apps` (for example, `bookstore-rest-api`)

Use local source files to verify implementation details, but prefer documented public APIs when changing examples or guidance for users.

## Installing Backpack agent instructions in a project

If a project uses Backpack packages and does not have an `AGENTS.md` file, suggest adding one at the repository root.

Do not create or modify `AGENTS.md` unless the user explicitly asks for it.

Use the canonical template:

* https://backpack.ns.nl/AGENTS.md

If an `AGENTS.md` file already exists:

* Do not overwrite it.
* Preserve project-specific instructions.
* Merge conservatively.
* Prefer adding a short Backpack section that links to the Backpack documentation.
* Explain what changed and why.

A user can ask an agent:

> Install Backpack agent instructions in this project. Use the canonical Backpack `AGENTS.md` template. If this repository already has an `AGENTS.md`, propose a minimal merge instead of overwriting it.

## General behaviour

Before changing code:

* Read the local `AGENTS.md`, if present.
* Inspect the existing project structure and follow local conventions.
* Check which `@backpack/*` packages are used in `package.json`.
* Prefer small, focused changes over broad rewrites.
* Preserve current behavior unless the task explicitly asks for a change.
* If docs and code conflict, state the conflict and ask before broad or breaking changes.

Local repository conventions override generic Backpack guidance.

## Baseline stack to assume

Backpack docs currently assume these defaults when a project does not specify otherwise:

* Node.js 24+
* ESM modules
* TypeScript 6+
* Vitest 4
* AWS CDK v2

Always use project-local versions and compatibility constraints when they differ.

## REST and Lambda guidance

When working on Lambda-based REST APIs:

* For API Gateway REST handlers, prefer documented helpers from `@backpack/aws-lambda`:
  * `defineRestLambda`
  * request parsing helpers such as `parseHeaders`, `parsePathParameters`, `parseQueryParameters`, `parseBody`, and `parseRequest`
  * response helpers such as `jsonOk` and `jsonResult`
  * default error handling utilities when applicable
* Validate external input with Zod at boundaries, such as request payloads, headers, query/path parameters, and external responses.
* For HTTP caching and conditional requests, use documented utilities from `@backpack/aws-lambda/rest` and `@backpack/http`, such as `CachePresets`, `handleConditionalRequest`, and `generateETag`, instead of ad hoc implementations.

For REST architecture decisions, Backpack docs currently mark API Gateway with single-purpose Lambdas as the recommended default. Do not rewrite architecture unless requested.

Do not introduce Hono, OpenAPI tooling, or other REST architecture changes unless the project already uses them, the Backpack docs recommend them for this use case, or the task explicitly asks for it.

## Infrastructure guidance

When working on CDK or infrastructure:

* Prefer existing `@backpack/cdk-constructs` where they fit the current stack.
* Be explicit about deployment impact, such as permissions, API Gateway behavior, domains, resources, and tags.
* Keep environment-specific config explicit and consistent with current project conventions.

## Testing guidance

When adding or changing tests:

* Use Vitest when the project does not specify another test framework.
* Prefer behavior-focused tests via public APIs.
* Prefer documented Backpack test utilities where useful, such as `@backpack/testing`, `@backpack/mockserver-client`, and `@backpack/hono-mockserver`.
* Run the project’s real scripts from `package.json`, such as `test`, `check:lint`, `check:types`, or `check:format`, before considering work complete.

Do not invent commands when the project already defines its own scripts.

## Recommended npm scripts

When changing npm scripts, or when the user asks for guidelines, prefer adding a minimal, consistent set of npm scripts:

* `check`: run type checks, lint, and formatting checks together.
* `check:types`: run `tsc`.
* `check:lint`: run `eslint`.
* `check:format`: run `prettier --check`.
* `build`: run the project build (if applicable).
* `test`: run tests once (for example `vitest run`).
* `test:watch`: run tests in watch mode.
* `test:coverage`: run tests with coverage.
* `lint`: run `eslint`.
* `lint:fix`: run `eslint --fix`.
* `format`: run `prettier --write`.

For CDK-based projects, also consider:

* `synth`: run `cdk synth`.
* Environment-scoped synth/deploy/destroy scripts, such as `synth:dev`, `deploy:dev`, and `destroy:dev`, with explicit config.

Use `prepare` for Git hooks setup, such as Husky, when the repository uses hook-based workflows.

## Package and import guidance

Before adding or changing Backpack imports:

* Verify exports in the current package documentation.
* Prefer public documented exports over deep or internal paths.
* Do not import from internal package paths unless the documentation explicitly allows it.

When changing Backpack versions, read:

* release notes
* the compatibility matrix
* the relevant upgrade guide or guides
* migration guides for non-version migrations

## Migration guidance

When helping with migrations:

* Identify current versions first.
* Apply upgrade guides step by step per version jump.
* Use migration guides for context-specific migrations, such as legacy package migrations.
* Prefer incremental, mechanical changes over broad rewrites.
* Call out required manual follow-up steps.

For migrations from deprecated packages or older Backpack patterns, prefer the current documented paved road.

## Documentation guidance

When editing Backpack documentation:

* Use clear, concise language.
* Use sentence case for headings.
* Prefer practical examples over abstract explanations.
* Keep examples realistic and copy-pasteable.
* Avoid unnecessary title case.
* Avoid horizontal rule separators.
* Keep the tone pragmatic and developer-friendly.

When documenting APIs, explain when to use the API, not only how to call it.

## Handling uncertainty

If documentation and local code disagree:

1. Preserve existing behavior unless asked to change it.
2. Use current Backpack docs for new code and migration direction.
3. Explain the mismatch and ask for confirmation before broad changes.

Do not guess Backpack APIs. Verify first.

[API reference](../../index.md) / @backpack/vite

# @backpack/vite

Backpack helpers for Vite.

## Vite 8 decorators compatibility

Vite 8 uses Rolldown/Oxc. Oxc does not yet lower stage 3 decorators directly, so
`@backpack/vite` provides a temporary compatibility transform through Babel.

Add `backpackVitePlugin()` to `vite.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import { backpackVitePlugin } from "@backpack/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [backpackVitePlugin()],
});
```

The transform uses `@rolldown/plugin-babel` with
`@babel/plugin-proposal-decorators` and the `2023-11` decorators version. It only
runs on code containing `@`.

When Vite/Oxc can lower native stage 3 decorators directly, this helper can
become a no-op.

## Vitest config

Projects with a separate `vitest.config.ts` can merge it with
`vite.config.ts` so tests use the same plugin setup:

```ts
import { defineConfig, mergeConfig } from "vitest/config";
import viteConfig from "./vite.config";

export default mergeConfig(
  viteConfig,
  defineConfig({
    test: {
      // project-specific Vitest options
    },
  }),
);
```

## Functions

* [backpackVitePlugin](functions/backpackVitePlugin.md)

# Announcing Backpack 0.10

Backpack 0.10 introduces important platform changes and a few powerful new libraries.

> \[!WARNING]
> This release contains **required migrations**.
> You must complete them before upgrading to `0.10.x`.

> \[!TIP]
>
> * For the full list of changes, see the [changelog].
> * For step-by-step instructions, check the [upgrade guide].

[changelog]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/CHANGELOG.md&_a=preview

[upgrade guide]: ../guides/upgrading/v0.10.md

## Required migrations ⚠️

### New Nexus registry (required)

Backpack originally emerged within the **NSAPP community**. Because of that, packages were published to a Nexus registry
closely tied to the NSAPP environment. We decided to change that, so it's easier to use Backpack in other projects.

Therefore, Backpack packages are now published to a **new Nexus registry**.

If you want to use Backpack `0.10.x`, you **must migrate** to this new registry first.
Projects that are not migrated will fail to install or resolve Backpack packages.

Please follow the dedicated migration guide:

👉 [Migrate to the new Nexus registry](../guides/migrating/nexus-registry.md)

### Node.js 24

Backpack `0.10.x` requires **Node.js 24**.

This aligns Backpack with the latest AWS Lambda runtime and enables modern
ECMAScript features. As part of this upgrade, you may need to:

* upgrade your local Node.js version
* update CI/CD pipelines to use Node.js 24
* upgrade `aws-cdk-lib` and Lambda runtimes where applicable

See the [upgrade guide] for detailed instructions.

## New library: `@backpack/i18n`

This release introduces a new, first-class internationalization library:
[`@backpack/i18n`](../packages/@backpack/i18n/index.md).

It is designed to be:

* fully TypeScript-first
* compile-time safe
* ergonomic for both frontend and backend use cases

If your project deals with translations or locale-specific formatting,
we strongly recommend checking it out.

## Preview: HTTP mockserver client

Backpack 0.10 includes a **preview** of a new HTTP mockserver library:
[`@backpack/mockserver-client`](../packages/@backpack/mockserver-client/index.md).

This library enables:

* programmatic control over HTTP mocks
* easy integration with Vitest
* a predictable, developer-friendly testing experience

⚠️ This is a preview release. APIs may change based on feedback.

## New Azure DevOps location

The Backpack repository has moved to a new, dedicated TOPAAS Azure DevOps project.

This is now the location for the Backpack source code, issues, and pull requests:

👉 https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/\_git/BACKPACK

Please update any existing bookmarks, links, or automation that still point to the old location.

## Documentation improvements

We've added:

* a new guide on [working with date and time](../guides/development/date-and-time.md);
* dedicated [upgrade guides](../guides/upgrading/index.md) to make upgrading between releases more explicit.

***

As always, feedback is very welcome.

# Announcing Backpack 0.11

Backpack 0.11 is another significant release with a wide range of improvements across our platform.

This release continues our focus on improving the developer experience, expanding our tooling,
and incorporating feedback from the growing Backpack community.

> \[!TIP]
>
> * For the full list of changes, see the [changelog].
> * For step-by-step instructions, check the [upgrade guide].

[changelog]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/CHANGELOG.md&_a=preview

[upgrade guide]: ../guides/upgrading/v0.11.md

## New: Datadog construct for Fargate

We finally adopted a Datadog construct for Fargate containers! 🎉

Our new [DatadogFargate construct] is an opinionated wrapper around the official `DatadogECSFargate`
construct from [datadog-cdk-constructs-v2].

It simplifies observability setup for container-based workloads by:

* automatically configuring the Datadog agent and extension;
* applying consistent tagging aligned with Backpack and NS standards;
* reducing boilerplate configuration in CDK stacks.

If you're running services on Fargate, this provides a much more streamlined way to integrate with Datadog.

Check out the [API docs][DatadogFargate construct] to learn more. If you are using the construct from `@ns/cdk-helper`,
please read the dedicated [migration guide].

[DatadogFargate construct]: ../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/classes/DatadogFargate.md

[datadog-cdk-constructs-v2]: https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-cdk-constructs

[migration guide]: ../guides/migrating/datadog-fargate.md

## New: Circuit breaker for `@backpack/rest-client`

As requested by the community, we added circuit breaker support to the Backpack REST client. This is implemented as
middleware and can be enabled per client with minimal configuration.

A circuit breaker helps protect your application from cascading failures by:

* temporarily blocking requests to failing services;
* reducing unnecessary load during outages;
* allowing systems time to recover.

> \[!note]
> In AWS Lambda environments, this is applied **per execution environment**.
> There is no shared state across Lambda instances, so the circuit breaker is most effective
> for short-lived bursts of failures rather than long-term global outages.

Read more in our [API reference](../packages/@backpack/rest-client/index.md#circuit-breaker).

## AWS Lambda improvements

We added several improvements to the `@backpack/aws-lambda` package.

### `Accept-Language` helpers

New helpers make it easier to parse and resolve `Accept-Language` headers.

```ts
import { defineRestLambda, parseHeaders, jsonOk } from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async (event) => {
  const headers = parseHeaders(event);

  const parsed = headers.parseAcceptLanguage();
  // LanguageCode[]

  const language = headers.resolveAcceptLanguage();
  // LanguageCode.nl | LanguageCode.en

  return jsonOk({ language });
});
```

[Check out the API reference](../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md#accept-language-helpers) to learn more.

### `defineAuthorizerLambda()` helper

A new helper
`defineAuthorizerLambda()` [has been added](../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md#definelambda-helpers).

Similar to the existing helpers, it provides strong typing and improved ergonomics
when implementing Lambda authorizers.

## MockServer improvements

The [Backpack MockServer](./../packages/@backpack/mockserver-client/index.md), introduced as preview feature in 0.10, is
now stable.

We've added several important improvements:

* Removed all `.mock...()` methods in favor of the more ergonomic `.when...()` API;
* Significantly improved error messages with clear explanations of near-misses, making debugging much easier;
* Expanded documentation for better onboarding;
* Reorganized module exports;
* Added support for Vitest asymmetric matchers:

```ts
await mockServer.verify({
  method: "POST",
  path: "/submit",
  headers: {
    authorization: expect.stringContaining("Bearer"),
  },
});
```

## Landing Zone additions

The `LandingZone` construct from `@backpack/cdk-constructs` has been extended with additional lookups for
`organizationId` and `vpc`.

## Dependency upgrades

Keeping dependencies up to date is a key part of Backpack.

We handle peer and transitive dependencies within the ecosystem, so upgrading Backpack
automatically gives you compatible versions of the underlying tooling.

### TypeScript 6

Backpack is now compatible with [TypeScript 6].

This release mainly acts as a transition towards future improvements in the TypeScript ecosystem,
including ongoing work towards faster tooling and new compiler capabilities.

If you're using `@backpack/typescript-config`, no changes are required.

[TypeScript 6]: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-6-0/

### ESLint 10

`@backpack/eslint-config` now supports [ESLint 10].

[ESLint 10]: https://eslint.org/blog/2026/02/eslint-v10.0.0-released/

We made a few changes to this ESLint package:

* `eslint-plugin-import` has been replaced with `eslint-plugin-import-x`, a modern and actively maintained fork with
  better compatibility and performance;
* As a nice side effect, this also resolves long-standing issues with the `no-extraneous-dependencies`
  rule in IntelliJ IDEA when installing new dependencies;
* The rule `vitest/no-standalone-expect` is now disabled by default to reduce noise in test setups (e.g. when using
  fixtures to implement expectations).

Check the [upgrade guide] for details.

### Datadog Lambda layers updates

We updated the [DatadogLambda] construct to use the latest Lambda layers:

* The Node.js layer got updated from v12.132.0 to
  v12.136.0 ([changelog](https://github.com/datadog/datadog-lambda-js/releases));
* The Datadog extension layer got updated from v91 to
  v94 ([changelog](https://github.com/datadog/datadog-lambda-extension/releases)).

[DatadogLambda]: ../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/classes/DatadogLambda.md

## What's next?

We are currently still exploring what the Backpack 1.0 paved road should look like.

This is not a trivial step. Backpack has grown into a widely used platform with an active community,
and we want to carefully balance standardization with flexibility.

We're actively exploring:

* where strong opinions add value;
* where flexibility should remain;
* how we can make the paved road clearer and easier to follow.

You can expect more updates soon as we continue shaping Backpack 1.0 together.

# Announcing Backpack 0.12

Backpack 0.12 contains improvements across testing, HTTP caching, linting, resource tagging, and messaging utilities.

> \[!TIP]
>
> * For the full list of changes, see the [changelog].
> * For step-by-step instructions, check the [upgrade guide].

[changelog]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/CHANGELOG.md&_a=preview

[upgrade guide]: ../guides/upgrading/v0.12.md

## New: test builder utility

We added a new test builder utility to `@backpack/testing`.

The new `createBuilder()` API makes it easier to create reusable test data builders with composable defaults, deep merge
semantics, and strong type inference. This is especially useful for nested test data, where you usually want to
define sensible defaults once and override only the fields that matter for a specific test.

```ts
import { createBuilder } from "@backpack/testing";

interface Device {
  deviceId: string;
  os: {
    name: "IOS" | "ANDROID";
  };
  preferences: {
    language: "NL" | "EN";
  };
}

const createDevice = createBuilder()
  .typed<Device>()
  .withDefaults({
    deviceId: "device-1",
    os: { name: "IOS" },
    preferences: { language: "NL" },
  });

const device = createDevice({
  os: { name: "ANDROID" },
});
```

The builder also supports `extend()`, `lazy()`, `REMOVE`, `.tap()`, and `.map()` for more advanced test workflows.

Check out the `@backpack/testing` [API reference](../packages/@backpack/testing/index.md) to learn more.

## New: HTTP caching utilities

We added first-class support for HTTP caching in Backpack applications.

For `@backpack/aws-lambda`, `jsonResult()` and `jsonOk()` now support explicit caching options. You can use the built-in
`CachePresets` to apply common caching strategies without manually constructing headers:

```ts
import {
  defineRestLambda,
  jsonOk,
  CachePresets,
} from "@backpack/aws-lambda/rest";

export const handler = defineRestLambda(async () => {
  const data = { /* ... */ };

  return jsonOk(data, {
    cache: CachePresets.FIVE_MINUTES,
  });
});
```

We also added a new `@backpack/http` package with generic HTTP utilities, including `cacheControl()`,
`durableCacheStorage()`, and `generateETag()`.

```ts
import { cacheControl } from "@backpack/http";

cacheControl().maxAge(300).mustRevalidate().build();
// → "max-age=300, must-revalidate"
```

Check out the [dedicated caching guide](../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md#http-caching) for more details.

## Type-checked ESLint rules

As of Backpack 0.12, the recommended ESLint preset now includes type-aware rules from `typescript-eslint`.

This makes the default linting setup stricter and more useful. Type-checked linting can catch issues that syntax-only
linting cannot reliably detect, such as unsafe values, floating promises, and incorrect type-driven usage patterns.

This has been included in the default `recommended` preset:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";
import backpack from "@backpack/eslint-config";

export default defineConfig(...backpack.configs.recommended);
```

If your project is not ready for type-checked linting yet, you can use the `legacy` preset instead.

Check the [upgrade guide](../guides/upgrading/v0.12.md) for migration details.

## Improvements for resource tagging

We made several improvements to resource tagging to better align Backpack with the latest tagging guidelines from other
platforms.

The following changes were made:

* our documentation and demo projects now reflect the correct tagging format;
* the `retrieve-tags` command in `@backpack/cli` has been updated to support the new tagging format;
* the `DatadogFargate` construct in `@backpack/cdk-constructs` now applies the correct sanitization rules;
* additional tagging utilities were added to `@backpack/cdk-constructs`, such as `resolveAndApplyTags()`.

These changes should make it easier to apply consistent tags across AWS resources, Datadog, and related platform
tooling.

## SQS batch publishing

The [`SqsPublisher`](../packages/@backpack/amazon-sqs/classes/SqsPublisher.md) in `@backpack/amazon-sqs` now supports
batch publishing.

You can publish multiple messages at once, and the publisher automatically chunks them into batches of 10 messages,
matching the AWS SQS batch limit.

```ts
await sqsPublisher.sendBatchJson([
  { message: "one" },
  { message: "two" },
  { message: "three" },
]);
```

## API Management improvements

Although not strictly part of the Backpack ecosystem, we also collaborated with our community to improve
the [APIM deploy brick].

[APIM deploy brick]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/CICD/_git/pipeline-templates?path=/jobs/deploy/api-management/apim-deploy.md&_a=preview

As of `8.15.0` of the CI/CD pipeline templates, you can associate an API with multiple products during deployment.
This makes it possible to link and unlink your API from multiple APIM products in a single deployment.

The existing `productId` parameter has been deprecated in favor of `productIds`.

```yaml
resources:
  repositories:
    - repository: CICD
      name: CICD/pipeline-templates
      type: git
      ref: refs/tags/8.15.0

stages:
  - stage: Deploy
    jobs:
      - template: jobs/deploy/api-management/apim-deploy.yml@CICD
        parameters:
          environment: "test"
          apiId: "backpack-bookstore"
          productIds:
            - "backpack-public"
            - "backpack-internal"
          # ...
```

# Announcing Backpack 0.13

Backpack 0.13 takes the first steps toward AI-assisted engineering, moves local REST API development to a Hono-based
setup, adds Vite 8 support, and improves Datadog tracing for Lambda applications that use the AWS SDK.

> \[!TIP]
>
> * For the full list of changes, see the [changelog].
> * For step-by-step instructions, check the [upgrade guide].

[changelog]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/CHANGELOG.md&_a=preview

[upgrade guide]: ../guides/upgrading/v0.13.md

## AI adoption: first steps

Backpack is starting to invest more deliberately in support for AI-assisted and agentic engineering.

As a first step, the documentation site now publishes AI-readable documentation through a `llms.txt`,
and Backpack-specific agent instructions. These files help coding agents discover the current Backpack documentation,
package APIs, migration guides, and examples instead of relying on stale model knowledge.

You can also make an existing Backpack project easier for agents to work with by adding an `AGENTS.md` file to the
project root. The Backpack CLI can create or update this file for you:

```shell
npx @backpack/cli agents init
```

This makes prompts such as *"upgrade this project to the latest Backpack version"* more reliable, because the agent can
find the Backpack upgrade guides, package documentation, and project conventions before changing code.

The documentation site now also includes an experimental chat widget.

See the [AI tooling guide](../guides/tooling/ai.md) for details.

## Hono for local development and testing

The old `@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda` package, which used an Express-based local development setup, has been
**deprecated**.

For local REST API development and testing, Backpack now provides `@backpack/hono`. It lets you mount existing API
Gateway Lambda handlers in a Hono application through `fromAwsLambdaHandler()`, run that app with
`@hono/vite-dev-server`, and test it directly with Hono's Fetch-style API or the new `createTestRestClient()` helper.

This is the first step in exploring Hono as part of the Backpack paved road. For now, the Hono setup is only about local
development and testing. It does **not** change the Lambda runtime, the API Gateway integration, or the production
programming model of existing Backpack Lambdas.

See the [local development guide](../guides/tooling/local-development.md) and the
[Hono migration guide](../guides/migrating/hono.md) for examples.

## Vite 8 support

Backpack 0.13 migrates the default tooling setup from Vite 7 to Vite 8.

Vite 8 uses Rolldown/Oxc. Oxc does not yet lower stage 3 ECMAScript decorators directly, which affects projects that
use decorators in code processed by Vite or Vitest. To support those projects, Backpack now includes
[`@backpack/vite`](../packages/@backpack/vite/index.md) with a temporary `backpackVitePlugin()` compatibility transform.

We realize it is annoying that some projects need a small config change for this. We would have preferred the Vite 8
upgrade to be purely a dependency update, but for decorator-based code there is currently no reliable way around adding
the compatibility plugin explicitly.

::: code-group

```ts [vitest.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";
import { backpackVitePlugin } from "@backpack/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [backpackVitePlugin()],
  test: {
    // project-specific Vitest options
  },
});
```

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import { backpackVitePlugin } from "@backpack/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [backpackVitePlugin()],
});
```

:::

If your Vitest config already merges your Vite config, adding the plugin to `vite.config.ts` is enough.

## Automatic Datadog instrumentation of AWS SDK calls

With a standard Backpack Lambda setup, distributed tracing across SNS and SQS flows was not visible correctly in
Datadog. The main issue was that AWS SDK clients were bundled into the Lambda asset, which meant the Datadog layer could
not patch those clients at runtime.

Backpack now changes the default behavior of the `LambdaFunction` construct. Direct `@aws-sdk/*` dependencies are
auto-detected from the nearest `package.json` and installed as separate `node_modules` in the Lambda runtime instead of
being bundled into the application file. This keeps AWS SDK clients patchable by the Datadog layer.

The `DatadogLambda` construct has also been updated with newer Datadog Lambda and extension layers. In most projects,
no code change is required to benefit from this.

## REST client OAuth bearer token middleware

The Backpack REST client now includes middleware for OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens.

Use `bearerToken()` with one of the provided token providers. For Azure Entra ID client credentials, use
`azureClientCredentials()`:

```ts
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";
import {
  azureClientCredentials,
  bearerToken,
  fromEnv,
} from "@backpack/rest-client/middleware";

const bookStoreClient = createRestClient({
  baseUrl: "https://my-book-store.com",
  middlewares: [
    bearerToken(
      azureClientCredentials({
        tenantId: fromEnv("AZURE_TENANT_ID"),
        clientId: fromEnv("AZURE_CLIENT_ID"),
        clientSecret: fromEnv("AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET"),
        scope: fromEnv("AZURE_SCOPE"),
      }),
    ),
  ],
});
```

Tokens are cached until shortly before expiry. For secrets stored in AWS Secrets Manager, use `fromAwsSecretsManager()`
with `@backpack/aws-secrets-manager`.

See the [REST client guide](../how-tos/rest-client.md#oauth-bearer-tokens) for more examples.

## Generated example project snapshots

To make it easier to inspect the structure of a newly generated Backpack project, we now publish snapshots of the
project template to a separate repository:

<https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/BACKPACK/_git/backpack-examples>

This repository is not meant for creating new projects. Use `npx @backpack/cli generate-project` for that. The example
repository is meant as a readable snapshot of how the generated project structure evolves over time.

Different CLI choices are visible as separate branches, such as `minimal`, `rest-api`, `dynamodb`, and `all`. This can
be useful when you want to compare template variants or copy a current best practice into an existing project.

## Other improvements

### Testing

`createMockedObject()` from `@backpack/testing` can now mock interfaces and type aliases:

```ts
import { createMockedObject } from "@backpack/testing";

type Book = { isbn: string };

interface BookRepository {
  findByIsbn(isbn: string): Promise<Book | undefined>;
  save(book: Book): Promise<void>;
}

const repository = createMockedObject<BookRepository>();

repository.findByIsbn.mockResolvedValue({ isbn: "9789027439642" });
```

Class-based mocks continue to work as before.

### AWS utilities

The `SnsPublisher` utility now supports batch publishing through `publishBatchJson()` and `publishBatchRaw()`. Messages
are automatically chunked into groups of 10, matching the SNS batch limit. Partial failures throw
`SnsBatchPublishError` with both failed and successful entries.

```ts
await publisher.publishBatchJson([
  { type: "BookCreated", isbn: "9789027439642" },
  { type: "BookCreated", isbn: "9789027439643" },
]);
```

The `DynamoDbRepository` utility now supports projected reads by passing a `readItem` mapper to `queryItems()`. This is
useful for GSI queries that return a narrower item shape than the repository's default item mapper expects.

```ts
const ids = await booksRepository.queryItems({
  KeyConditionExpression: "genre = :genre",
  ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":genre": "FANTASY" },
  IndexName: "GenreIndex",
  ProjectionExpression: "id",
  readItem: (item) => ({ id: item.id as string }),
});
```

`DynamoDbRepository` also includes `transactWrite()` for atomic multi-item writes.

### Backpack config

Invalid configuration now throws an `InvalidConfigError` with human-readable Zod output. This should make configuration
mistakes easier to diagnose during local development, CI, and Lambda startup.

### CDK constructs

The `LambdaFunction` construct now defaults to the `ARM_64` Lambda architecture to reduce runtime costs. Projects that
need another architecture can override this in the construct configuration.

The `DatadogLambda` construct now configures a Python Datadog layer version as well, so it can instrument Python Lambda
functions added to the construct.

The `DatadogFargate` construct is now NSCF compliant with read-only root filesystem access enabled by default. It also
adds the writable mount points that Fluent Bit needs when the root filesystem is read-only.

Datadog defaults were updated to newer versions:

* `DatadogLambda`: Node layer `v140` and extension layer `v98`;
* `DatadogFargate`: Datadog agent `v7.80.3`.

# Announcing Backpack 0.3

## New in Backpack: error handling

Backpack now includes some best practices regarding [error handling](../guides/development/error-handling.md). There are
also some nice utilities included in the new [`@backpack/error-handling`](../packages/@backpack/error-handling/index.md) package.

Go check it out, and please share your feedback!

## Migrate your AWS Lambda functions to Node v22

We upgraded the recommended runtime for your AWS Lambda functions from Node v20 to Node v22.

* Make sure to upgrade `aws-cdk-lib` to `v2.168.0` or higher first.
* In your CDK code, change the `runtime` of your lambda to `NODEJS_22_X`.

## Changed entry points of `@backpack/aws-lambda`

All REST-related utilities in `@backpack/aws-lambda` have been moved to `@backpack/aws-lambda/rest`.
This means you have to update all your existing imports.

* [Express 5 release notes](https://expressjs.com/2024/10/15/v5-release.html)
* [Vite 6 release notes](https://vite.dev/blog/announcing-vite6)

# Announcing Backpack 0.5

For full details, please refer to our [changelog].

[changelog]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/CHANGELOG.md&_a=preview

## Adopted utilities from `@ns/common-serverless-library`

We adopted most of the utilities from `@ns/common-serverless-library`. They can be found in the following packages:

* [`@backpack/aws-secrets-manager`](../packages/@backpack/aws-secrets-manager/index.md): utilities for AWS Secrets Manager
* [`@backpack/amazon-dynamodb`](../packages/@backpack/amazon-dynamodb/index.md): utilities for interacting with a DynamoDB table
* [`@backpack/amazon-sns`](../packages/@backpack/amazon-sns/index.md): utilities for publishing messages to Amazon SNS
* [`@backpack/amazon-sqs`](../packages/@backpack/amazon-sqs/index.md): utilities for publishing messages to Amazon SQS
* [`@backpack/amazon-s3`](../packages/@backpack/amazon-s3/index.md): utilities for interacting with an Amazon S3 bucket

If you plan to migrate, make sure to consult the [migration guide][migration guide common-serverless].

[migration guide common-serverless]: ../guides/migrating/common-serverless-library.md

## New: Backpack REST client

We explored common practices for REST clients and have introduced a pre-configured REST client in Backpack. It
uses [Wretch] under the hood and allows seamless integration with any REST API in a straightforward manner while keeping
dependencies minimal:

```ts
import { createRestClient } from "@backpack/rest-client";

const bookStoreClient = createRestClient({
  baseUrl: "https://my-book-store.com",
  apiManagementApiKey: '...',
  timeout: 5_000,
  // ...
});

const books = await bookStoreClient
  .get("/api/v1/books")
  .json();
```

Explore the new [`@backpack/rest-client`] package to learn more!

[Wretch]: https://github.com/elbywan/wretch

[`@backpack/rest-client`]: ../packages/@backpack/rest-client/index.md

## Added `@backpack/testing`

We also extracted a popular testing utility function into [`@backpack/testing`](../packages/@backpack/testing/index.md).

## Improved the entire documentation

We have completely restructured the documentation and added many new pages. For example, check out the
new [how-to guides], which focus on common tasks, or visit the updated [CDK snippets] page.

We also now have a dedicated [migration guide] on how to migrate your existing project to Backpack!

[how-to guides]: ../how-tos/lambda.md

[CDK snippets]: ../guides/infrastructure/cdk-snippets.md

[migration guide]: ../guides/migrating/existing-project-to-backpack.md

# Announcing Backpack 0.7

We're happy to announce the release of Backpack 0.7.

> \[!TIP]
>
> * For the full list of changes, please refer to our [changelog].
> * For step-by-step instructions, check the [upgrade guide].

## New CDK constructs library

We’ve added a new package to Backpack: `@backpack/cdk-constructs`. It contains reusable CDK constructs that help you
build serverless applications with less boilerplate code. It also helps to rollout generic platform capabilities. Check
out [the docs](../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/index.md) to learn more.

## Improved project template

When you generate a new project using the [Backpack CLI](../packages/@backpack/cli/index.md), you’ll notice several
improvements:

* The default template now uses the new `@backpack/cdk-constructs` library.
* Datadog dashboards in infrastructure-as-code are now optional.

Zod 4 brings major performance improvements, smaller bundles, and new features like metadata registries, JSON Schema
support, and better error handling. Read more about the changes [here](https://zod.dev/v4).

### Wretch 3

We’ve upgraded Wretch — the foundation of `@backpack/rest-client` — to version 3.\
Wretch 3 now targets modern browsers and Node 22+, removes legacy APIs, and improves immutability, modularity, and
TypeScript support. See the [migration guide] for renamed methods and updated error-handling behavior.

workflow, we added [a new CI/CD brick] to the Azure DevOps CI/CD pipelines library.

* When generating a new project with the Backpack CLI, it will be automatically included in the generated CI/CD
  pipeline;
* To add it to your existing project:
  * generate [a new CI/CD pipeline] with the Backpack CLI;

# Announcing Backpack 0.9

This release delivers a lot of improvements.

> \[!TIP]
>
> * For the full list of changes, please refer to our [changelog].
> * For step-by-step instructions, check the [upgrade guide].

[changelog]: https://dev.azure.com/ns-topaas/_git/BACKPACK?path=/CHANGELOG.md&_a=preview

[upgrade guide]: ../guides/upgrading/v0.9.md

## Major documentation overhaul

First of all: the docs site has now moved to [backpack.ns.nl](https://backpack.ns.nl) :tada:. This is part of a bigger
effort to position Backpack more and more as an official (and wider adopted) initiative.

We've also made some big changes to the documentation itself. One important change is that we have reorganized the
in-depth guides
into clearer categories, such as developer tooling, CI/CD, infrastructure and development.

We have also added several new pages, for example:

* [Linting and formatting]
* [Using Vitest] and [testing strategies]
* [Logging and metrics]
* [Monitoring and alerts]

[Linting and formatting]: ../guides/tooling/linting-and-formatting.md

[Monitoring and alerts]: ../guides/observability/monitoring-and-alerts.md

Missing something? Please let us know.

## CDK construct enhancements

We refined several CDK constructs to further improve the developer experience.

### API Gateway

The [ApiGateway] construct has received the following updates:

* Added `FileApiDefinition` for file-based OpenAPI specs ([example][FileApiDefinition]);
* The `apiDefinition` and `lambdaFunctions` options are now optional;
* You can now enable access logging using the `enableAccessLogging` [feature toggle][access logging].

[ApiGateway]: ../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/classes/ApiGateway.md

[FileApiDefinition]: ../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/classes/FileApiDefinition.md
