#### AWS Lambda

* Added `vpc` and `vpcSubnets` options to the `LambdaFunction` construct.

### Datadog monitoring

We updated the [DatadogLambda] construct to use the latest Lambda layers:

* The Node.js layer got updated from v12.128.0 to
  v12.132.0 ([changelog](https://github.com/datadog/datadog-lambda-js/releases));
* The Datadog extension layer got updated from v86 to
  v91 ([changelog](https://github.com/datadog/datadog-lambda-extension/releases)).

[DatadogLambda]: ../packages/@backpack/cdk-constructs/classes/DatadogLambda.md

## Linting and formatting improvements

To enhance linting and formatting across projects — without disrupting your workflow, we've introduced the
following:

* **Improved default project template:**
  * includes default ESLint and Prettier configurations for IntelliJ IDEA and VS Code;
  * adds a `lint-staged` + Husky setup to automatically lint and format staged files before committing;
  * updated npm scripts to make local validation easier.
* **For existing projects:** a dedicated [how-to guide][Linting/formatting how-to guide] has been added. Check it out
  and, if you want to, update your project accordingly.

[Linting/formatting how-to guide]: ../guides/tooling/linting-and-formatting.md

## Added Change API to the standard CI/CD pipeline

To make it easier to publish your changes to ServiceNow, we added Change API integration to
the [standard CI/CD pipeline](../guides/cicd/standard-pipeline.md).

## New helper: `defineScheduledLambda()`

For scheduled Lambda functions that need access to the `EventBridgeEvent`, you can now use:

```ts twoslash
import { defineScheduledLambda } from "@backpack/aws-lambda";

const handler = defineScheduledLambda(async (event) => {
  //                                         ^?
  // ...
});
```

Check out the [API reference](../packages/@backpack/aws-lambda/index.md) for similar helper functions.

## Renovate improvements

We spotted some issues with Renovate and have updated the standard configuration accordingly. Please check out our new
[Renovate how-to guide] for more details.

[Renovate how-to guide]: ../guides/cicd/renovate.md

## What's next?

A few hot topics on our roadmap:

* Support for monorepos / npm workspaces;
* Start adopting Hono for code-first OpenAPI support;
* Further improvements to optimize the overall developer experience.

# Backpack 1.0: paved road for REST APIs

This document outlines our plan to explore and define the paved road for Backpack 1.0 around developing REST APIs.

> This document is intended as a **discussion paper for the workshop**.\
> It contains initial directions and recommendations, but does **not** represent a final decision.

## Goal

For the Backpack 1.0 paved road, we aim to:

* **explore** a set of **capabilities** currently missing or inconsistent;
* **clarify** the **problems and limitations** in today’s paved road;
* **determine** what should be standardized and what should remain flexible;
* **define direction**, not finalize all implementation details.

## Context

The following RFC has been proposed to the community:\
https://backpack.ns.nl/rfcs/hono-adoption.html

After receiving feedback, we concluded:

* the RFC introduced significant changes to the programming model without clearly explaining the underlying problems;
* it focused too much on a specific implementation (Hono), instead of the capabilities we aim to achieve;
* it implicitly enforced decisions (e.g. code-first), without sufficiently exploring alternatives.

## Stakeholders

* **key engineers** across teams/clusters within ComIT
* **solution architects** from the involved clusters;
* team **Fundamentals** (acting as the current Backpack core team)

## Why?

Standardization helps us:

* reduce cognitive load across services
* improve maintainability and consistency
* speed up onboarding
* enable better tooling and automation

A paved road provides a **clear, opinionated default**, while still allowing flexibility where needed.

However, there is an inherent tension:

* too much standardization → rigid, low adoption
* too little standardization → fragmentation, low effectiveness

This effort aims to strike the right balance.

## Decision framing

We are **not deciding whether to adopt Hono**.

We are deciding:

* which **capabilities** Backpack should standardize;
* which capabilities should have a **default implementation**;
* and whether Hono is a good candidate for some of those defaults.

## How?

* Create a **task force** (5–10 engineers/architects)
* Run one or more **workshop sessions**
* For each capability:
  * understand the problem
  * explore solution directions
  * identify a preferred direction (not finalize)
* Use outcomes to refine a new RFC
* Implement decisions in Backpack 1.0

## Scope

Backend services implementing **TypeScript-based REST APIs on AWS Lambda**

## Capability 1: runtime agnostic handlers

> Goal: promote a **consistent, web-standard-based programming model**

### Problem

AWS-native handlers are awkward and inconsistent across teams.

Most engineers implement REST endpoints using "native" AWS-handlers:

```ts
import type { APIGatewayProxyEvent, APIGatewayProxyResult } from "aws-lambda";  
  
export const handler = async (event: APIGatewayProxyEvent) => {  
  return { statusCode: 200, body: "Hello world!" }
}  
```

Working with raw `APIGatewayProxyEvent` and `APIGatewayProxyResult` often proved to be a bit awkward.  Examples include: normalizing (multi-value) parameters/headers, dealing with case sensitivity, etc.

Many teams have introduced their own custom utilities to make working with AWS objects more ergonomic.

This leads to fragmentation:

* Backpack utilities (`@backpack/aws-lambda`)
* [Middy]-based middleware
* decorator-based approaches (e.g. MijnNS)
* custom per-team solutions

Result: no consistent mental model across teams.

[Middy]: https://middy.js.org/

### Solution direction

Adopt Fetch-based handlers (`Request` / `Response`).

### Explanation

Instead of implementing AWS-specific handlers, we can change the current programming model to work with standard  `Request` and `Response` classes instead.

> \[!info] Industry direction\
> Using a "Fetch-like" interface is an industry direction that has been standardized by [WinterTC](https://wintertc.org/work).
> This means code written against these APIs becomes portable across runtimes such as Node.js, Deno, AWS Lambda, etc.

To apply this technique, you don't need to use a framework. A simple adapter for AWS Lambda is enough:

```ts
import { handleFetch } from "@backpack/aws-lambda" // (does not exist yet)  
  
const requestHandler = (request: Request) => {
  return new Response("Hello world!");
}  
  
export const handler = handleFetch(requestHandler); // AWS-specific adapter  
```

This allows engineers to work with a **single mental model** across:

* AWS Lambda runtime
* local development
* integration tests

Instead of switching between different abstractions (APIGateway events, custom utilities, mocks),  we align on one consistent interface while relying on standardized APIs such as `Request`, `Response`, `URL`, `Headers` .

#### Request model ergonomics

Modern web APIs provide ergonomic helpers such as:

```ts
return Response.json(data)
```

Header normalization:

```ts
request.headers.get(...)   
```

#### Testing & client interoperability

Fetch-style handlers can be invoked directly in tests using standard `Request` objects:

```ts
const response = await myHandler(new Request("/api/v1/hello"));  
// or, with proper normalization: await myHandler("/api/v1/hello");    

expect(response.status).toBe(200);  
expect(await response.json()).toEqual({ message: "Hello world!" });  
```

Without the need for AWS-specific mocks (`APIGatewayProxyEvent`), this enables fast and lightweight integration tests (with no HTTP socket needed), and you interact with local in-memory app code the same way as with remote environments.

### Possible default implementation: Hono

[Hono] is a lightweight web framework that builds on top of the Fetch model and adds higher-level abstractions such as routing and middleware.

[Hono]: https://hono.dev/

Even though a standardized `Request` handler is a solid foundation, it can still feel a bit clunky to implement certain things. For example, when obtaining query parameters:

```ts
const url = new URL(request.url);  
const names = url.searchParams.getAll("name");  
```

With [Hono](https://hono.dev/), you get a more ergonomic approach, as it provides some shorthands:

```ts import { Hono } from "hono";  
import { handle } from "hono/aws-lambda";  
  
const app = new Hono();  
  
app.all((c) => {  
  const names = c.req.queries("name") ?? ["World"];
  const formatted = names.join(", ");  
  
  return c.text(`Hello ${formatted}!`);
});  
  
export const handler = handle(app);  
```

This example shows a single "catch-all" Hono handler, which under the hood works similar to our previous example: it accepts a request, and delegates it to a handler.

#### Middleware-support

Hono also allows us to introduce reusable **type-safe [middleware]**:

[middleware]: https://hono.dev/docs/middleware/third-party

```ts import { Hono, type MiddlewareHandler } from "hono";  
import { cors } from "hono/cors";  
  
const app = new Hono();  
  
app.use(cors()); // standard middleware
app.use(myCustomMiddleware()); // custom middleware    

app.all("*", (c) => {  
  return c.text("Hello world!!");
});  
  
function myCustomMiddleware(): MiddlewareHandler {  
  return async (c, next) => {
    console.log(`Request method: ${c.req.method}`);
    await next();
  };
}  
```

This makes it easier to reuse middleware across different projects and teams.

#### Error handling

Hono also makes **error handling** more ergonomic:

```ts
app.onError((err, c) => {  
  console.error(err);  
  return c.json({ title: "Unknown error" }, 500);
});    
```

This allows us to easily implement standardized error handling across Backpack projects.

#### Final notes

> \[!warning] Important limitation: path parameters
>
> A plain `Request` does not include route information such as named path parameters. These need to be resolved using a routing layer (e.g. `URLPattern` or a router like Hono, see capability #3).

Adopting Hono as a default introduces:

* a middleware model
* request/response helpers
* validation integrations
* testing utilities

This means choosing Hono is not just a technical detail,  but a broader platform decision.

### Recommendation

Adopt Fetch-based handlers as the **foundational abstraction**.

Consider Hono as a **recommended default implementation** for teams that benefit from:

* routing
* middleware
* improved ergonomics

but do not enforce it as the only model.

## Capability 2: local development support

> Goal: improve developer productivity

Some teams prefer the option for local development because it improves:

* feedback speed during development
* debugging capabilities
* confidence when making changes

However, the current setup does not consistently deliver these benefits.

### Problem

Local development for REST Lambdas today introduces:

* additional setup (Express server, custom adapters)
* a different programming model than production
* duplication of routing logic
* slower feedback loops

As a result, local development is not consistently used across teams,  and does not provide a reliable or ergonomic developer experience.

### Solution

Introduce a Hono-based development server that can:

* run Fetch-based handlers directly
* adapt AWS-native handlers using lightweight adapters
* provide a consistent developer experience across environments

This approach builds on Capability #1 (Fetch-based handlers), allowing the same handler model to be reused across local development and production.

#### Current approach (`@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda`)

The current approach in Backpack involves setting up a local Express.js app (e.g. `server.ts`) where we use a custom adapter to integrate one or more AWS-handlers. This can then be served using Vite as development server.

```ts
import express from "express";  
import { lambdaHandlers } from "@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda";  
  
const app = express(); // <- Express.js app  
  
app.use(
    lambdaHandlers({ // <- existing custom adapter from Backpack
        handlers: {
            "/api/v1/books": {
                get: {
                    handler: () => import("./app/lambdas/get-books.lambda.ts")
                        .then((it) => it.handler),
                },
                post: {
                    handler: () => import("./app/lambdas/add-book.lambda.ts")
                        .then((it) => it.handler),
                },
            },
        },
    })
);  
```

Limitations:

* Express is not aligned with modern web standards;
* handler registration is not ergonomic;
* adds additional abstraction layer;
* requires a custom Vite plugin maintained by Backpack (`@backpack/vite-plugin-lambda`)

#### Hono-based approach  (new paved road)

With Hono, we can use `@hono/vite-dev-server` combined with more ergonomic adapters.

```ts import { Hono } from "hono";  
  
// custom adapters, do not yet exist  
import { fromLambda, fromFetch } from "@backpack/hono";  
  
import { handler as getBooks } from "./get-books.lambda";  
import { handler as addBook } from "./add-book.lambda";  
import { requestHandler as helloWorld } from "./hello-world.lambda";
  
const app = new Hono();  
  
// adapter for AWS-native handlers:  
app.get("/api/v1/books", fromLambda(getBooks));  
app.post("/api/v1/books", fromLambda(addBook));  
  
// adapter for Fetch-like request handlers:  
app.get("/api/v1/hello", fromFetch(helloWorld));
```

### Important consideration

In this setup, routing exists outside the Lambda runtime and is **not the source of truth**. API Gateway remains the authoritative routing layer in production.

### Recommendation

Prefer a Hono-based local development model as the default approach.

This provides a consistent developer experience aligned with Fetch-based handlers.

At the same time:

* AWS-native handlers should remain fully supported
* local development should remain optional
* teams should not be forced into a single development workflow

## Capability 3: route-aware handlers inside the runtime

> Goal: support route semantics such as named path parameters and route-level middleware on top of Fetch-based handlers.

### Problem

A plain Fetch-based handler models HTTP transport well, but does not include route semantics such as named path parameters.

For many REST APIs, those semantics are useful in practice, for example:

* extracting path parameters in a standardized way
* applying middleware to specific route groups
* keeping handlers ergonomic and expressive

### Solution direction

Introduce a route-aware runtime abstraction on top of Fetch, for example using Hono.

```ts
app.get("/api/v1/hello/:name", (c) => {
  const { name } = c.req.param();
  return c.text(`Hello ${name}!`);
});
```

This allows handlers to work with route semantics such as:

* named path parameters
* route matching
* route-level middleware

### Recommendation

Support **route-aware handlers** as a recommended capability on top of the Fetch-based foundation.

This improves ergonomics and makes runtime-agnostic handlers more practical.

> Important: this does **not** imply that multiple endpoints need to be implemented in a single Lambda.

## Capability 4: multiple handlers inside one Lambda

> Goal: support grouping multiple related endpoints into a single Lambda where this is beneficial.

### Problem

Some use cases benefit from combining multiple related handlers into one Lambda, for example:

* internal tools
* mock servers
* grouped endpoints with shared middleware
* specific BFF-style compositions

However, this introduces architectural trade-offs around service boundaries, deployment blast radius, and observability.

### Solution direction

Use a runtime router such as Hono to host multiple handlers inside a single Lambda when needed.

```ts
const app = new Hono();

app.get("/api/v1/hello", (c) => c.text("Hello world!"));

app.get("/api/v1/hello/:name", (c) => {
  const { name } = c.req.param();
  return c.text(`Hello ${name}!`);
});

export const handler = handle(app); // single handler to serve both endpoints
```

### Trade-offs

* duplicates routing concerns already present in API Gateway
* introduces an additional abstraction layer inside the runtime
* can blur service boundaries when overused
* increases deployment blast radius compared to single-purpose Lambdas

### Recommendation

Support **multiple handlers inside one Lambda** as an optional architectural pattern.

For most services, Backpack should continue to prefer **single-purpose Lambdas** with routing handled by API Gateway.

Runtime routing is most valuable in specific scenarios, such as:

* grouped endpoints with shared middleware
* local development integration
* internal tools or mock servers

It should be treated as a pragmatic option, not as the default architecture.

## Capability 5: runtime validation

### Problem

There is currently no consistent way to:

* validate incoming data
* transform data into usable domain objects
* ensure type-safety across runtime and TypeScript

API Gateway validation can act as a first-line guard, but it does not solve these problems.

### Solution

Adopt [Zod](https://zod.dev/) validation as a unified approach for validation, transformation, and typing.

### Explanation

Using Zod is as simple as:

```ts
const UpdateBook = z.object({    
  title: z.string().min(1).max(255).nonempty(),
});    

const result = UpdateBook.safeParse(json);    
    
if (!result.success) {    
  return { statusCode: 400, body: "Bad request" };  
}    
```

This effectively creates a single pipeline:

* input validation
* data transformation
* strongly-typed domain objects

Benefits:

* expressive validation logic;
* transformations and normalization (e.g. parsing strings into domain types)
* shared runtime + TypeScript types;
* consistent error handling.

#### Examples

Using Zod in a native AWS-handler:

```ts
const UpdateBook = z.object({    
  title: z.string().min(1).max(255).nonempty(),
});    
    
const UpdateBookRequest = z.object({    
  params: z.object({    
    isbn: z.string().transform((it) => it.trim()),    
  }),
  body: UpdateBook,    
});    
    
export const handler = async (event: APIGatewayProxyEvent) => {    
  const parseRequest = UpdateBookRequest.safeParse({    
    params: event.pathParameters,    
    body: JSON.parse(event.body ?? "{}"), // or use Backpack utilities    
  });    
    
  if (!parseRequest.success) {    
    return { statusCode: 400, body: "Bad request" };    
    // Future consideration: standardize validation error handling
  }    
    
  const request = parseRequest.data;    
    
  const { isbn } = request.params;    
  const updateBook = request.body;    
    
  return {    
    statusCode: 200,    
    body: `Updated title of book ${isbn} to "${updateBook.title}"!`    
  };
};  
```

In Hono, you can benefit from built-in [validator](https://hono.dev/docs/guides/validation) support, such as `@hono/zod-validator`:

```ts
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { zValidator } from "@hono/zod-validator";
import { z } from "zod";    
    
const UpdateBook = z.object({    
  title: z.string().min(1).max(255).nonempty(),
});    
    
const UpdateBookParams = z.object({    
  isbn: z.string().min(10).max(13),
});    
    
const app = new Hono();    
    
app.put("/api/v1/books/:isbn",    
  zValidator("param", UpdateBookParams),    
  zValidator("json", UpdateBook),    
  (c) => {    
    const { isbn } = c.req.valid("param");    
    const updateBook = c.req.valid("json");    
      
    return c.text(`Updated title of book ${isbn} to "${updateBook.title}"!`);    
  });  
```

### Recommendation

Standardize on **Zod** as the primary runtime validation library, to:

* validate incoming requests
* transform data into domain-friendly shapes
* provide a single source of truth for TypeScript types

Validation should be implemented inside the runtime, regardless of whether API Gateway validation is used.

Framework integrations (such as Hono) are optional and build on top of this foundation.

## Capability 6: spec-first OpenAPI

> Goal: support contract-first API design for teams that prioritize explicit API specifications.

### Context

There are two fundamentally different approaches to API design:

* **spec-first**: the API contract (e.g. OpenAPI) is the source of truth
* **code-first**: the implementation (e.g. Zod schemas) is the source of truth

Both approaches are valid, but they lead to different workflows, tooling, and trade-offs.

### Approach

In a spec-first workflow:

* API contracts are defined using OpenAPI (e.g. YAML)
* code is generated from the specification (e.g. TypeScript types or Zod schemas)
* runtime validation is based on generated models

### Examples

Using OpenAPI-generated models with Zod schemas is very powerful when combined with Hono:

```ts
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { zValidator } from "@hono/zod-validator";    
    
// generated using your favorite OpenAPI generator:  
import { UpdateBookRequest, UpdateBookParams } from "./generated/v1/books";    
    
const app = new Hono();

app.put(
  "/api/v1/books/:isbn",
  zValidator("param", UpdateBookParams),    
  zValidator("json", UpdateBookRequest), (c) => {    
    const { isbn } = c.req.valid("param");    
    const updateBook = c.req.valid("json");    
        
    return c.text(`Updated title of book ${isbn} to "${updateBook.title}"!`);    
  });  
```

### Trade-offs

While spec-first provides strong contract guarantees, it also introduces trade-offs:

* requires additional tooling (generators, pipelines)
* limited control over generated validation logic
* divergence between spec and implementation is still possible

> \[!warning] Challenges
>
> * There is currently no standardized OpenAPI generator across teams;
> * custom post-processing is sometimes needed (e.g. lint/format).

### Recommendation

This remains a **valid and supported approach**.

However, Backpack will **not optimize the paved road primarily for spec-first workflows**.

Instead:

* support spec-first where needed
* avoid blocking teams that rely on it
* do not standardize on a specific generator or toolchain

> See capability #7 for the primary (code-first) approach.

## Capability 7: code-first OpenAPI

> Goal: define API contracts from code, using a single source of truth for validation, types, and documentation.

### Context

In a **code-first** workflow:

* API contracts are derived from implementation code
* validation, typing, and documentation are defined in one place
* OpenAPI is generated from runtime models

### Solution

This approach extends the Zod-based validation model (capability #5),\
turning it into a single source of truth for:

* runtime validation
* TypeScript types
* OpenAPI documentation

This eliminates duplication between:

* validation logic
* TypeScript types
* API documentation

reducing the risk of inconsistencies between these layers.

#### Using `@asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi`  (paved road)

This library allows you to define your OpenAPI model programmatically:

```ts
const UserSchema = z
  .object({
    id: z.string().openapi({ example: '1212121' }),
    name: z.string().openapi({ example: 'John Doe' }),
    age: z.number().openapi({ example: 42 }),
  })
  .openapi('User');

registry.registerPath({
  method: 'get',
  path: '/users/{id}',
  summary: 'Get a single user',
  request: {
    params: z.object({ id: z.string() }),
  },

  responses: {
    200: {
      description: 'Object with user data.',
      content: {
        'application/json': {
          schema: UserSchema,
        },
      },
    },
  },
});
```

This can then be used to generate an OpenAPI document, while still using Zod schemas for runtime safety.

Note that this library does not require you to use Hono.

#### Using `@hono/zod-openapi` (experimental)

This builds on top of  `@asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi`. After defining your OpenAPI models programmatically, you can use them to leverage type-safe Hono handlers:

```ts
import { OpenAPIHono } from '@hono/zod-openapi'

const app = new OpenAPIHono()

app.openapi(route, (c) => {
  const { isbn } = c.req.valid('param') // type-safe params
  const updateBook = c.req.valid('json') // type-safe params
  
  return c.text(`Updated title of book ${isbn} to "${updateBook.title}"!`);
})

// The OpenAPI documentation will be available at /doc
app.doc('/doc', {
  openapi: '3.0.0',
  info: {
    version: '1.0.0',
    title: 'My API',
  },
})
```

This provides a very integrated developer experience when using Hono,  but introduces tighter coupling to the framework and its abstractions.

> \[!warning] Challenges
>
> * strong request validation, but limited response validation
> * no Zod 4.1 codec support yet
>
> → treat as experimental for now.

### Recommendation

Code-first OpenAPI should be the **primary approach** for Backpack.

This approach:

* builds on the Zod validation model (capability #5)
* provides a single source of truth
* provides a strong and consistent developer experience
* reduces duplication and inconsistencies

Backpack should invest primarily in tooling and documentation for this approach.

## Workshop format

This session is designed to balance structure, alignment, and open discussion.

We aim to:

* align on the **capabilities** that matter for our paved road;
* explore **solution directions** for each capability;
* identify **preferred directions**, not finalize every detail;
* collect input to shape a refined RFC proposal.

> Important: this session is **not** intended to finalize the RFC.\
> It is intended to **inform** the next version of the proposal.

### Workshop principles

To keep the session effective and focused:

* We discuss **principles and direction**, not edge cases.
* We aim for **alignment**, not perfection.
* We prefer **clear defaults with flexibility**, not rigid rules.
* Everyone contributes, no one dominates.
* Disagreement is fine — we capture it and move on.

### Time schedule

| Time        | Activity               |\
|-------------|------------------------|\
| 09:00–09:30 | Walk-in                |\
| 09:30–09:45 | Introduction & framing |\
| 09:45–10:25 | Capabilities 1 & 2     |\
| 10:25–10:35 | Break                  |\
| 10:35–11:15 | Capabilities 3 & 4     |\
| 11:15–11:25 | Break                  |\
| 11:25–11:45 | Capability 5           |\
| 11:45–12:00 | Synthesis & wrap-up    |

### Introduction (09:30–09:45)

We start with:

* Context of this session and relation to the earlier RFC
* Goals of the workshop
* Explanation of the capability-based approach
* Explanation of the format per capability
* Alignment on workshop principles

### Capability format (±20 minutes each)

Each capability follows the same structure:

#### 1. Problem framing (±5 min)

* Short explanation of the problem
* Why this matters at scale
* Current limitations / fragmentation

#### 2. Solution directions (±5 min)

* Present 1–2 possible approaches
* Highlight trade-offs
* Keep it focused (avoid too many variants)

#### 3. Group input (±7 min)

* Do you recognize this problem?
* Are we missing important aspects?
* What feels like a natural direction?

#### 4. Direction signal (±3 min)

We capture a quick signal from the group:

* 👍 Recommended / strong support
* 😐 Acceptable / neutral
* 👎 Not preferred

> Goal: identify direction, not finalize decisions.

#### 5. Facilitator summary (±1 min)

The facilitator summarizes in **one sentence**:

* e.g. “Zod as the validation standard”
* e.g. “Hono as recommended default, not enforced”

### Synthesis & wrap-up (11:45–12:00)

At the end of the session:

1. **Recap per capability**

* One-line summary of the preferred direction

2. **Combine into a coherent model**

* What becomes the **default**?
* What remains **optional**?
* What is **experimental**?

3. **Validate with the group**

* Does this feel consistent?
* Are we missing major concerns?

### Outcome

After the workshop:

* A refined **RFC draft** will be created based on the outcomes
* The draft will be shared with participants for review
* After incorporating feedback, it will be presented to the broader community
* The RFC will be finalized after a defined feedback period

## Current working hypothesis

### 🧱 Paved road v1.x

* **Primary model:** Hono-based runtime (recommended, not enforced)
* **Validation:** Zod (standard)
* **OpenAPI:** both spec-first and code-first supported
* **Routing:** Hono-based routing (recommended)
* **Local dev:** Hono-based approach
* **Hono Zod OpenAPI:** experimental

> \[!important] Key principle\
> We standardize on **capabilities**, not strictly on tooling.

### 🧓 Legacy support

* AWS-native handlers remain supported
* no forced migration
* Express-based local development will be **deprecated**
* gradual adoption path

# Backpack 1.0: request handling & API design decisions

**Status:** Proposed\
**Version:** 0.2.1\
**Author:** Dirk Luijk\
**Created:** 2026-03-31\
**Last updated:** 2026-03-31

> This RFC supersedes the earlier "Hono adoption discussion" RFC by restructuring the discussion into three independent decision axes.

## Goal

This document describes how we want to structure the paved road for building REST APIs in Backpack 1.0.

Rather than defining a fixed set of capabilities, we describe a small number of **key decisions** that teams can make when building services.

These decisions are largely independent, but do influence each other in practice.

Our goal is to:

* make these decisions explicit and easy to understand;
* clarify which options are **supported**;
* clarify which options are **recommended and optimized** by Backpack.

## Background

In the current Backpack paved road, several concerns are implicitly coupled:

* AWS-native handlers (API Gateway events)
* validation (often implicit or limited)
* OpenAPI (mostly spec-first)
* local development (limited or ad-hoc)
* middleware (via patterns like Middy or custom solutions)

At the same time, we see increasing demand for:

* better local development experience
* runtime validation
* more portable and testable handlers
* clearer separation between infrastructure and application logic

The introduction of Web APIs (Request/Response), Fetch-based handlers, and tools like Hono and Zod allows us to rethink how we structure these concerns.

## Overview

When building a service with Backpack, there are three main decision axes:

1. **Validation model** – how do you validate and model your data?
2. **Request handling model** – how do you structure your handlers and runtime?
3. **API contract model** – where does your OpenAPI specification come from?

Each of these decisions is described below.

## Decision 1: validation model

### Summary

Backpack strongly recommends using Zod for runtime validation and type-safe data modelling.

However, Zod is **not a hard prerequisite** for all other choices.

Zod is not just a validation library. It also enables:

* default values
* transforms
* codecs
* custom domain validation

This makes it a strong foundation for both API validation and internal domain modelling.

### Example: basic schema

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

export const getUserResponseSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  name: z.string(),
});

export type GetUserResponse = z.infer<typeof getUserResponseSchema>;
```

### Example: defaults, transforms and custom validation

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

export const createUserRequestSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().trim().min(1),
  email: z.email().transform((value) => value.toLowerCase()),
  locale: z.string().default("nl-NL"),
  birthDate: z.string().refine(
    (value) => !Number.isNaN(Date.parse(value)),
    "birthDate must be a valid ISO date"
  ),
});
```

### Example: codec

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

const epochMillisToInstantCodec = z.codec(
  z.number(),
  Temporal.Instant,
  {
    decode: (value) => Temporal.Instant.fromEpochMilliseconds(value),
    encode: (value) => value.epochMilliseconds,
  }
);

const bookingSchema = z.object({
  departureTime: epochMillisToInstantCodec,
});
```

### Example: AWS-style 400 validation error

```ts
import { z, ZodError } from "zod";

const paramsSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(1),
});

export async function handler(event: { pathParameters?: Record<string, string | undefined> }) {
  try {
    const params = paramsSchema.parse(event.pathParameters ?? {});

    return {
      statusCode: 200,
      body: JSON.stringify({
        message: `Hello ${params.name}`,
      }),
    };
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof ZodError) {
      return {
        statusCode: 400,
        body: JSON.stringify({
          message: "Invalid request",
          issues: error.issues.map((issue) => ({
            path: issue.path.join("."),
            message: issue.message,
          })),
        }),
      };
    }

    throw error;
  }
}
```

### Positioning

* **Recommended (default):** use Zod
* **Supported:** other validation approaches

Backpack will optimize for Zod-based workflows.

## Decision 2: request handling model

### Summary

Teams can choose how they structure their request handling and runtime model.

This ranges from fully AWS-native handlers to a Fetch-based model using Hono.

### Option A: AWS-native handlers

```ts
import type { APIGatewayProxyHandler } from "aws-lambda";

export const handler: APIGatewayProxyHandler = async (event) => {
  const name = event.pathParameters?.name ?? "world";

  return {
    statusCode: 200,
    body: JSON.stringify({
      message: `Hello ${name}`,
    }),
  };
};
```

### Option B: Hono in dev/test only

Hono is used as a **local development and testing layer**, while production continues to use AWS-native Lambda handlers.

A thin adapter allows existing Lambda handlers to be exposed as Fetch-based endpoints.

### Example: reuse an AWS Lambda handler in Hono

```ts
import { Hono } from "hono";
import type { APIGatewayProxyHandler } from "aws-lambda";

// existing AWS-native handler
const getHelloHandler: APIGatewayProxyHandler = async (event) => {
  const name = event.pathParameters?.name ?? "world";

  return {
    statusCode: 200,
    body: JSON.stringify({
      message: `Hello ${name}`,
    }),
  };
};
```

Expose it via Hono:

```ts
import { lambdaHandler } from "@backpack/hono-adapter";

const app = new Hono();

app.get("/api/v1/hello/:name", lambdaHandler(getHelloHandler));

export default app;
```

### Run a local dev server

```ts
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";

serve({
  fetch: app.fetch,
  port: 3000,
});
```

### Test using Fetch API

Note: this doesn't require running a separate HTTP server.

```ts
const response = await fetch("http://localhost:3000/api/v1/hello/john");

expect(response.status).toBe(200);

const body = await response.json();

expect(body).toEqual({
  message: "Hello john",
});
```

### Positioning

* **Recommended stepping stone**
* ideal for teams that want improved DX without changing production architecture

## Decision 3: API contract model

### Summary

Backpack supports both **spec-first** and **code-first** approaches for OpenAPI.

Both are valid, but they fit differently with the other decisions in this RFC.

In particular:

* **spec-first** fits naturally with AWS-native handlers;
* **code-first** fits more naturally with Zod-based validation and Hono-based request handling.

Backpack therefore supports both approaches, while having a **strong preference for code-first** as the optimized paved road.

### Option A: spec-first

In a spec-first approach, the OpenAPI document is the source of truth.

From that specification, teams generate TypeScript types, validation schemas, or other supporting artifacts.

#### Example: OpenAPI-first contract

```yaml
paths:
  /hello/{name}:
    get:
      parameters:
        - name: name
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Successful response
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required:
                  - message
                properties:
                  message:
                    type: string
```

Generated TypeScript-only types might look like:

```ts
type GetHelloPathParams = {
  name: string;
};

type GetHelloResponse = {
  message: string;
};
```

This works well, but TypeScript-only generation does not provide runtime safety by itself.

#### Note on Zod-based generators

There are generators that produce **Zod schemas** from OpenAPI specifications.

That is often a significant improvement over generating TypeScript types only, because it provides **runtime validation for free**.

For example:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

export const GetHelloPathParamsSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string(),
});
```

However, this can still be a missed opportunity when teams want to add richer application-specific behaviour such as:

* transforms
* codecs
* defaults
* domain-specific refinements
* custom business validation

In practice, generated schemas often still need manual extension.

Another limitation is that generators currently do not provide an elegant path towards generating a fully integrated Hono application or routing model.

#### Positioning

* **Supported**
* natural fit with **AWS-native handlers**
* workable with Zod-based generation
* not the primary optimization target for Backpack

***

### Option B: code-first

In a code-first approach, the API contract is defined in TypeScript and OpenAPI is generated from that implementation model.

In practice, this usually means using Zod schemas as the source of truth and enriching them with OpenAPI metadata.

#### Example: code-first with zod-to-openapi

```ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { OpenAPIRegistry, OpenApiGeneratorV3, extendZodWithOpenApi } from "@asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi";

const registry = new OpenAPIRegistry();

const HelloPathParamsSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(1).openapi({
    example: "Dirk",
    description: "Name of the person to greet",
  }),
}).openapi("HelloPathParams");

const HelloResponseSchema = z.object({
  message: z.string().openapi({
    example: "Hello Dirk",
    description: "Greeting message",
  }),
}).openapi("HelloResponse");

registry.registerPath({
  method: "get",
  path: "/hello/{name}",
  request: {
    params: HelloPathParamsSchema,
  },
  responses: {
    200: {
      description: "Successful response",
      content: {
        "application/json": {
          schema: HelloResponseSchema,
        },
      },
    },
  },
});

const generator = new OpenApiGeneratorV3(registry.definitions);

export const openApiDocument = generator.generateDocument({
  openapi: "3.0.0",
  info: {
    title: "Example API",
    version: "1.0.0",
  },
});
```

This keeps the runtime schema and the generated OpenAPI document closely aligned.

It also leaves room for richer runtime models, for example:

```ts
const CreateUserRequestSchema = z.object({
  email: z.email().transform((value) => value.toLowerCase()),
  locale: z.string().default("nl-NL"),
});
```

#### Optional variant: code-first with Hono

```ts
import { createRoute, OpenAPIHono } from "@hono/zod-openapi";
import { z } from "zod";

const app = new OpenAPIHono();

const getHelloRoute = createRoute({
  method: "get",
  path: "/hello/{name}",
  request: {
    params: z.object({
      name: z.string().min(1),
    }),
  },
  responses: {
    200: {
      description: "Successful response",
      content: {
        "application/json": {
          schema: z.object({
            message: z.string(),
          }),
        },
      },
    },
  },
});

app.openapi(getHelloRoute, (c) => {
  const { name } = c.req.valid("param");

  return c.json({
    message: `Hello ${name}`,
  });
});
```

#### Positioning

* **Recommended and optimized path**
* strongest fit with **Zod**
* strongest fit with **Hono**
* primary focus for Backpack tooling and documentation

***

### Key trade-off

The main question is:

> Where do we want the source of truth to live, and how tightly do we want contract, validation and runtime behaviour to be integrated?

For Backpack:

* support **spec-first** where it fits naturally;
* optimize for **code-first** where stronger runtime validation and tighter integration are desired.

***

### Interaction with Decision 2

* **AWS-native + spec-first** → very natural
* **AWS-native + code-first** → valid
* **Hono + spec-first** → possible but less elegant
* **Hono + code-first** → most natural

[API reference](../../../index.md) / [@backpack/cdk-constructs](../index.md) / AccountDomainName

# Class: AccountDomainName

Represents a subdomain under the current AWS account domain name, as provisioned by the Landing Zone.

It creates the required AWS certificate and can target different resources such as API Gateway or CloudFront.

## Examples

To create a domain name such as `api.bookstore.my-account-p.cla.ns.nl`, you only need to specify the subdomain:

```ts
new AccountDomainName(this, "AccountDomainName", {
  subDomain: "api.bookstore"
});
```

If your domain name already exists (e.g., what it was created in another stack), you can also import it.
This will skip the creation of the certificate.

```ts
const accountDomainName = AccountDomainName.fromExisting(this, "AccountDomainName", {
  subDomainName: "api.bookstore"
});
```

To target an API Gateway instance, you can use the [ApiGateway](ApiGateway.md) construct:

```ts
const accountDomainName = new AccountDomainName(this, "AccountDomainName", {
  subDomainName: "api.bookstore"
});

new ApiGateway(this, "BookStoreApiGateway", {
  restApiName: "Bookstore API",
  // ...
  customDomain: {
    accountDomainName: accountDomainName;
  }
});
```

To target other L2 constructs, such as a CloudFront distribution, you can use the `addTarget` method
which will add the required DNS records.

```ts
const domainName = new AccountDomainName(this, "AccountDomainName", {
  subDomainName: "api.bookstore"
});

domainName.addTarget(this, "CfTarget", new CloudFrontTarget(myDistribution));
```

## Extends

* `Construct`

## Implements

* [`IAccountDomainName`](../interfaces/IAccountDomainName.md)

```ts
   scope,

   options): AccountDomainName;
```


### addTarget()

```ts

   scope, 
   id, 
   target): void;
```

Adds any `AliasRecordTarget` to this domain, adding the required DNS records.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `scope` | `Construct` | The scope in which to define this construct |
| `id` | `string` | The scoped construct ID. Must be unique amongst siblings. |
| `target` | `IAliasRecordTarget` | Valid alias record targets, like CloudFront distributions and load balancers. |

#### Returns

`void`

***

### fromExisting()

```ts
static fromExisting(
   scope, 
   id, 
   options): IAccountDomainName;
```

Imports an existing account domain name, preventing the creation of new certificates.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `scope` | `Construct` |
| `id` | `string` |
| `options` | [`AccountDomainNameOptions`](../interfaces/AccountDomainNameOptions.md) |

#### Returns

#### Example

```ts

AccountDomainName.fromExisting(this, "AccountDomainName", {
  subDomainName: "api.bookstore"
});
```


The AWS certificate created for this domain name.


[API reference](../../../index.md) / [@backpack/cdk-constructs](../index.md) / ApiGateway

# Class: ApiGateway

Creates an Amazon API Gateway for REST APIs, created using OpenAPI specifications.

## Example

```ts
new ApiGateway(this, "BookstoreApiGateway", {
  restApiName: "Bookstore API",

  // optionally, provide an OpenAPI spec file used for routing,
  // with optionally, serving a Swagger UI in its gateway
  apiDefinition: new FileApiDefinition("./path/to/openapi.yaml"), // (or JSON)
  swaggerUI: true,

  // optionally, pass your Lambda functions to arrange invocation permissions.
  lambdaFunctions: [ /* lambda functions here  */ ],

  // enable API Management ACL
  enableApiManagementAcl: true,

  // optionally, enable a custom domain
  customDomain: {
    accountDomainName: new AccountDomainName(this, "AccountDomainName", {
      subDomainName: "api.bookstore"
    });
  }
});
```

## Extends

* `SpecRestApi`

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new ApiGateway(
   scope, 
   id, 
   options): ApiGateway;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `scope` | `Construct` |
| `id` | `string` |
| `options` | [`ApiGatewayOptions`](../interfaces/ApiGatewayOptions.md) |

#### Returns

`ApiGateway`

#### Overrides

```ts
SpecRestApi.constructor
```

[API reference](../../../../index.md) / [@backpack/error-handling](../../index.md) / [async-result](../index.md) / AsyncResult

# Class: AsyncResult\<T>

Extension of a `Promise<T>`, providing some nice additional operators for
improved error handling.

## Extends

* `Promise`<`T`>

## Type Parameters

| Type Parameter | Description |
| ------ | ------ |
| `T` | Represents the type of the resulting value, if successful. |

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new AsyncResult<T>(executor): AsyncResult<T>;
```

Creates a new AsyncResult.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `executor` | (`resolve`, `reject`) => `void` |

#### Returns

`AsyncResult`<`T`>

#### Overrides

```ts

```

## Methods

### asResult()

```ts
asResult(): Promise<Result<T>>;
```

Converts the `AsyncResult<T>` into a `Promise<Result<T, unknown>>`.

Can be used in combination with async/await to handle the `Result` in a more imperative style.

#### Returns

### match()

```ts
match<TResult1, TResult2>(onSuccess, onError): AsyncResult<TResult1 | TResult2>;
```

Maps the value if successful, or else the error if failed.

For example, `.match(x => 1, e => 2)` would be similar to `.map(x => 1).recover(e => 2)`

#### Type Parameters

| `TResult2` |

# Class: CacheControlBuilder

Fluent builder for constructing `Cache-Control` header values.

## Example

```ts
cacheControl().maxAge(300).mustRevalidate().build();
// "max-age=300, must-revalidate"
```

```ts

```

the server before using a cached copy.

#### Returns

`this`

***

### noStore()

```ts

```

Use for error responses or sensitive data.

#### Returns

`this`

***

### private()

```ts

```

Shared caches like CDNs must not store the response.

#### Returns

`this`

***

### proxyRevalidate()


#### Returns

`this`


#### Returns

`this`

### stackTraceLimit

```ts
static stackTraceLimit: number;
```

The `Error.stackTraceLimit` property specifies the number of stack frames
collected by a stack trace (whether generated by `new Error().stack` or
`Error.captureStackTrace(obj)`).

The default value is `10` but may be set to any valid JavaScript number. Changes
will affect any stack trace captured *after* the value has been changed.

If set to a non-number value, or set to a negative number, stack traces will
not capture any frames.

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.stackTraceLimit
```

## Methods

### captureStackTrace()

```ts
static captureStackTrace(targetObject, constructorOpt?): void;
```

Creates a `.stack` property on `targetObject`, which when accessed returns
a string representing the location in the code at which
`Error.captureStackTrace()` was called.

```js
const myObject = {};
Error.captureStackTrace(myObject);
myObject.stack;  // Similar to `new Error().stack`
```

The first line of the trace will be prefixed with
`${myObject.name}: ${myObject.message}`.

The optional `constructorOpt` argument accepts a function. If given, all frames
above `constructorOpt`, including `constructorOpt`, will be omitted from the
generated stack trace.

The `constructorOpt` argument is useful for hiding implementation
details of error generation from the user. For instance:

```js
function a() {
  b();
}

function b() {
  c();
}

function c() {
  // Create an error without stack trace to avoid calculating the stack trace twice.
  const { stackTraceLimit } = Error;
  Error.stackTraceLimit = 0;
  const error = new Error();
  Error.stackTraceLimit = stackTraceLimit;

  // Capture the stack trace above function b
  Error.captureStackTrace(error, b); // Neither function c, nor b is included in the stack trace
  throw error;
}

a();
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `targetObject` | `object` |
| `constructorOpt?` | `Function` |

#### Returns

`void`

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.captureStackTrace
```

***

### isError()

```ts

```

Indicates whether the argument provided is a built-in Error instance or not.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |

[API reference](../../../index.md) / [@backpack/cdk-constructs](../index.md) / DatadogFargate

# Class: DatadogFargate

Opinionated AWS CDK wrapper around the official `DatadogECSFargate`
construct from `datadog-cdk-constructs-v2`.

This construct provides sensible defaults so teams only
need to supply service identity, tags, and optional overrides. It:

* Creates a Fargate task definition instrumented with the Datadog agent and
  Fluent Bit log router.
* Configures the EU Datadog site for both agent and Fluent Bit output.
* Enables JSON log parsing and multiline log reassembly
* Optionally sends logs to a CloudWatch log group as a secondary output
* Automatically retrieves the Datadog API key from the landing zone
* Normalizes tag keys and values to comply with Datadog's tag format

After construction, add your application containers to
[DatadogFargate.taskDefinition](#taskdefinition) — the official construct automatically
instruments added containers with the correct log driver.

## Example

```ts
// First, create Datadog construct:
const monitoring = new DatadogFargate(this, "DatadogFargate", {
  service: "bookstore-api",
  env: "development",
  version: "1.0.0",
  source: "java",
  tags: {
    team: "team_fundamentals",
    application: "NS App Core",
    applicationserviceid: "ASID0007799",
    department: "RG2",
    owner: "my.po@ns.nl",
  },
});

// Add your application container to the instrumented task definition
const appContainer = monitoring.taskDefinition.addContainer("app", {
  image: ecs.ContainerImage.fromRegistry("my-app:latest"),
  // ...
});

// Explicitly set the default container for ALB target-group registration
monitoring.taskDefinition.defaultContainer = appContainer;
```

## See

Migrating from `DatadogEcsMonitoring`? See the [migration guide](https://backpack.ns.nl/guides/migrating/datadog-fargate.html).

## Extends

* `Construct`

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new DatadogFargate(
   scope, 
   id, 
   options): DatadogFargate;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `scope` | `Construct` |
| `id` | `string` |
| `options` | [`DatadogFargateOptions`](../interfaces/DatadogFargateOptions.md) |

#### Returns

`DatadogFargate`

#### Overrides

```ts
Construct.constructor
```

## Properties

### taskDefinition

```ts
readonly taskDefinition: DatadogECSFargateTaskDefinition;
```

The instrumented Fargate task definition.
Add your application containers to this — they will automatically be
configured with the Datadog FireLens log driver and UST environment variables.

# Class: DynamoDbRepository\<TItem, TKey>

A repository for a DynamoDB table. Provides methods for getting, putting, deleting, and querying items.

## Type Parameters

| Type Parameter | Default type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `TItem` | `Record`<`string`, `unknown`> | The type of the persisted item. |
| `TKey` *extends* `Partial`<`Record`\<keyof `TItem`, `unknown`>> | `Partial`<`Record`\<keyof `TItem`, `unknown`>> | The type used as (composite) key for the item. |

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new DynamoDbRepository<TItem, TKey>(client, options): DynamoDbRepository<TItem, TKey>;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `client` | `DynamoDBDocumentClient` | The DynamoDBDocumentClient from `@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb`. |
| `options` | [`DynamoDbRepositoryOptions`](../interfaces/DynamoDbRepositoryOptions.md)<`TItem`> | Additional options for this repository. |

#### Returns

### queryItems()

#### Call Signature

```ts
queryItems<TProjection>(queryOptions): Promise<TProjection[]>;
```

Returns specific items using a `QueryCommand`.

##### Type Parameters

| Type Parameter |
| ------ |
| `TProjection` |

##### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `queryOptions` | [`QueryItemsOptions`](../interfaces/QueryItemsOptions.md)<`TProjection`> |

##### Returns

`Promise`<`TProjection`\[]>

##### Examples

```ts
const books = await booksRepository.queryItems({
  KeyConditionExpression: "genre = :genre",
  ExpressionAttributeValues: {
    ":genre": "FANTASY",
  },
  IndexName: "GenreIndex",
});
```

**Reading a projected shape (e.g., a global secondary index projection)**

by supplying a `readItem` mapper, which replaces the repository's `itemMapper`:

```ts
const ids = await booksRepository.queryItems({
  KeyConditionExpression: "genre = :genre",
  ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":genre": "FANTASY" },
  IndexName: "GenreIndex",
  ProjectionExpression: "id",
  readItem: (item) => ({ id: item.id as string }),
});
```

#### Call Signature


***

### transactWrite()

```ts
transactWrite(actions, options?): Promise<void>;
```

Performs an atomic multi-item write using a `TransactWriteCommand`.

All actions succeed or all fail. The 100-item / 4 MB transaction cap of
DynamoDB is enforced server-side; this method does not chunk because
chunking would break atomicity.

If the transaction is canceled (e.g., a condition check fails), a
[TransactWriteCancelledError](TransactWriteCancelledError.md) is thrown with per-action reasons
indexed against the input `actions` array.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `actions` | [`TransactWriteAction`](../type-aliases/TransactWriteAction.md)<`TItem`, `TKey`>\[] | Non-empty list of actions to execute atomically. |
| `options?` | [`TransactWriteOptions`](../type-aliases/TransactWriteOptions.md) | Transaction-level options forwarded to the `TransactWriteCommand` (e.g. `ClientRequestToken`, `ReturnConsumedCapacity`). |

#### Returns

`Promise`<`void`>

#### Example

```ts
await repository.transactWrite([
  { type: "put", item: parent, condition: { ConditionExpression: "attribute_not_exists(version)" } },
  { type: "put", item: child },
  { type: "delete", key: { id: orphanId } },
]);
```

***

### updateItem()

```ts
updateItem(options): Promise<void>;
```

Updates an item using a `UpdateCommand`.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `options` | [`UpdateOptions`](../type-aliases/UpdateOptions.md) |

#### Returns

`Promise`<`void`>

#### Example

```ts
await booksRepository.updateItem({
  Key: { id: myId },
  UpdateExpression: 'set foo = :foo',
  ExpressionAttributeValues: {
    ':foo': foo,
  },
});
```

# Class: DynamoDbStore

DynamoDB-backed store for the mockserver.

Assumed table schemas (v1):

1. Mappings table
   * PK: id (string)

2. Requests table
   * PK: scope (string) // default: "global"
   * SK: sk (string) // "{millis}#{uuid}" for time ordering
   * TTL: ttl (number) optional epoch seconds (configure DynamoDB TTL on this attribute)

# Class: FileApiDefinition

Refers to an API specification from a local file.

## Example

```ts
new ApiGateway(this, "BookstoreApiGateway", {
  restApiName: "Bookstore API",

  // optionally, provide an OpenAPI spec file used for routing,
  // with optionally, serving a Swagger UI in its gateway
  apiDefinition: new FileApiDefinition("./path/to/openapi.yaml"), // (or JSON)
});
```

## Extends

* `ApiDefinition`

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new FileApiDefinition(filePath): FileApiDefinition;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `filePath` | `string` | OpenAPI specification file path relative to the CDK app root. Supports both JSON and YAML formats. |

#### Returns

`FileApiDefinition`

#### Overrides

```ts

```

### stackTraceLimit

```ts

```

The `Error.stackTraceLimit` property specifies the number of stack frames
collected by a stack trace (whether generated by `new Error().stack` or
`Error.captureStackTrace(obj)`).

The default value is `10` but may be set to any valid JavaScript number. Changes
will affect any stack trace captured *after* the value has been changed.

If set to a non-number value, or set to a negative number, stack traces will
not capture any frames.

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.stackTraceLimit
```

## Methods

### captureStackTrace()

```ts
static captureStackTrace(targetObject, constructorOpt?): void;
```

Creates a `.stack` property on `targetObject`, which when accessed returns
a string representing the location in the code at which
`Error.captureStackTrace()` was called.

```js
const myObject = {};
Error.captureStackTrace(myObject);
myObject.stack;  // Similar to `new Error().stack`
```

The first line of the trace will be prefixed with
`${myObject.name}: ${myObject.message}`.

The optional `constructorOpt` argument accepts a function. If given, all frames
above `constructorOpt`, including `constructorOpt`, will be omitted from the
generated stack trace.

The `constructorOpt` argument is useful for hiding implementation
details of error generation from the user. For instance:

```js
function a() {
  b();
}

function b() {
  c();
}

function c() {
  // Create an error without stack trace to avoid calculating the stack trace twice.
  const { stackTraceLimit } = Error;
  Error.stackTraceLimit = 0;
  const error = new Error();
  Error.stackTraceLimit = stackTraceLimit;

  // Capture the stack trace above function b
  Error.captureStackTrace(error, b); // Neither function c, nor b is included in the stack trace
  throw error;
}

a();
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `targetObject` | `object` |
| `constructorOpt?` | `Function` |

#### Returns

`void`

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.captureStackTrace
```

***

### isError()

```ts
static isError(error): error is Error;
```

Indicates whether the argument provided is a built-in Error instance or not.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `error` | `unknown` |

#### Returns

`error is Error`

#### Inherited from



# Class: LambdaFunction

Creates an AWS Lambda function using a Node.js runtime.

Bundles the entry point using `esbuild`. Based on `NodejsFunction`, using different default options.

It sets up bundling using `esbuild` (ESM, minify, optional source maps), configures environment variables,
denies CloudWatch logs to cut costs, and overrides the logical ID for OpenAPI compatibility.
It can be optimized for production use and external logging.

## Example

```ts
new LambdaFunction(this, "AddBookV1", {
  entryPath: "./app/books/lambdas/add-book.handler.ts",
  handler: "handler",
  environment: {
    POWERTOOLS_SERVICE_NAME: "bookstore",
    APP_PROFILE: `AWS_DEV`,
  },
});
```

## Extends

* `NodejsFunction`

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new LambdaFunction(
   scope, 
   id, 
   options): LambdaFunction;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `scope` | `Construct` |
| `id` | `string` |
| `options` | [`LambdaFunctionOptions`](../interfaces/LambdaFunctionOptions.md) |

#### Returns

`LambdaFunction`

#### Overrides

```ts
NodejsFunction.constructor
```

[API reference](../../../index.md) / [@backpack/amazon-s3](../index.md) / S3Service

# Class: S3Service

Utility class to interact with an S3 Bucket.

## Example

```ts
import { S3Client } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { S3Service } from "@backpack/amazon-s3";

const client = new S3Client();
const service = new S3Service(client, "my-bucket-name");

// puts an object
await service.putObject("your/object.json", "...");

// retrieves the object as text
const myObjectAsText = await service.getObject("your/object.txt", {
  type: "text",
});

// retrieves the object as json
const myObjectAsJson = await service.getObject("your/object.json", {
  type: "json",
});

// retrieves the object as stream
const myObjectAsStream = await service.getObject("your/large-object.csv", {
  type: "stream",
});

// deletes the object
await service.deleteObject("your/object.json");
```

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new S3Service(
   client, 
   bucketName, 
   logger?): S3Service;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `client` | `S3Client` | The S3 client from AWS SDK. |
| `bucketName` | `string` | The name of the bucket. |
| `logger?` | `Logger` | Pass a PowerTools logger instance to enable logging. |

#### Returns

`S3Service`

## Methods

[API reference](../../../index.md) / [@backpack/aws-secrets-manager](../index.md) / SecretsManagerService

# Class: SecretsManagerService

Retrieves secrets from AWS Secret Manager.

## Example

```ts
import { SecretsManagerClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-secrets-manager";
import { SecretsManagerService } from "@backpack/aws-secrets-manager";

const client = new SecretsManagerClient();
const service = new SecretsManagerService(client);

const mySecret = service.getJsonSecret("/my/secret-id");
//    ^ inferred as `unknown`, throws error if not found

type MySecret = { foo: string; bar: string; };
const typedSecret = service.getJsonSecret<MySecret>("/my/secret-id");
//    ^ inferred as `MySecret`, throws error if not found

const optionalSecret = service.getJsonSecret<MySecret>("/my/secret-id", { required: false });
//    ^ inferred as `MySecret | undefined`
```

## Extended by

* [`CachedSecretsManagerService`](CachedSecretsManagerService.md)

***

### stackTraceLimit

```ts
static stackTraceLimit: number;
```

The `Error.stackTraceLimit` property specifies the number of stack frames
collected by a stack trace (whether generated by `new Error().stack` or
`Error.captureStackTrace(obj)`).

The default value is `10` but may be set to any valid JavaScript number. Changes
will affect any stack trace captured *after* the value has been changed.

If set to a non-number value, or set to a negative number, stack traces will
not capture any frames.

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.stackTraceLimit
```

## Methods

### captureStackTrace()

```ts
static captureStackTrace(targetObject, constructorOpt?): void;
```

Creates a `.stack` property on `targetObject`, which when accessed returns
a string representing the location in the code at which
`Error.captureStackTrace()` was called.

```js
const myObject = {};
Error.captureStackTrace(myObject);
myObject.stack;  // Similar to `new Error().stack`
```

The first line of the trace will be prefixed with
`${myObject.name}: ${myObject.message}`.

The optional `constructorOpt` argument accepts a function. If given, all frames
above `constructorOpt`, including `constructorOpt`, will be omitted from the
generated stack trace.

The `constructorOpt` argument is useful for hiding implementation
details of error generation from the user. For instance:

```js
function a() {
  b();
}

function b() {
  c();
}

function c() {
  // Create an error without stack trace to avoid calculating the stack trace twice.
  const { stackTraceLimit } = Error;
  Error.stackTraceLimit = 0;
  const error = new Error();
  Error.stackTraceLimit = stackTraceLimit;

  // Capture the stack trace above function b
  Error.captureStackTrace(error, b); // Neither function c, nor b is included in the stack trace
  throw error;
}

a();
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `targetObject` | `object` |
| `constructorOpt?` | `Function` |

#### Returns

`void`

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.captureStackTrace
```

***

### isError()

```ts
static isError(error): error is Error;
```

Indicates whether the argument provided is a built-in Error instance or not.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `error` | `unknown` |

`error is Error`

# Class: SnsPublisher

Utility for publishing messages to Amazon SNS.

## Example

```ts
import { SNSClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-sns";
import { SnsPublisher } from "@backpack/amazon-sns";

const client = new SNSClient();
const publisher = new SnsPublisher(client, "my-topic-arn");

// publishes the message as raw payload
await publisher.publishRaw("raw payload");

// publishes the message as JSON payload
await publisher.publishJson({ foo: 'Foo' });
```

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new SnsPublisher(
   snsClient, 
   topicArn, 
   logger?): SnsPublisher;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `snsClient` | `SNSClient` | The SNSClient from AWS SDK. |
| `topicArn` | `string` | The ARN of the topic to publish to. |
| `logger?` | `Logger` | The PowerTools logger instance to enable logging. |

#### Returns

`SnsPublisher`

## Methods

### ~~publish()~~

```ts
publish(
   message, 
   topicArn, 
options?): Promise<PublishCommandOutput>;
```

Publishes a single message via SNS.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `message` | `string` | The raw message payload. |
| `topicArn` | `string` | The ARN of the topic to publish to. |
| `options?` | [`PublishOptions`](../type-aliases/PublishOptions.md) | Additional publish options. |

#### Returns

`Promise`<`PublishCommandOutput`>

#### Deprecated

Please use [SnsPublisher#publishRaw](#publishraw) or [SnsPublisher#publishJson](#publishjson) instead.

***

### publishBatchJson()

```ts
publishBatchJson(messages, options?): Promise<PublishBatchResultEntry[]>;
```

Publishes multiple messages as JSON to an SNS topic.
Messages are automatically chunked into groups of 10 (the SNS batch limit).
Note that this is not atomic: on partial failure, some messages may already
have been delivered.

The `Id` field on returned entries and error entries corresponds to the
index in the input array (i.e. `Number(entry.Id)` gives the original position).

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `messages` | `unknown`\[] | The message objects which will be published as JSON. |
| `options?` | [`BatchPublishOptions`](../type-aliases/BatchPublishOptions.md) | SNS options applied to every entry in the batch. |

#### Returns

`Promise`<`PublishBatchResultEntry`\[]>

The successful entries from SNS.

#### Throws

When one or more messages in the batch fail.

***

### publishBatchRaw()

```ts
publishBatchRaw(messages, options?): Promise<PublishBatchResultEntry[]>;
```

Publishes multiple raw messages to an SNS topic.
Messages are automatically chunked into groups of 10 (the SNS batch limit).
Note that this is not atomic: on partial failure, some messages may already
have been delivered.

The `Id` field on returned entries and error entries corresponds to the
index in the input array (i.e. `Number(entry.Id)` gives the original position).

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `messages` | `string`\[] | The raw message payloads. |
| `options?` | [`BatchPublishOptions`](../type-aliases/BatchPublishOptions.md) | SNS options applied to every entry in the batch. |

#### Returns

`Promise`<`PublishBatchResultEntry`\[]>

The successful entries from SNS.

#### Throws

When one or more messages in the batch fail.

***

### publishJson()

```ts
publishJson(message, options?): Promise<PublishCommandOutput>;
```

Publishes a message as JSON via SNS.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `message` | `unknown` | The message which will be published as JSON. |
| `options?` | [`PublishOptions`](../type-aliases/PublishOptions.md) | Additional publish options. |

#### Returns

`Promise`<`PublishCommandOutput`>

***

### publishRaw()

```ts
publishRaw(message, options?): Promise<PublishCommandOutput>;
```

Publishes a raw message via SNS.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |

[API reference](../../../index.md) / [@backpack/amazon-sqs](../index.md) / SqsPublisher

# Class: SqsPublisher

Utility for publishing messages to Amazon SQS.

## Example

```ts
import { SQSClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";
import { SqsPublisher } from "@backpack/amazon-sqs";

const client = new SQSClient();
const publisher = new SqsPublisher(client, "my-queue-url");

// sends the message as raw payload
await publisher.sendRaw("raw payload");

// sends the message as JSON payload
await publisher.sendJson({ foo: 'Foo' });

// sends a batch of JSON messages (automatically chunked if >10)
await publisher.sendBatchJson([{ foo: 'Foo' }, { bar: 'Bar' }]);

// sends a batch with per-message SQS options
await publisher.sendBatchJson([{ foo: 'Foo' }], { MessageGroupId: 'group-1' });
```

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new SqsPublisher(
   sqsClient, 
   queueUrl, 
   logger?): SqsPublisher;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| `sqsClient` | `SQSClient` | The SQS client from AWS SDK. |
| `queueUrl` | `string` | The URL of the SQS queue to publish to. |
| `logger?` | `Logger` | A PowerTools logger instance, to enable additional logging. |

#### Returns

`SqsPublisher`

## Methods

```ts
   message, 
   queueUrl,
```

#### Returns

`Promise`<`void`>

#### Deprecated

# Class: StackArchiver

Utility to automatically delete a CloudFormation stack.
Useful for scheduling cleanups in development/testing environments.

## Example

```ts
// automatically clean up this stack after 2 weeks:
new StackArchiver(this, "AutoDeleteStack", {
  targetStack: this,
  deletionSchedule: Schedule.rate(Duration.days(14)),
});
```

# Class: SwaggerUi

Adds a Swagger UI to an API Gateway using OpenAPI specs. Currently only supporting `InlineApiDefinition`.

Note: this is already included in the [ApiGateway](ApiGateway.md) construct, and can be enabled using the `swaggerUI` option.

Adds three additional routes:

* `/`: redirects to `/swagger-ui`
* `/swagger-ui`: the Swagger UI interface
* `/openapi`: exposes the OpenAPI specs as JSON

## Example

```ts
new SwaggerUi(this, "SwaggerUi", {
  restApi: myRestApi,
  apiDefinition: myApiDefinition,
});
```

## Extends

* `Construct`

## Constructors

### Constructor

```ts
new SwaggerUi(
   scope, 
   id, 
   options): SwaggerUi;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `scope` | `Construct` |
| `id` | `string` |
| `options` | [`SwaggerUiOptions`](../interfaces/SwaggerUiOptions.md) |

#### Returns

`SwaggerUi`

#### Overrides

```ts
Construct.constructor
```

The `Error.stackTraceLimit` property specifies the number of stack frames
collected by a stack trace (whether generated by `new Error().stack` or
`Error.captureStackTrace(obj)`).

The default value is `10` but may be set to any valid JavaScript number. Changes
will affect any stack trace captured *after* the value has been changed.

If set to a non-number value, or set to a negative number, stack traces will
not capture any frames.

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.stackTraceLimit
```

## Methods

### captureStackTrace()

```ts
static captureStackTrace(targetObject, constructorOpt?): void;
```

Creates a `.stack` property on `targetObject`, which when accessed returns
a string representing the location in the code at which
`Error.captureStackTrace()` was called.

```js
const myObject = {};
Error.captureStackTrace(myObject);
myObject.stack;  // Similar to `new Error().stack`
```

The first line of the trace will be prefixed with
`${myObject.name}: ${myObject.message}`.

The optional `constructorOpt` argument accepts a function. If given, all frames
above `constructorOpt`, including `constructorOpt`, will be omitted from the
generated stack trace.

The `constructorOpt` argument is useful for hiding implementation
details of error generation from the user. For instance:

```js
function a() {
  b();
}

function b() {
  c();
}

function c() {
  // Create an error without stack trace to avoid calculating the stack trace twice.
  const { stackTraceLimit } = Error;
  Error.stackTraceLimit = 0;
  const error = new Error();
  Error.stackTraceLimit = stackTraceLimit;

  // Capture the stack trace above function b
  Error.captureStackTrace(error, b); // Neither function c, nor b is included in the stack trace
  throw error;
}

a();
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `targetObject` | `object` |
| `constructorOpt?` | `Function` |

#### Returns

`void`

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.captureStackTrace
```

***

### isError()

```ts
static isError(error): error is Error;
```

Indicates whether the argument provided is a built-in Error instance or not.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `error` | `unknown` |

#### Returns

`error is Error`

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.isError
```

***

### prepareStackTrace()

```ts
static prepareStackTrace(err, stackTraces): any;
```

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `err` | `Error` |
| `stackTraces` | `CallSite`\[] |

#### Returns

`any`

#### See

https://v8.dev/docs/stack-trace-api#customizing-stack-traces

#### Inherited from

```ts
Error.prepareStackTrace
```
